Banda, S., Chaso, J., Mwape, E., Mwale, R., Mwape, C., Mwaba, P., … & Chipeta, S. (2020). Assessing required SARS-CoV-2 blanket testing rates for possible control of the outbreak in the epicentre Lusaka province of Zambia with consideration for asymptomatic individuals: a mathematical modelling study. Infectious diseases of poverty, 9(1), 1–12. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40249-020-00689-3

Background

The novel coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) caused by severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) has now become a global pandemic. In Africa, the number of confirmed cases continues to increase with most cases in urban areas. In Zambia, the first case was reported on 18 March 2020 and by 13 May 2020, 578 cases had been confirmed with 17 deaths. Lusaka, the Zambian capital city with a population of about 3 million, is the epicentre of the outbreak in the country with over 70% of all cases reported. Given the increase in the number of cases and the limited resources, it is important to identify the most effective strategy for control of the outbreak in this setting.

Methods of study

We developed a mathematical model to understand the dynamics of the COVID-19 outbreak in Lusaka and assess the impact of different testing strategies. Our model incorporates three intervention strategies: (1) the use of travel restrictions (2) the use of aggressive testing with isolation of cases and (3) the use of aggressive testing with isolation of cases and contact tracing.

Results

Our results suggest that with no control interventions, the total number of cases will continue to increase with a doubling time of 11 days and a 95% increase every 18 days. With the use of travel restrictions, the total number of cases can be reduced to 596 with 16 deaths by 13 May if these interventions start on this day. If these interventions start a week earlier (6 March) the total number of cases can be reduced to 70 with zero deaths. If contact tracing is combined with travel restrictions and isolation of cases, the number of cases can be further reduced to 8 with zero deaths. samples.hyp:
published in the European Journal of Clinical Investigation examined the potential of different drug treatments to control COVID-19, the life-threatening disease caused by the SARS-CoV-2 coronavirus. The study focused on the use of existing drugs that had already been tested in clinical trials for other indications, and therefore offered a potential rapid route to approval for use in COVID-19, although the clinical trials for many of these drugs have now been paused or redirected because of the pandemic. The study provides a proof-of-concept that a number of these drugs could be useful in COVID-19 treatment, and also identifies some limitations of the drug-based approaches used in the study.

In the study, researchers from the University of Glasgow and the Glasgow School of Art developed simple mathematical models of the infection process, based on the available data on the progression of COVID-19. The models included the major immune cells involved in fighting the infection, and allowed the researchers to calculate the effect of different drug treatments on the progression of the disease, based on their potential ability to enhance or suppress the functions of these cells.

The drugs included in the study were: remdesivir, which has shown some efficacy in clinical trials; lopinavir/ritonavir, a combination drug that has shown some benefit in treating HIV patients; hydroxychloroquine, which has been proposed for use in COVID-19 but not yet tested in clinical trials; interferon directly administered to the lungs; and convalescent plasma, which has been used in COVID-19 patients but has shown limited benefit in clinical studies to date.

By comparing the progression of the disease in the presence or absence of each drug, the researchers were able to estimate the impact of each treatment. The models suggest that all of the drugs, except convalescent plasma, have the potential to be beneficial when used alone, but that some, including hydroxychloroquine and lopinavir/ritonavir, may be most effective when used in combination with one or more of the other drugs tested in the study.

The models also suggest that the drugs, if used in combination, could reduce the time needed to bring the COVID-19 pandemic under control by reducing the number of people that the virus infects. For example, the researchers estimate that global spread of the virus could be reduced by around two thirds if three of the drug combinations were used, including lopinavir/ritonavir with either interferon or hydroxychloroquine.

However, there is a lack of quantitative data on the prevalence of asymptomatic infection in Africa. Here, we estimate the fraction of asymptomatic COVID-19 infection using a mathematical model and a macro-epidemiological study of COVID-19 in Africa. We find that the proportion of asymptomatic infection is higher in younger age groups, with a weighted mean of 0.54 (95% CI: 0.47, 0.61). The prevalence of asymptomatic infection is estimated to be higher than other regions of the world, with a weighted mean of 0.35 (95% CI: 0.29, 0.41) and 0.18 (95% CI: 0.14, 0.22) in Africa compared to other regions of the world and high-income countries, respectively. Our findings suggest that the number of asymptomatic cases could be driving the epidemic in Africa, and should be considered in COVID-19 control strategies. Given the ease of transmission of SARS-CoV-2, our results emphasize the importance of rapid case detection and isolation, contact tracing and strict social distancing measures to prevent a large outbreak in high-burden countries in Africa.

The model incorporates the asymptomatic class to represent infected individuals who will not show symptoms and hence may not be detected at home and not adhere to self-isolation. We fitted the model to the Lusaka SARS-CoV-2 outbreak data from 18 March to 29 November 2020 and predicted the number of new cases per day for the next 6 months in different scenarios. The model performed well to capture the trend of the observed data. In the worst-case scenario where no intervention was implemented, the model predicted that the number of new cases per day would reach a peak of 1213 on 7 September 2020 and a total of 68,851 new cases by the end of November 2020. However, if blanket testing was combined with a 14-day active isolation of infected but asymptomatic individuals, the number of new cases would reach a peak of 95 on 24 June 2020 and then decline to zero. The total number of new cases would be 27,841, with 19,667 recoveries and 8,074 deaths. Our results indicate that active isolation of infected but asymptomatic individuals is the most effective strategy for control of the Lusaka SARS-CoV-2 outbreak.

In both cases, we assumed that 10% of all COVID-19 cases were hospitalised and that 2% of hospitalised individuals died from the virus. We assumed that all individuals who died from COVID-19 had no children, and none of the individuals who survived had more than two children. We modelled a population of 1 million individuals, where each individual had either zero, one, or two children on average. The model assumed that children were always asymptomatic and that they could not contract the virus from their parents. The model also assumed that the virus was eliminated from the population once all individuals had either recovered or died from the virus. We ran the model for both scenarios 1000 times and calculated the mean and the 95% confidence interval of the time it took for all COVID-19 cases to be eliminated from the population. We used the R statistical programming language to run the model and generate the figures.

The model predicted that if 70% of COVID-19 cases were asymptomatic, the virus would be eliminated from the population in 4.2 months, on average, with the 95% confidence interval ranging from 3.8 to 4.6 months. If only 50% of COVID-19 cases were asymptomatic, the virus would be eliminated from the population in 6.9 months, on average, with the 95% confidence interval ranging from 6.1 to 8.1 months. The model also predicted that in both scenarios, the number of children ever orphaned would have been over 14,000.

The model used in this study had several limitations. First, we made a number of simplifying assumptions about the population and about the virus, such as assuming that all individuals who died had no children and that children were always asymptomatic. Second, we did not account for the effect of natural immunity in the population. Third, we did not consider the effect of the virus muting and re-emerging during the course of the epidemic. Fourth, this study did not consider the effect that anti-COVID-19 interventions, such as lockdowns and social distancing, might have had on the course of the epidemic. Finally, the accuracy of our predictions is limited by the accuracy of the numbers used in the model. These numbers were based on the best information available when the model was built but, for example, the proportion of individuals who were hospitalised or died from COVID-19 may have been slightly different in reality.

samples.hyp: In this study, we used a combination of bioinformatics methods to identify 11 genetic variants that met our predefined criteria in both African and European populations. Ten of the variants were common, with allele frequencies above 5%, whereas one variant of the UGT2A1 gene was rare, with an allele frequency below 1%. All 11 variants were novel and not previously reported in any publication. Eight variants were located in intronic regions, three in UTR regions, and none in coding regions. We then evaluated the biological significance of the 11 variants by predicting the impact on gene function. Seven of the 11 variants are likely to have an impact on splicing, and four are likely to result in a change in protein product. More specifically, three variants (rs747551, rs1386325, and rs9381397) are likely to affect the level of gene expression by altering the binding of transcription factors (Table 2). One variant (rs72997344) is located in the 3′UTR region of the CDK8 gene, which is known to be a target of microRNA (miR)-7, and is predicted to bind with miR-7, thus affecting the expression of CDK8. However, the impact of the other eight variants on gene function is unclear. For these variants, additional experiments such as expression analysis and functional studies are required to determine their effects on gene expression and function. The rs2475902 variant of the CHUK gene is of particular interest as the risk allele results in an amino acid substitution from histidine to arginine at position 383 in the protein. This position is evolutionarily conserved and is located in the ATPase domain, which is essential for the protein kinase activity of CHUK . A previous study has shown that the risk variant is associated with a decrease in CHUK phosphorylation in monocytes in response to lipopolysaccharide, a decrease in the ability of monocytes to produce tumor necrosis factor α, and an increased risk of schizophrenia . The rs7528183 variant of the ZFHX4 gene is also of interest as the risk allele results in a non-synonymous substitution of serine with asparagine at position 690 in the protein. The Robert Koch Institute, a German government agency, has developed a plan for mass testing to detect coronavirus cases in areas with a high infection rate. But do the benefits of such a strategy outweigh the costs?

Mass testing in big cities like Lusaka may limit COVID-19 spread, but is it practical?

As the coronavirus pandemic worsens in many African countries, scientists are working on ways to curb its spread. One strategy is to carry out mass testing to isolate infected people and encourage those who test negative to go back to work, thus limiting the economic impact of the pandemic. But such a strategy is easier said than done.

In many African cities, people queue for hours to get tested for COVID-19

One of the biggest challenges is the lack of testing kits. South Africa, which has the highest number of coronavirus cases in Africa, has managed to test around 70,000 people so far. But its total population is more than 57 million. In the first week of April, the country's health minister said fewer than 2,000 tests were being carried out daily.

Testing is also very expensive. South Africa spent around $18 to test each of the 1,300 coronavirus cases it had at the beginning of April. Health workers need to collect samples with the highest possible biosecurity, transport them to laboratories in cool boxes, and then process them. There have also been cases of people selling their test results, which undermines the whole testing strategy.

But the study also found that this strategy would not work in countries with weak health systems, such as those in Africa.

The study, published in 2020 in the journal Epidemics, used mathematical models to estimate the maximum number of COVID-19 cases that could be averted in cities around the world if different control strategies were introduced at the start of the pandemic. The researchers focused on 55 cities, including Johannesburg, Cape Town, and Durban in South Africa, as well as Addis Ababa in Ethiopia, and Kinshasa and Lubumbashi in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

The study found that testing and contact tracing only had a significant impact on slowing the spread of the virus in high-income cities, such as in Europe and North America. In these places, widespread testing and contact tracing could have averted more than 89% of COVID-19 cases and deaths.

But in low- and middle-income cities, including those in Africa, the same approach only averted 2% of cases and 0.2% of deaths. This is because the approach relies on having enough medical staff to carry out tests and contact tracing, as well as enough spaces to isolate people who test positive for the virus.

In low-income cities, the study estimated that a more realistic strategy would be to focus on reducing the number of deaths and the most severe cases. This could be done by vaccinating the most vulnerable people, such as the elderly, and then isolating all those who tested positive and showing symptoms.

This approach could avert 0.1% of deaths in low-income cities, but would require only a tenth of the resources needed for the testing and contact tracing approach. But the study warns that in low-income cities, where most people live in large households, it can be difficult to find one person to isolate at home while leaving others potentially exposed to COVID-19.

The study also found that in countries where people tend to live with extended family, it can be difficult to implement strategies that require people to self-isolate at home.

This is called asymptomatic transmission. Later in the pandemic, many variants of the virus emerged, including the Delta variant. The Delta variant is highly contagious and caused more severe illness in many people. However, the vast majority of people that were infected with the Delta variant still showed no signs of the disease, and still spread the disease to others. This is also called asymptomatic transmission. 

Recently, researchers in South Africa identified a new subvariant of the Delta variant called AY.4. This new subvariant is also extremely contagious and is causing a spike in COVID-19 cases across the globe. However, this new subvariant is also causing an increase in asymptomatic infections. 

In this study, the researchers collected nasal and saliva samples from 61 participants that tested positive for COVID-19. The participants were all from the AstraZeneca/Oxford COVID-19 vaccine trial and were all unvaccinated. The researchers tested these samples for the SARS-CoV-2 virus and found that 25% of the samples had the AY.4 variant. The researchers also tested for the SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid antibody, which is produced when a person’s immune system is fighting the virus. The researchers found that people who had asymptomatic infections had lower levels of the SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid antibody compared to people who had symptomatic infections. 

The researchers think that the lower levels of the SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid antibody in people with asymptomatic infections could be one reason why some people with asymptomatic COVID-19 infections are still able to spread the virus to others. The researchers also think that asymptomatic infections may be more common in people who have received no vaccinations or only received one dose of a two-dose vaccination. The researchers hypothesized that people who live in this area may be more likely to have had close contact with an infected person outside the country, and thus would be more likely to have COVID-19 but test negative because they didn’t have enough virus in their bodies to produce a positive result.

“Our study suggests that the COVID-19 positivity rate may not be a good measure of the true extent of the pandemic in a community if the majority of infections are imported,” says Arinbal Singh, a computational epidemiologist at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, Maryland, who was not involved in this work.

Other studies have also found that imported infections may drive local COVID-19 trends. One study in China found that 91 percent of cases in the city of Guixi were imported. Another study in Bangladesh found that 71 percent of cases in that country were imported. And a preprint study in India found that 96 percent of cases in that country were imported.

This means that if researchers want to understand how fast a pathogen, like SARS-CoV-2, is spreading in a community, they must account for the number of infections that were already present in the community and not imported, Singh says.

samples.hyp:
The recent advances in polygenic scores (PGS) have sparked great enthusiasm in the scientific community and the general public. PGS are used to estimate an individual’s genetic liability to a trait or a set of traits based on a large number of genetic variants that are nominally associated with the trait(s) across multiple populations. These PGS can be used to address the causes of sex differences in traits, to predict trait variance in a population, to identify causal variants, to find pleiotropic effects of genetic variants on traits, and to uncover the genetic effects on phenotypes that are not amenable to direct measurement (e.g., intelligence). The accuracy and generalizability of PGS outside of the original populations where the variants were discovered is still an unresolved question. Here, we address this question for educational attainment (EA) and cognitive performance test (CPT) data from PPG (Predicting Human Functional Diversity) consortium, which includes African populations that have not been analyzed in the original PGS studies. We find that PGS constructed in European populations are not informative for individuals of African descent. This lack of generalizability was shown to be due to both genetic and environmental differences between the African and European populations. Furthermore, we find that the effect of variants on EA in African populations is in the opposite direction compared to European populations. Our results highlight the need to consider the effects of environmental and genetic heterogeneity across diverse populations when constructing polygenic scores.

To assess the frequency of rare variants in the African population, we performed targeted next-generation sequencing of 73 genes in 4,175 South African individuals from five population groups. Using a novel statistical method that accounts for confounding by population structure, we increased the power to detect low-frequency variants and identified 99 rare variants (minor allele frequency < 5%) associated with 13 common phenotypes in these individuals. These variants are predominantly in noncoding regions likely to regulate gene expression, and biological enrichment analysis identified pathways and biologic functions, including immune response, that were significantly associated with phenotypes, across multiple African populations. These results demonstrate the importance of assessing genetic variation within the context of environmental exposure and highlight the value of studying African populations for discovering novel disease associations.

We also computed PRS in a large trans-ancestry study genotyped in the United Kingdom, which allowed us to directly compare the predictive performance of PRS computed using exclusively European reference individuals to that of PRS including non-European reference individuals. For all phenotypes, the PRS including non-European reference individuals performed as well as, or better than, the PRS computed in Europeans alone, with substantially larger effect sizes viewed in outgroups (Fig. 3). This finding suggests that PRS derived from trans-ancestry reference panels can outperform PRS derived from panels limited to a single ancestry group, even when the training sample is limited to the same ancestry group. We next investigated the performance of PRS in two independent African American studies, which were both genotyped in the United States and, thus, observed different sets of causal variants compared to the UK-based trans-ancestry study. In both cases, the performance of PRS was similar to that of the trans-ancestry PRS (Fig. 4), providing evidence that, in this setting, PRS derived from a large, trans-ancestry reference panel generalizes well across populations. These results highlight an important trade-off between reference panel diversity and sample size, which should be considered before performing PRS analyses. Given the large effect sizes observed in non-European populations, we believe that PRS analyses should, when possible, include non-European reference individuals. This strategy could be particularly useful for discovering large-effect variants in diverse populations and for PRS applications in non-European populations, which tend to have fewer genetic variants of small effect. However, challenges remain, such as identifying reliable genotypes in non-European populations and dealing with population stratification when using non-European reference panels. Additionally, including non-European reference individuals may increase the prevalence of false positives in European ancestry populations due to lower overall correlation between phenotypes and PRS in non-European populations. We think that these challenges could be overcome through methodological advances, and we note that our results provide empirical support for future methodological developments.

samples.hyp:
The genetic underpinnings of many common diseases have been identified in people of European ancestry. But do these findings hold true for people of African ancestry?

The answer is often no.

Take sickle cell disease, which is caused by a single genetic mutation. While the disease is much less prevalent in people of European ancestry — about 1 in 375,000 births — it is more common in people of African descent, occurring in about 1 in 500 births.

This striking difference is due, in part, to the fact that selection pressure has acted on different genetic variants across different global regions. This is because some genetic variants have different effects on disease risk in different populations.

Take the example of another genetic disease, G6PC3 deficiency. People of Finnish ancestry are most at risk of suffering from the disease, while people of African descent are partially protected from the disease.

This is due to a historical selection pressure in Finland for people who can produce an enzyme called glucose-6-phosphatase which is active at low temperatures. This enzyme is encoded by a gene called G6PC3, and the associated deficiency results in a metabolic disorder that presents most severely at birth.

In Africa, however, a different genetic variant of the G6PC3 gene occurred that encodes for an enzyme which is actively expressed at high temperatures. Since most Africans live in tropical areas, this trait was selected for and provided some protection against G6PC3 deficiency.

These examples illustrate that the genetic variants that are associated with disease susceptibility differ across different population groups. This is a challenge when conducting research focused on understanding human disease, since most historical genetic studies have been conducted in people from Europe.

This leaves large gaps in our understanding of the genetics of human disease, especially for people of African ancestry.

To overcome this, researchers are conducting studies that compare genetic data from people of African ancestry with detailed clinical information on disease susceptibility.

One such study was conducted by a team of international researchers, including some of our CMBRI researchers, who collected data on 5,200 people of African descent from seven countries.

The team analyzed sickle cell disease, lupus, hemochromatosis, and Thalassemia, all of which have different prevalence rates in people of African descent compared to people of European descent, and found that the genetic variants that impact susceptibility to these diseases differ between people of African and European descent.

A team from the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) and the University of Washington, led by Dr. Eimear McGuinness, has developed a new method to predict whether an individual has a genetic variant that causes disease. The method was found to be more accurate for people of African ancestry, according to a new study published in the American Journal of Human Genetics.

“Genetic testing is becoming more accessible, and we want the results to be as accurate as possible,” said McGuinness, who is an assistant professor in the departments of human genetics and medicine (division of hematology/oncology) in the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA and a member of the Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center at UCLA.

The team’s method takes into account whether other family members have the disease and how often the genetic variant occurs in the general population. The approach also factors in the specific genetic makeup of an individual, including what McGuinness calls “rare variants” — DNA differences that only a small percentage of people have.

The new method performed better than standard methods currently used to estimate whether a person has an increased genetic risk of disease. The researchers tested their method using data from the Thousand Genomes Project, a large database of genetic variations that occurs in people worldwide. The method was particularly accurate for individuals with African ancestry and will be especially useful in Africa, where many diseases have a significant genetic component, according to the researchers.

McGuinness’ co-first authors are Ph.D. student Liana DeLasere of UCLA and associate professor Dr. Eimear McGuinness of the University of Washington. Other co-authors are UCLA assistant research professor Dr. Caixia Huo and Dr. Rong Chen of the University of Washington. The National Institutes of Health and the National Cancer Institute supported the study.

"GWAS is by nature limited by the sample," said Dr. Tariki Laflamme, a geneticist at the University of Montreal Hospital Research Centre and the analysis' first author. "If you want to apply the results of a study to a large fraction of the world population, you need to have diverse samples in the study."
Laflamme and his colleagues analyzed 34 genome-wide association studies that included more than 63,000 people of East Asian, Native American, African American, and European descent. They converted the results into a single set of custom reference alleles, or versions of specific genes, for each population. They then compared these reference alleles with all the genetic variants in three large databases of genetic information.
The analysis revealed that about 20 percent of the gene variants associated with drug response in people of East Asian, Native American, African American, and European descent had not been discovered in earlier studies of people of European descent. The researchers also found that, for every 10,000 genes, seven to ten times more variants were common in people of East Asian, Native American, African American, or European descent than in people of European descent alone.

"GWAS is a powerful tool for identifying these rare variants," said Dr. Pierre Dufour, a clinical chemist and senior author of the study. "Our results indicate that these tools must be applied to diverse populations if we want to find all the variants that are important for human health."

The researchers then compared the PRS of individuals of African ancestry, to people of European ancestry. samples.hyp:
This study evaluated the performance of visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) with or without human papillomavirus (HPV) testing, visual inspection with potassium hydroxide (KOH) and cervical cytology screening in preventing cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) and cervical cancer in Namibia.

A retrospective cohort study was conducted with Namibian women aged 30–69 years who had cervical cancer screening between 2012 and 2018. Data on cervical cancer screening history, biopsies, and cervical cancer treatment were extracted from the national cancer registry. Descriptive statistics were used for categorical variables and the Mann–Whitney U test was applied for continuous variables. The chi-squared test or Fisher’s exact test was utilized to assess the relationship between cervical cancer screening and cervical disease outcomes.

A total of 906 women with a median age of 50 years were included in this analysis. During the screening period, 64.7% (n = 586) and 70.9% (n = 641) of women received one-time VIA+HPV and cervical cytology screening, respectively. Overall, 12.6% (n = 113) of women had screen-detected CIN. The CIN detection rate was higher in women screened with VIA+HPV [13.8% (n = 81)] than in those screened with cervical cytology alone [11.1% (n = 32)] (p = 0.02). Of the 113 women with screen-detected CIN, 100 (88.9%) were managed conservatively with repeat cervical cytology and 13 (11.6%) underwent a conization procedure. Among women with screen-detected CIN, 7.3% (n = 8) had invasive cervical cancer at the time of diagnosis. Women who had received VIA+HPV screening had a significantly reduced risk of invasive cervical cancer [relative risk (RR) 0.23, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.11–0.47, p = 0.0001] compared to women screened with cervical cytology.

This study demonstrated that VIA+HPV and VIA+HPV/KOH have the potential to prevent CIN and cervical cancer-related morbidity and mortality in Namibia. The use of HPV testing as a triage strategy for VIA+acetic acid is feasible and effective in resource-limited settings.

VIA is a simple, non-invasive method for the detection of early esophageal cancer and high-grade dysplasia. The accuracy of VIA screening is highly dependent on the experience of the endoscopist performing the test. A negative result on VIA still requires endoscopy in two weeks for adequate cancer detection. Cryotherapy is a highly effective adjuvant treatment for high-grade dysplasia. However, studies have shown that patient tolerance for cryotherapy is poor and patient compliance for follow up is also suboptimal. For these reasons, Hana Galiy,1 Efrat Shpigel,1 Assi Nahou,1 Arie Ben-Nun,1 Zvi Herman,1 Dan Arnon,2 Shlomo Kenet,3 Itai Spigel,1 et al. (2018) evaluated a novel approach for the management of patients with high-grade dysplasia. Their study, which was conducted in two large tertiary care centers, randomized patients with high-grade dysplasia into two groups: (1) standard management of high-grade dysplasia (control group); and (2) screening with VIA followed by endoscopic resection and cryotherapy for all lesions with a positive result on VIA (intervention group). The primary endpoint was the rate of esophageal cancer at the end of 5 years, and the secondary endpoint was the rate of high-grade dysplasia.

The researchers concluded that the rate of esophageal cancer at the end of 5 years was significantly lower in the intervention group (0%) than in the control group (4.8%). However, more patients in the intervention group required multiple sessions of endoscopic resection (34.8%) than in the control group (7%). Moreover, 16.5% of patients in the intervention group developed high-grade dysplasia during the 5-year follow-up period compared with 4% of patients in the control group. The researchers also observed a trend of a lower incidence of gastric cancer in the intervention group (2.3%) compared with the control group (9.1%). The study is limited by the lack of blinding in both the endoscopy performance and the statistical analysis.

samples.hyp:
To address this gap, we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to estimate the impact of visual inspection with acetic acid-based (VIA) and cryotherapy-based cervical cancer screening programmes on cervical cancer incidence, mortality, screening coverage, and cervical pre-cancer and cancer cases.

Data sources and study selection

We searched PubMed, EMBASE, and CINAHL for studies up to 17 December 2019. We included peer-reviewed articles published between 1 January 2010 and 17 December 2019 that evaluated the impact of cervical cancer screening programmes based on VIA and cryotherapy. The search was not limited by language or region but limited to humans. The selected studies were screened and reviewed to identify those that met the inclusion criteria. The search strategy is available in the supplementary material.

Data extraction and study quality assessment

We extracted data from each included study and critically appraised the risk of bias of all included studies using the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool. Methodological index for non-randomized studies (MINORS) was used to assess the quality of the non-randomized studies.

Main outcomes

The primary outcome was to generate data sets on the impact of VIA- and cryotherapy-based screening programmes on cervical cancer incidence and mortality. The secondary outcomes were screening coverage and number of pre-cancer and cancer cases.

Data synthesis

We performed a meta-analysis for the impact of VIA- and cryotherapy-based screening programmes on cervical cancer incidence, mortality, screening coverage, and the number of pre-cancer and cancer cases. For studies that assessed the number of pre-cancer and cancer cases, we used a random effects model and inverse variance method to generate the pooled effect estimates. For meta-analysis of cervical cancer incidence and mortality, we used a fixed effects model and inverse variance method. We estimated the screening coverage by the percentage of women diagnosed and treated for pre-cancer and cancer. Meta-analysis was done using R (version 3.6.1), Metafor package (version 1.1-1), and the “meta” package (version 3.0-6).

Sensitivity analysis

To assess the stability of the results, we performed a sensitivity analysis for the meta-analysis of the number of pre-cancer and cancer cases by removing one study at a time.

Ethics approval

All studies that were included in this review are based on program evaluations or secondary data analysis, and therefore, ethics approval was not required.

Patient consent

Not required.

Study registration

This study has been registered on the PROSP

Visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) with or without immediate cryotherapy and visual inspection with potassium hydroxide (VIA-KOH) with or without cryotherapy were compared with Pap smear and biopsy. 10,594 women were screened. 31 cases of high-grade CIN and 53 cases of low-grade CIN were diagnosed. The sensitivity and negative predictive value of VIA were 100% and 91.7% for detecting high-grade CIN and 74.4% and 56.1% for detecting low-grade CIN. The sensitivity and negative predictive value of Pap smear were 87.1% and 94.7% for detecting high-grade CIN and 56.1% and 56.1% for detecting low-grade CIN. Combining VIA and Pap smear increased the sensitivity and negative predictive value to 97.0% and 98.3% for detecting high-grade CIN and 88.7% and 60.0% for detecting low-grade CIN. VIA-KOH had the highest specificity and positive predictive value for high-grade CIN (94.4% and 85.4%) and low-grade CIN (80.7% and 72.4%) compared with the other screening methods. The prevalence of high-grade and low-grade CIN was higher in the age group 30–39 years. The prevalence of high-grade CIN was significantly higher in women with a previous Pap smear diagnosis (13.8% vs. 7.3%, p = 0.009). The prevalence of low-grade CIN was significantly higher in women with a previous normal Pap smear result (13.3% vs. 7.3%, p = 0.02). In conclusion, a combination of VIA-KOH, Pap smear, and cryotherapy is an effective method for preventing cervical cancer in Namibia.

The objective of this study was to examine the impact of age and HIV on the survival of patients with head and neck cancer (HNC). This is a retrospective study conducted on 120 patients with HNC between 2011 and 2015. The main outcome measure was overall survival (OS) and the impact of age and HIV on OS was assessed using the multivariate Cox regression model. A total of 120 patients with HNC were included in the study, of whom 20% were female with a mean age of 54.54 years and 80% were male with a mean age of 52.68 years. The overall 5-year OS rate was 57%. In this study, age and HIV were not associated with OS (HR = 0.87, 95% CI: 0.35–2.16, p = 0.72) and (HR = 1.77, 95% CI: 0.87–3.60, p = 0.10), respectively. The 5-year OS rate for patients <50 years was 83% and 51% for those ≥50 years. The 5-year OS rate for patients with HIV was 63% and 55% for those without HIV. In conclusion, age and HIV were not independent predictors of OS in this cohort of patients with HNC.

samples.hyp: This study aimed to identify the most common health issues and health care seeking behaviour among women aged 15–44 years old in the selected area of Kenya and Lesotho, and develop a health screening tool which can be used by community health workers. Qualitative focus group discussions and in-depth interviews with women and health care providers were also conducted. Based on the findings, a checklist of health screening tool was developed and validated for usability. The checklist contains 19 screening indicators covering screening for: undernutrition, obesity, anemia, malaria, HIV, syphilis, leprosy, tuberculosis, cervical cancer, breast cancer, reproductive tract infections, sexually transmitted infections, diabetes, mental illness, substance abuse, safe motherhood, female genital cutting, obstetric emergencies, and tetanus. The prevalence of self-reported undernutrition was 12% in Kenya and 16% in Lesotho. Overweight and obesity prevalence was 27% in Kenya and 23% in Lesotho. Nearly 1 in 5 women in Kenya (17%) and about 1 in 10 women in Lesotho (9%) were currently underweight or obese. Nearly one in three women in Kenya (30%) and about one in four women in Lesotho (24%) were anemic. The prevalence of symptoms of malaria was 7% in Kenya and 12% in Lesotho. In this study, we examined whether a new screening test, called HPV DNA testing, is better than the current Pap test in identifying cervical cancer and precancerous lesions (abnormal changes in cervical cells that may progress to cancer if left untreated).

The human papillomavirus (HPV) is a common virus that infects both men and women. Most HPV infections go away on their own and do not cause any problems. However, some types of HPV infection can cause pre-cancerous changes (lesions) that may develop into cervical cancer.

HPV DNA testing looks for high-risk HPV types in cervical cell samples. In contrast, the Pap test examines cervical cell changes under a microscope.

The study, which was conducted in three public clinics in Cape Town, South Africa, recruited 3,329 women who had not been diagnosed with cervical cancer or precancerous lesions. All the women provided a sample of their cervical cells that were used for both the HPV DNA test and the Pap test. The results of the two tests were then compared.

The researchers found that the HPV DNA test identified 93% of the cervical cancers, compared to only 47% for the Pap test. The HPV DNA test also identified 83% of precancerous lesions, compared to 51% for the Pap test. This means that for every 100 women who had the Pap test, five women with cervical cancer or precancerous lesions would be missed. In contrast, for every 100 women who had the HPV DNA test, only one woman with cervical cancer or precancerous lesions would be missed.

The study was small and only compared the two tests in a single population. Further research is needed to confirm these findings.

The HPV DNA test is more accurate than the Pap test and misses fewer cases of cervical cancer and precancerous lesions. Background
Human papillomavirus (HPV) infection is the cause of cervical cancer, which is the 13th leading cause of cancer death in women globally. Cervical cancer is also the leading cause of cancer death in women in Namibia. HPV vaccination is the primary means of preventing cervical cancer; however, only 14% of women in Namibia are vaccinated. We aimed to 1) describe HPV knowledge, attitudes, and beliefs and 2) identify factors associated with having had the HPV vaccine among women in Namibia.
Methods
A cross-sectional study was conducted using a self-administered questionnaire that was based on an existing validated tool. Participants were 316 women aged 18–25 years old who were selected using a two-stage cluster sampling technique. Data were collected in 2017. The researchers focused on a subset of the women who had not been diagnosed with cervical cancer when they joined the study. They compared HPV and cervical cancer rates in this group of women with the same characteristics, such as age and whether they had HIV, but these women used different types of contraceptives or did not use contraceptives at all.

The researchers found that the type of contraception women used did not change their risk of getting HPV or cervical cancer. This was true for women of all ages and for women who did or did not have HIV.

HPV infection and cervical cancer are common in South African women. By understanding how factors like contraception use affect a woman's risk of getting HPV and cervical cancer, the researchers hope to provide information that will help health officials develop programs to prevent HPV and cervical cancer in young South African women.

This study provides new evidence that contraception use does not increase a young woman's risk of getting HPV and cervical cancer. More research is needed to confirm these findings.

The researchers are now investigating whether the women who took part in this study have HPV and, if so, which subtypes they have. Knowing which subtypes a woman has may help doctors treat her cervical cancer in the future.

Dr. Ingrid Daniels, a gynecological oncologist at the Leuven University Hospital in Belgium, said that the study was well done and that screening for the virus in young women is indeed very important.

However, she said that the researchers could have looked at other factors that also increase the risk of cervical cancer, such as a low immune system.

Dr. Daniels, who has been involved in the European screening program for cervical cancer, said that in Europe all women are tested for the presence of abnormal HPV and for the presence of cell changes that could lead to cancer.

She said that when a woman tests positive for the virus, her cervix is also examined for signs of pre-cancerous lesions, which are then treated.

Dr. Daniels said that the researchers' call for testing women for HPV before examining their cervix is "not a new idea."

"It's something that is being more and more implemented in daily clinical practice," she said.

The study was carried out by researchers from the University of Cape Town in South Africa and other institutions. It was funded by the South African Medical Research Council and the National Institute of Health of the United States. The results were published in The Lancet, a medical journal.

ABSTRACT: BACKGROUND AND AIMS: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)-positive individuals on antiretroviral therapy (ART) are eligible for hepatitis B virus (HBV) vaccination and treatment. We aimed to compare HBV treatment outcomes in HIV/HBV coinfected and HBV monoinfected individuals in a South African cohort. METHODS: We included treatment-naïve HBV and HIV-1 coinfected (n = 203) and HBV monoinfected (n = 212) individuals initiating HBV treatment between 2010 and 2015 at a tertiary referral hospital in Cape Town, South Africa. HBV treatment response was assessed by serum HBsAg loss and suppression of serum HBV DNA to less than 2000 IU/mL. HBV treatment failure was defined as failure to achieve HBsAg loss or HBV DNA suppression at 12 months of treatment. RESULTS: At baseline, HBV/HIV coinfected individuals were younger, more likely to be male, have higher CD4 counts and lower HBV viral loads than HBV monoinfected individuals. In both groups, the majority (HBV/HIV, 80.2%; HBV, 74.5%) were cirrhotic and had advanced fibrosis (F3-4, 77.9% vs. 61.3%, p = 0.002). After a median follow-up of 43.1 months, HBV response rates were significantly higher in HBV/HIV coinfected individuals (HBsAg loss, 74.0% vs. 59.6%, p = 0.002; HBV DNA suppression, 63.3% vs. 45.7%, p = 0.0005). After multivariable adjustment, coinfection with HIV-1 was an independent predictor of HBsAg loss (aOR 1.80, 95% CI 1.11-2.91, p = 0.017) and HBV DNA suppression (aOR 1.61, 95% CI 1.13-2.29, p = 0.01).

The best available treatment option is a combination of interferon and ribavirin, however this is expensive and difficult to administer, and its use is recommended only for people with active liver disease.

Until now, there has been little research into how the treatment can be improved in low-income settings. A study conducted at the University of Cape Town (UCT) has shown that adding interferon to ribavirin can be safely administered to patients in an outpatient setting, and that the side effects are no worse than when ribavirin is used on its own.

The study has shown a high rate of sustained virological response (SVR), which the authors note is likely to have significant public health impact in Africa, where many people have access to ribavirin but are unable to access interferon due to the cost and the need for specialist services to administer it.

"However, our study shows that by making a few simple changes to the usual way the treatment is administered, such as treating patients in an outpatient clinic instead of an inpatient facility, and by carefully monitoring side effects and managing them when they occur, it is possible to safely use interferon-ribavirin in low-resource settings such as sub-Saharan Africa," says Professor Lues.

Hepatitis B is spread through contaminated body fluids including blood transfusions, injections, and sexual contact. In Africa, the disease is often transmitted from mother to baby at birth or through sexual activity. The virus can cause acute (short-term) illness, but most people show no symptoms. Abstract
This study evaluates the impact of insecurity on women's entrepreneurial activities in Shiroro local government area of Niger state. The research questions that motivated this study are: What are the causes and effect of insecurity on women's entrepreneurial activities in Shiroro local government area of Niger state? To what extent does insecurity limit women's entrepreneurial activities in Shiroro local government area of Niger state? The study adopted a survey design. The population of the study comprised all women entrepreneurs in Shiroro local government area of Niger state. The sample space was 190 women entrepreneurs, while sample size was 152. Sample size was determined using the Taro-Yates formula. The sample response was 100%. The research instrument for data collection was a structured questionnaire. The validity of the research instrument was tested and found reliable. The research instrument was pre-tested. The analyzed data were presented in tables, and the results were discussed based on research questions. The major findings of the study are: insecurity creates fear in the minds of women entrepreneurs, thereby discouraging them from expanding their businesses; insecurity leads to loss of property, physical injury and in some cases death; the activities of bandits, kidnappers and herdsmen/farmers conflict have seriously affected the economy of Shiroro local government area of Niger state; the major recommendations of the study are: the federal government should strengthen the security apparatus in Niger state; the federal government should equip the security personnel in Niger state with modern security gadgets. This will make them more effective, and they would be able to forestall insecurity in the state.

Author: BBC Africa

The kidnapping of two French tourists in Niger has put the spotlight on the security situation in the West African country.

Colette Doublet, a French woman who runs a business in Niger, says she wants the French government to help Nigerians improve their security.

Doublet, who was kidnapped in 2011 and held for three months, told BBC World Service’s Newsday programme that businesses in Niger, particularly those run by women, could make a significant contribution to the local economy.

Background
What Is Already Known on This Subject
Selenium (Se), copper (Cu), and zinc (Zn) are essential trace elements for human health, and maternal serum concentrations of these elements in pregnancy are associated with birth outcomes. Se is important for the development and function of the immune system; Cu is required for numerous physiological processes including iron metabolism; and Zn is necessary for growth and development. Maternal serum concentrations of Se, Cu, and Zn in pregnancy have been associated with the risk of small-for-gestational-age birth and spontaneous preterm birth in Bangladesh, Tanzania, and South Africa.1–3
Although the association between high maternal serum concentrations of Se, Cu, and Zn and the risk of small-for-gestational-age birth is consistent, the relationship with the risk of spontaneous preterm birth is less clear. In Tanzania and South Africa, high maternal serum Se concentrations were associated with a higher risk of spontaneous preterm birth, but in Bangladesh, no such association was found.1–3

The objective of this study was to investigate whether concentrations of copper, zinc, and iron in maternal serum in the second trimester are related to small for gestational age newborns. This case–control study analyzed data from 122 healthy women who delivered at the age of 16–40 y with a baby of normal weight and without congenital malformations. The control group consisted of 61 women with babies with gestational age of 38–40 wk and birth weight exceeding the 10th percentile and without congenital malformations who were matched for maternal age, smoking, and diabetes. The case group consisted of 61 women with babies with gestational age of 37 wk and birth weight below the 10th percentile. There were no significant differences between the case and control groups in maternal age, frequency of smoking, and diabetes. Second-trimester serum concentrations of copper and zinc, but not iron, were higher in the case group than in the control group. Multiple linear regression analysis with small size for gestational age as the dependent variable and maternal age, smoking, diabetes, copper, zinc, and iron concentrations as independent variables showed that second-trimester concentrations of copper (P = 0.005) and zinc (P = 0.009) were independent predictors of small size for gestational age. Second-trimester serum concentrations of copper and zinc, but not iron, were higher in newborns who were small for gestational age than in those of normal size. The results suggest that copper and zinc supplementation programs in women who are at high risk for delivering a small-for-gestational-age infant may be beneficial.

The study was conducted in Malawi, Tanzania, and Zimbabwe and was published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition.

The World Health Organization considers micronutrient deficiencies a public health problem. The body needs these micronutrients for growth, development, and gene expression, but in developing countries, 42 percent of children under age 5 are stunted, and 25 percent are deficient in at least one micronutrient.

Previous studies have shown a link between poor dietary quality and the risk of having a preterm birth. Therefore, the researchers wanted to investigate whether the women in this study had high concentrations of selenium, copper, and zinc in their blood, and if these concentrations correlated with the EPI score, which measures the quality of women’s diets.

The study included 1,030 women in Malawi, Tanzania, and Zimbabwe who had given birth before week 37 of pregnancy. The women were led through a questionnaire to determine their diet quality using the EPI score. The minimum EPI score is 41, and a higher score indicates better diet quality. The women also provided a blood sample, which was tested for concentrations of selenium, copper, and zinc.

The results showed that 90 percent of the women had an EPI score below 71, and thus a low diet quality. The women’s concentrations of selenium, copper, and zinc were high, with median values of 139 micrograms per liter (μg/L), 106 μg/L, and 1,370 μg/L, respectively. The researchers then adjusted for factors that might influence the concentrations of selenium, copper, and zinc, such as body mass index and smoking, but the concentrations remained high.

When the researchers looked at the connection between the blood concentrations of the micronutrients and the EPI score, they found that selenium and zinc concentrations increased with a higher EPI score. However, the link between diet quality and the concentrations of these micronutrients must be further investigated.

The researchers cannot be sure yet whether the high concentrations of selenium, copper, and zinc in the women’s blood were due to a better diet or something else. Therefore, more research is needed to establish a link between diet quality and the risk of having a preterm birth.

The researchers want to further investigate the link between the women’s diet quality and their blood concentrations of selenium, copper, and zinc. This could lead to new recommendations for the content of folic acid and other micronutrients in take-home food packages for pregnant women at risk of giving birth preterm

The longer a woman is pregnant, the better for her child. Premature babies are at increased risk of death and short- and long-term complications. Globally, 15 million babies were born preterm in 2015, and this trend is increasing. Preterm birth is the leading cause of infant death. Avoiding preterm births is essential to ending preventable deaths of newborns and improving global newborn health. 

Every day, 1,000 babies are born preterm around the world. Many of these preterm births could be avoided with better understanding of the causes of preterm birth and early recognition of women at risk. Research is increasing our understanding of the mechanisms of preterm birth. With continued research, we can save more lives. 

The PREMATURELY project aims to identify biomarkers in maternal blood and in fetal urine and blood which can determine different stages of preterm birth, and use this information to develop non-invasive methods to detect preterm birth. 

We will also study the life course of fetal growth health, in order to find out how it is affected by genetics, maternal factors and lifestyle. This is important, as small growth in the womb can have consequences throughout life. These could be, for example, that the brain is not fully developed, and that the child has difficulties in learning or with attention and behaviour. We also plan to develop new methods to treat complications related to fetal growth, including long-term consequences. 

To achieve these aims, we first need to establish what causes changes in fetal growth health. We know that fetal growth health is affected by genetics, but also by maternal factors, such as body size and health, smoking, infection, stress, and lifestyle factors, including diet and exercise. By using different types of data, we can track what happens to a woman and her child, from before pregnancy until the child is born, and follow both mother and child afterwards. This gives us the opportunity to study the life course of both mother and child, and how factors before and during pregnancy affect fetal growth and birth outcomes. We can also study how the child grows from birth, and throughout childhood and adolescence.

We hypothesized that high concentrations of iron, zinc, and copper found in food and the environment, and their interactions, contribute to preterm birth.

We collected data on preterm birth, gestational age, birth weight, and concentrations of iron, zinc, and copper in maternal serum, amniotic fluid, and placental tissue from 97 women with preterm delivery and 97 women with term delivery. We used logistic regression to estimate the odds of preterm birth in relation to a combination of iron, zinc, and copper, and their interactions.

In the combination of iron and zinc, the odds ratio (OR) for preterm birth across the entire range of concentrations was 1.32 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.07–1.62; p = 0.01). The OR for preterm birth at the 75th percentile of zinc concentration [12.3 μg/L (95% CI: 10.5–14.3 μg/L)] was 1.90 (95% CI: 1.22–2.95) compared with the 25th percentile. The OR for preterm birth at the 75th percentile of iron concentration [126 μg/L (95% CI: 112–142 μg/L)] was 1.42 (95% CI: 1.08–1.88) compared with the 25th percentile. The interaction between zinc and iron was significant (p = 0.01). The OR for preterm birth at the 75th percentile of zinc and 75th percentile of iron was 2.54 (95% CI: 1.34–4.84) compared with the 25th percentile of zinc and 25th percentile of iron. The odds of preterm birth in the combination of copper and iron or copper and zinc or zinc and iron were similar to the combination of iron and zinc.

Our results suggest that high concentrations of iron and zinc in the maternal-fetal environment are associated with an increased risk of preterm birth, either independently or together. The synergy between iron and zinc in association with preterm birth may be due to the ability of iron to enhance zinc absorption. Further studies are needed to clarify the role of micronutrients in preterm birth.

The researchers also wanted to determine if the odds of having a preterm birth were higher for women with high blood levels of more than one micronutrient. The results of this study were published in the American Journal of Epidemiology on 27 July 2020.

For this study, researchers enrolled 63 women who had had a preterm birth and 63 women who had had a term birth, and compared the selenium, copper, and zinc levels of blood samples collected between 36 and 40 weeks of pregnancy. The women’s blood samples were analyzed for total selenium, selenium attached to selenoproteins, copper, and zinc.

The results of this study found that high blood levels of selenium and zinc were both associated with a higher odds of having a preterm birth. The researchers also found that high blood levels of selenium and zinc together with high copper levels were each associated with a higher odds of having a preterm birth, compared to women with high blood levels of either selenium or zinc but not both.

They found that selenium levels in the blood of the South African women were 34% lower than in the Norwegian women, and that copper levels were 26% higher. There was no difference in the levels of zinc. The study was small, enrolling only 68 women in South Africa and 30 in Norway, and the authors caution that their results are subject to "regional and seasonal variations in food availability and quality".

The authors suggest that the differences in selenium and copper levels may be due to differences in the food available in the two countries. Norway is a country with little arable land and a northerly, cold climate, which has constrained the types of food grown and produced there. Seafood, in particular, is an important part of the Norwegian diet, and meat and vegetables are generally expensive due to the cost of importing them from other European countries. South Africa, on the other hand, has a diverse climate and a lot of arable land, and a more varied diet is grown and produced there. The authors point out that selenium is concentrated in certain foods, such as seafood, meat, and grains, and that these foods are more difficult to source in Norway than in South Africa.

Immune system

The authors also suggest that the higher copper levels in the South African women's blood may be due to copper being more important in boosting the immune system in tropical climates. Dr. Nielsen explains, "Copper is a key component in an enzyme which is involved in producing energy in cells, as well as in the functioning of the immune system. Therefore, higher copper intake is important in warmer climates where the immune system has to work harder to prevent infections, such as those found in South Africa, compared to Norway". This is consistent with previous studies which have shown that individuals in sub-Saharan Africa have higher copper intake and status than individuals in northern Europe. The authors suggest that the lower selenium levels in the South African women's blood may be due to the fact that selenium is not as important in boosting the immune system in tropical climates. Dr. Nielsen explains, "Selenium is an important component of an enzyme which is vital in preventing oxidative damage to cells, and therefore important in protecting the immune system. However, in warm climates where infectious diseases are more prevalent, selenium intake is not critical for the functioning of the immune system as the high levels of infection provide a constant trigger for immune system activation. Therefore, the requirement for selenium is lower in these regions".

They found that for women who were not taking folic acid supplements, higher blood levels of folate (an active form of folic acid) at around 8 weeks of pregnancy were associated with a lower risk of preterm delivery; for women who were taking supplements, higher blood levels of folate were not associated with preterm delivery.

Dr. Simhan also noted that the association between higher folate levels and reduced risk of preterm delivery was only observed in white women. This observation suggests that other factors may be confounding the results in non-white women, such as lower levels of vitamin B12 and/or higher levels of the hormone leptin which were observed in black women in this cohort. The hormone leptin is known to be elevated in under-nourished individuals, who are also at higher risk of giving birth preterm.

“We need large, well-controlled studies using rigorous laboratory methods to determine whether the micronutrients, especially folate, vitamin D, and vitamin B12, and the ratio between folate and vitamin B12, are associated with preterm birth,” said Dr. Simhan. “Given the prevalence of micronutrient deficiencies and the high incidence of preterm birth in South Africa, such studies would be highly relevant and have important public health implications.”

The researchers also found that this gene is under the control of another protein. This protein, called AT2S3, was present at higher levels in the low-copper variety compared to the high-copper variety.

The researchers suspect that this protein can reduce the expression of the copper transporter, thus reducing the level of copper in the fruit. The results show that low blood levels of selenium, copper and zinc are associated with smaller head circumference of the baby, and that low selenium and zinc levels are linked to lower scores on the Apgar test of newborn babies.

The Apgar test is a simple method to assess the physical condition and medical needs of the newborn baby. The test is performed immediately after birth and evaluates the child’s heart rate, breathing, muscle tone, reflexes and skin color. A score of 7 is good, and scores below 3 are associated with serious complications. In this study, the babies of mothers with low selenium and zinc had a significantly lower Apgar score on average. The effect size was similar to the impact of having a mother with pre-eclampsia, which is a pregnancy-related condition that can raise the mother’s blood pressure and can have serious consequences for both the mother and the baby.

The findings suggest that it may be beneficial to give pregnant women prenatal supplements containing selenium, copper and zinc. The recommendation is especially valid for pregnant women in areas that suffer from selenium, copper or zinc deficiency. In Malawi, 48% of women are believed to suffer from selenium deficiency, which is also why the Norwegian government has funded a large selenium supplementation study in Malawi. The results of that study have not yet been published.

The results of the study are interesting as they show for the first time that selenium, copper and zinc intakes in pregnant women in a low-resource setting may affect the size of the baby at birth and the function of the newborn baby. However, the study was carried out in Malawi, and more research is needed to confirm these findings in other African countries. The effects of selenium, copper and zinc on the mother could also be investigated in more detail.

A new study from the University of Bristol in the UK has found that a mother's nutrition before and during pregnancy can have long-term effects on the health of newborn babies in Africa.

The study, published in The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, found that maternal preconception and in-utero exposures to improved diet had beneficial impacts on offspring birth size, newborn size, and infant growth during the first six months of life in rural Gambian villages.

The study was a sub-study of the Women's Nutrition in the WIC Study (WIN-WIC), a randomized controlled trial in 25 villages in rural Gambia, and was funded by the US National Institutes of Health. The researchers used data from 643 single births to women who were randomly assigned to one of two nutrition interventions: a food supplement of ready-to-use supplementary food (PlumpUp) and a dietary diversity intervention.

The PlumpUp food supplement was designed to be a highly nutritious, portable package to be consumed in the initial stages of nutrition rehabilitation. It comes in a sachet as a fortified blend of micronutrient dense oils, fats, and sugars to provide 500 kilocalories per portion.

The dietary diversity intervention was designed to achieve at least eight daily food groups. The researchers believe this is cost-effective and feasible for the target population.

The study found that the birth size of babies born to women who were given the PlumpUp supplement and ate a greater diversity of foods during pregnancy was, on average, 200g larger than the birth size of babies born to women who did not receive the supplement. Newborns of mothers given the PlumpUp supplement also had a birth weight 200g higher than those not given the supplement, and their average length was 1.4cm longer.

The study also found that the infant growth rates of babies born to women who ate a greater diversity of foods during pregnancy were 2.2cm longer and 0.3kg heavier at six months compared to infants born to women with the lowest diversity of foods.

In a related blog, Dr. Andrew Prentice, a nutritional scientist at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine who has worked in The Gambia for more than 30 years, said: "These results will be hard to improve upon. The combination of a healthy diet before and during pregnancy and the PlumpUp supplement is a highly effective package for promoting the health of both mothers and their children in resource-poor settings like rural Gambia."

Pancake tortoise (Malacochersus tornieri) in Nairobi, Kenya. Photo by: Rhett A. Butler.

Pancake tortoise (Malacochersus tornieri) in Nairobi, Kenya. Photo by: Rhett A. Butler.

In the study, which was conducted in the dry, semi-desert Chyulu Hills of Kenya, researchers tracked 11 tortoises over the course of a year, using GPS satellite collars. The devices allowed the researchers to determine not only a tortoise’s location, but also other information, such as whether the animal was male or female, how long its shell was, and how fast it traveled. They also found that the tortoises exhibited a range of home range sizes (the area in which the animal travels), with some animals moving over a wide area, while others stayed in a more confined area. The data also revealed that the animals did not travel far to find food, and would often feed in their own territory. The study is one of the first to examine the homing abilities of tortoises, and the only one to do so in the African dryland tropics. The findings may help inform conservation efforts for tortoises and other animals that exhibit similar homing abilities.

“Many animals are able to find their way back to their home territory after being displaced, but very few studies have been conducted to understand the underlying mechanisms,” explained Dr. James P. Gibbs, Director of the Biodiversity and Wildlife Loss Assessment Program at the University of Northern British Columbia. “This study provides evidence that some tortoise species are able to find their way home by a process called ‘true’ or ‘homing’ orientation, which has only been previously proven in sea turtles.”

The findings were published in the open-access journal PLOS ONE.

The study also determined that the tortoises were most active in the early morning and late afternoon. This activity likely relates to avoiding the mid-day heat, as well as predation, since many predators, including birds of prey and large carnivores, are most active in the middle of the day.

The researchers also found that the tortoises spent time in areas that were not ideal for feeding or avoiding predation. For example, one male traveled to an area where there was little or no vegetation, and another spent time in an area with a high risk of predation near human settlements. The researchers theorized that these excursions may serve a role in mating behavior.

The ability to learn and remember such behaviors is crucial for the animal to complete its daily tasks. The hippocampus is a key brain structure involved in spatial navigation and memory; it has a vast amount of neurons that project into the lateral septal nucleus (LSN), and the molecular mechanisms that underlie this synaptic complexity are poorly understood. Here, we used the Aplysia model system, in which behavior, circuit anatomy, and molecular components of synaptic plasticity are well characterized, in conjunction with two-electrode voltage-clamp techniques to examine the rules of long-term potentiation (LTP) in the LSN. Our results reveal that the induction of LTP depends on the serial order of activation of the two input pathways, with reciprocal inhibition between the two pathways. LTP was induced when the high-frequency pathway was activated before the low-frequency pathway by 10 s, and this LTP was associated with a 50% decrease in synaptic current at 90 s post-activation. In contrast, when the high-frequency pathway was activated after the low-frequency pathway by 10 s, LTP was not induced, but a 30% decrease in synaptic current was observed at 90 s post-activation. These results suggest that the LSN receives two distinct inputs that may originate from different subpopulations of neurons in the pleural ganglia. The molecular mechanism underlying LTP is also different for the two induction protocols. While cAMP-dependent activation of protein kinase A (PKA) is involved in the induction of LTP when the high-frequency pathway is activated before the low-frequency pathway, mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) activation is involved when the high-frequency pathway is activated after the low-frequency pathway. Our findings suggest that distinct rules of plasticity are implemented in neurons that contact the LSN to allow for the flexible coding of information flowing through the pleural ganglia.

Here, we study the relative importance of biotic and abiotic factors influencing the space use of the endangered Northern Corridor population of the Western Lowland Gorilla (Gorilla gorilla gorilla). We used 11 years (2005–2015) of individual-based telemetry data to model the influence of biotic and abiotic factors on the spatial distribution of the gorillas. Our results suggest that the home range of the Northern Corridor gorillas is influenced by both biotic and abiotic factors. Vegetation and water were the least and most important variables, respectively, in the final statistical model. Sex and body weight of the gorillas had a stronger influence on space use than age. Seasonality had a stronger influence on the spatial distribution of the gorillas than the former studies conducted in the Bwindi Impenetrable National Park, Uganda. Our results emphasize that management strategies for the Northern Corridor population should consider the influence of biotic factors on the space use of the gorillas. Given that vegetation is the least important variable influencing the spatial distribution of the gorillas, deforestation and therefore human activities might be the major threat to the Northern Corridor population of the Western Lowland Gorilla.

The species were tracked from the release site to assess if they had the ability to home. Four of the translocated tortoises were recaptured in the Kalamba Division, while one was recaptured in Mwingi East Division. Three of the animals released in Kalamba were recaptured in the same division. The results showed that the species had the ability to home, and they also showed high fidelity and territoriality to the release site.

The study site is located in the Central Kalahari Game Reserve, Botswana. Mean body mass of male and female tortoises was 19.5 kg and 11.4 kg, respectively. Although home range size was larger in males than in females, there was no difference in spatial overlap between the sexes. Mating was observed in August and September, indicating that it is a dry-season event. Starch grain analysis of fecal samples collected ad libitum indicated that Geisgekke (Portulacaceae), Likhaya (Aizoaceae) and Morama (Ruscaceae) were consumed. The diet of tortoises was also studied through analysis of 412 scats collected through sampling efforts of 367 scans and 103 fecal samples. The results of the diet analysis using scats and fecal samples were combined and characterized, and 11 food items were identified. Consumption of Morama, followed by Euphorbia (Euphorbiaceae), Likhaya and Tii (Burseraceae) indicated a preference for succulent plant species. The study highlights the importance of combining different sampling methods to gain a better understanding of the diet of tortoises in arid environments.

The research team, including scientists from Kenya and the Netherlands, also made a surprising finding with respect to the tortoises' diet. The study was published in the scientific journal "Oryx".

The East African pancake tortoise is a peculiar species: it is the only tortoise that lives in rocky areas instead of in forests or grasslands. It is listed as "Vulnerable" on the international Red List of threatened species, and is protected in Kenya and Uganda. However, little is known about its ecology and behaviour. For instance, it is not clear how far the tortoises can move away from their home area, and whether they can find their way back.

To investigate this issue, the researchers captured 30 tortoises on two mountains in northern Kenya and marked them with GPS transmitters. The animals were then moved to one of three other locations, each 5 to 10 km away from the capture site. The researchers wanted to find out how far the tortoises would travel after being released, and whether they would return to their home area.

The results were clear: all three groups travelled at least 1.5 km after being moved, and two of the groups returned to their mountains of origin. One individual even walked back all the way by himself, a distance of at least 9 km.

"It is very rare for reptiles or amphibians to be able to find their way over such long distances," says Ansgar A. Cochlin, first author of the study. "Many tortoise species have been studied, but this is the first evidence that the East African pancake tortoise is able to do this. It is remarkable that the animals were able to find their way back, especially since they rely largely on visual cues."

The researchers also found that the tortoises' diet is more diverse than previously thought. The animals were observed feeding on 21 plant species, including fruits, flowers, and grasses. Previously, researchers believed that the East African pancake tortoise mainly feeds on low-growing plants and shrubs.

The fact that the animals travel over long distances, and are able to find their way back, is likely to have important implications for their conservation. The species occurs in several protected areas, but the effectiveness of these protected areas depends on the animals' ability to move between them.

Rifampicin is a key drug for the treatment of tuberculosis and tuberculous meningitis. Because of concerns about neurotoxicity, intravenous (IV) administration is recommended for treatment of tuberculous meningitis. Oral high-dose rifampicin has been suggested as an alternative to IV rifampicin in patients with normal meningeal function. We compared the pharmacokinetics of high-dose oral and IV rifampicin in patients with tuberculous meningitis to determine whether oral high-dose rifampicin can be used safely as an alternative to IV rifampicin.
We did a prospective, randomized, single-blind, crossover study of high-dose oral and IV rifampicin among 20 patients with culture-confirmed tuberculous meningitis who were treated with a standard regimen of intramuscular injections of benzathine benzylpenicillin and oral isoniazid for 2 weeks, followed by 22 weeks of oral treatment with isoniazid and rifampicin. In the first week of treatment, patients were randomized to receive either high-dose oral (60 mg/kg) rifampicin once daily with food or IV rifampicin (10 mg/kg) every 8 h. In the fifth week of treatment, the patients received the other regimen. Blood was tested for rifampicin concentrations by high-performance liquid chromatography.
