This study tested the effects of JASPER, a naturalistic, embedded intervention for young children with autism in a randomized controlled trial in Uganda. Children (N = 39) with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) were recruited from government and NGO clinics and schools and assessed prior to a 6-month intervention. During the intervention, normally developing peers (N = 11) received JASPER; children with ASD (N = 20) were randomized to receive JASPER or usual care. Intervener raters and observers assessed child social communication skills, and interviewees assessed reliability of intervention implementation. Intervened children showed significant improvements in initiation of social interaction, maintenance of social engagement, and frequency of social initiation. Intervention fidelity was high. Peers of children with ASD showed significant improvements in responding to social initiations. This is the first controlled trial of an evidence-based intervention for children with ASD in a low-resource setting and provides evidence that such an approach is feasible and produces gains for both peers and children with ASD. © 2017 Society for Research in Child Development.

We investigated if higher doses of rifampicin could be administered by the intramuscular route in a pharmacokinetic study in Ugandan adults with tuberculous meningitis.
Pharmacokinetic analysis of rifampicin was performed in 20 Ugandan adults with culture-confirmed tuberculous meningitis. Patients received intramuscular injections of rifampicin 10 mg/kg body weight with oral doses of 300 mg daily. Concentrations of rifampicin were measured in plasma and cerebrospinal fluid. Non-linear mixed-effects modelling was used to analyse pharmacokinetic data.
The median (IQR) dose-adjusted area-under-the-curve (AUC) was 69.2 (55.7-107.7) mg.h/L and individual AUC values were highly variable (range 7.1-477.7 mg.h/L). The median (IQR) peak plasma concentration was 14.2 (10.1-19.8) mg/L. Concentrations of rifampicin in cerebrospinal fluid were low, with a median (IQR) of 0.52 (0.39-0.81) mg/L and a cerebrospinal fluid to plasma concentration ratio of 0.032 (0.023-0.045). There was a trend towards an association between higher dose-adjusted AUC and shorter time to cure meningitis (p=0.1).
Higher doses of intramuscular rifampicin can be given to patients with tuberculous meningitis, although concentrations in cerebrospinal fluid are low. The high variability in rifampicin exposure requires further investigation. The association between dose-adjusted AUC and shorter time to cure suggests that higher doses of rifampicin may be more effective in treating meningitis. The results support the ongoing Meningitis II trial (ISRCTN72902759).

The pharmacokinetic analysis was conducted on data from 16 children with bacterial meningitis enrolled in a randomized controlled trial comparing intravenous rifampicin 20 mg/kg with oral rifampicin 35 mg/kg. Non-parametric methods were used to estimate area-under-the-curve (AUC) of rifampicin in both groups.

The median rifampicin AUC was 2610 μM·h/L (interquartile range 2210-3230) after oral dosing and 2570 μM·h/L (interquartile range 2280-3100) after intravenous dosing. The difference between the median AUC of the oral and intravenous groups was -4.9% (95% CI -19.3 to 12.5, p=0.6233). There was great intersubject variability, and AUC values were not significantly related to body weight or age in either group.

Our results suggest that the exposure achieved with intravenous rifampicin 20 mg/kg is similar to that achieved with oral rifampicin 35 mg/kg. These findings support the use of a rifampicin dose of 20 mg/kg intravenously, which may be useful in trials of rifampicin-containing regimens in children with meningitis.

This is according to a study by the Desmond Tutu HIV Centre at the University of Cape Town, which was published in The Lancet Global Health on Monday.

The study, which was conducted over 10 years, found that the majority of HIV-positive patients who developed TB meningitis died within a year of being diagnosed with the condition.

Co-lead author Laura Bowring said in a statement that although TB meningitis is a rare form of TB, it accounts for almost one in every 10 cases of TB in South Africa.

“Because it is a disease that attacks the brain and spinal cord, it causes high levels of death and disability,” Bowring said.

The study looked at 1 698 patients who had been diagnosed with HIV and TB meningitis between 1 January 2006 and 31 December 2015 at three sites in Cape Town.

The researchers found that, of the patients who died, two-thirds died within six months of diagnosis and 80% died within a year. The average time to death was 7.5 months.

According to the World Health Organization, TB meningitis usually develops in the later stages of TB infection. It is difficult to diagnose because symptoms overlap with those of other diseases.

The most common symptoms are fever, drowsiness, confusion, headache, lack of appetite, nausea, vomiting, stiff neck and seizures. The disease causes inflammation of the lining of the brain and spinal cord.

The researchers found that the use of highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART), a combination of several antiretroviral (ARV) drugs to maximise the suppressive effect of the drugs, did not improve survival rates among patients with TB meningitis.

Bowring said this could be because HAART was started later in the course of illness, when the meninges had already been inflamed for some time.

Co-lead author Francesca Conradie said in the statement that the findings show that patients with HIV and TB meningitis are a particularly vulnerable group.

She said the high levels of death and disability among this group of patients call for targeted interventions, which could include identifying the patients before they show typical symptoms and treating them with different or additional medications.

The tablets are printed with a special 3D printer that uses a special polymer material that hardens when exposed to light. The researchers have now been able to adjust the composition of the material used, so that it becomes even easier to break down the tablets.

“We added a plastic, polyethylene, to the tablets so that they become more brittle and easier to break,” says Oscar Hultgren, PhD student at the Department of Materials and Manufacturing at Chalmers University of Technology.

The researchers also wanted to find out if they could use a non-invasive breath test to see if the body is producing the drug, and how much. The researchers will present their findings on Monday, 12 July.
Dr. Mariam Koster, a researcher at UMC Utrecht in the Netherlands and one of the principal investigators of the study, says: “Rifampicin is a powerful drug that can clear tuberculosis (TB) in only two months. It is also one of the drugs of choice against multidrug-resistant and extensively drug-resistant TB. However, many patients develop resistance to it, and we need to find ways to give them the best possible treatment and prevent resistance from developing in the first place. This is why we wanted to find out more about the pharmacokinetics of high-dose rifampicin.”
Pharmaceutical company MyDx Pharmaceuticals developed the breath test that the researchers will use. It can show whether a person’s body is producing a drug, and how much. The test works by having a patient breathe into a device that contains a sensor. The test will be able to detect the drug’s by-products, which are created when the body breaks down the drug. Since these by-products are not absorbed into the body, they remain in the lungs, from where they can be easily measured in the breath. The researchers will use the test to see if a person’s body breaks down high-dose rifampicin differently from standard-dose rifampicin.
The researchers will also use the test to see if they can use a model to calculate the amount of drug that a person’s body is producing. This would be a major breakthrough in TB treatment, as it would mean that a person’s treatment could be tailored to them. Currently, doctors have to make a diagnosis based on a patient’s symptoms and a visual assessment of their x-ray results. “If we can develop this model, it would be a major breakthrough in TB treatment,” says Dr. Koster. “It would mean that we could test a patient’s sputum sample to see if the treatment is working, and if not, change it immediately. This is a much better way of treating TB than the method we use at the moment.”
The researchers will present their findings on Monday, 12 July, at the 11th Conference of the International Union of Tuberculosis and Lung Disease in Cape Town, South Africa.

The researchers then looked at the genetic makeup of the bacteria from each patient and used this information to determine which treatment each patient received. 

They found that the new treatment was much more effective than the standard treatment at wiping out all the bacteria from the blood and skin of the patients. 

However, the bacteria from three of the patients developed a resistance to dapsone during the course of the study, and so the researchers then added the antibiotic clofazimine to the combined treatment. 

This new combination was highly effective at wiping out the bacteria and was not met with the development of any drug resistance. 

The researchers also found that the course of moxifloxacin could be reduced to just 4 weeks without reducing the effectiveness of the treatment. 

This new treatment is now being prepared for testing in larger clinical trials. 

Lead researcher Dr. Chetan Chauhan from the Institute of Tropical Medicine Antwerp in Belgium said: “Leprosy remains a major public health problem in many parts of the world, and it is very important to highlight the fact that the current treatment is not always effective. We found that by personalising the treatment according to the genetic make-up of the bacteria that cause the disease, we were able to greatly improve the efficacy of the treatment.”

One year later, 90% of the girls who received Cervarix were protected against HPV 6, 11, 16 and 18, compared with 70% of those who received placebo.

Protection was longer in girls who received the vaccine before they became sexually active. In those who had ever had sex, the vaccine was 60% effective in protecting them against cervical cancer and the HPV 6, 11, 16 and 18 infections.

Dr Mark Doorbar, director of the HPV research group at the Cancer Council Victoria, said the results were exciting.

"It's a very important step forward in providing a vaccine to help protect young women against cervical cancer," he said. "But it's not the whole answer, because even in those who get the vaccine, if they do become infected, they will still get cancer.

"It really should be seen as one tool in a toolkit that includes existing treatments and prevention strategies such as Pap smears and condoms."

Dr Doorbar said the vaccine could potentially be given to boys as well as girls, which would have the added benefit of protecting against genital warts.

The World Health Organization and many public health groups want to see the vaccine included in childhood immunisation programs. The WHO wants to see it added to the routine immunisations given to girls aged 9-10 years old.

But the WHO and many health groups have also called for the vaccine to be given to boys as well as girls to protect everyone from the virus.

The research was a collaborative project between the Research Institute for Tuberculosis and the Department of Chemistry at Stellenbosch University in South Africa.

Dr. Frans van der Westhuizen, a researcher at the Research Institute for Tuberculosis, said that the DPAE4 compound was identified through a process of rational drug design. Unlike other compounds that are currently being used to treat tuberculosis, the new compound is composed of four components that can be easily recognized by the bacteria that cause tuberculosis, which then allows the bacteria to take up the compound.

This compound is then able to accumulate within the bacteria to a much higher level than the other compounds that are currently used in the clinic. It is this accumulation that leads to the high level of toxicity towards the bacteria.

A major advantage of this new compound is that it is effective against all types of mycobacteria that are either natural pathogens of animals and humans or that are opportunistic pathogens, which means that it can be used to treat many more patients than are currently treated for tuberculosis.

The main focus in this study was to investigate the mechanism by which the compound kills mycobacteria. Using a series of biochemical experiments, the researchers were able to show that the DPAE4 compound kills mycobacteria by inhibiting the synthesis of lipids within the bacteria. It is this process that is essential for the survival of mycobacteria as a species. Without being able to synthesize lipids, the bacteria are not able to survive.

This compound is also effective against tuberculosis in mice. Since the compound is effective in mice at very low doses, it is hoped that it will also be effective in humans at low doses. If this is the case, it will allow the treatment of tuberculosis to be less toxic to humans and also less expensive since the dosage will be much lower than that of currently available anti-tuberculosis drugs.

A laboratory incubation study

Soil and Environmental Sciences Research Group, Department of Soil Science, University of Saskatchewan, Saskatoon, SK, Canada S7N 5A2

*Corresponding author: E-mail: firstname.lastname@example.org

The quality of highly weathered coastal savanna soils is often low and they are generally deficient in plant nutrients and organic matter. Combining compost and biochar could increase nutrient retention and availability, nutrient use efficiency, and soil organic matter content. The objective of this study was to investigate the individual and interactive effects of compost and biochar, as well as compost x biochar interactions on soil chemical properties after 30 d of incubation. Compost and biochar were applied at rates of 0, 4, and 8 Mg ha−1. Results showed that compost and biochar, individually, increased soil organic carbon (C), potentially mineralizable soil C, soil temperatures, basal respiration, and microbial biomass. Interactions between compost and biochar resulted in a synergistic effect on soil C, microbial biomass, basal respiration, and dehydrogenase activity, but a mitigating effect on mineralizable C. Compost plus biochar, at 8 Mg ha−1, resulted in soil C and microbial biomass contents similar to those found in less-weathered soils from other land uses. The combination of compost and biochar application is an easy and effective way to improve soil quality and microbial function in highly weathered coastal savanna soils.

Keywords: Compost; Biochar; Soil organic carbon; Microbial biomass; Basal respiration.

Soils in coastal savanna regions are unique in their geology, topography, vegetation, and climate (Miles et al. 2014). In these regions, soils are often highly weathered, with low soil organic carbon (C) content and have low fertility (Miles et al. 2014). In addition, these soils are generally acidic with a high level of iron and aluminium toxicity (Su et al. 2014). As a result, these soils are often N and P limited and have low soil quality (Miles et al. 2014). Improving soil quality in coastal savanna regions is important to support increased crop productivity and crop yield stability, which is required to sustain the needs of a growing global population (Kassam et al. 2015).

In order to develop successful strategies to improve crop productivity, an in-depth understanding of the factors controlling soil organic carbon (SOC) dynamics is essential. Soil microbial communities regulate C dynamics, both directly through their lability of soil organic matter (SOM) and indirectly through their impact on soil inorganic C and N cycles. We used a combined 13C-labeling and soil respiration measurements approach to quantify the response of C sequestration to changes in plant input and soil microbial community composition in a field experiment with C3 and C4 species under two N input levels (no N fertilizer and N fertilizer at 150 kg N ha−1 y−1). We estimated that, under no N input, the net C accumulation in the live SOM and detritus pools was 0.95 and 0.44 kg C m−2 y−1, respectively, and the C sequestration rate was 0.30 kg C m−2 y−1. N fertilization increased plant biomass production, and C input from plant material to soil organic matter, by 102%. As a result, net C accumulation in live SOM and detritus pools increased to 1.23 and 0.97 kg C m−2 y−1, respectively, and the C sequestration rate increased to 0.41 kg C m−2 y−1. The change in soil microbial community composition, as a result of changes in plant input and soil management, was assessed by pyrosequencing of the 16S ribosomal RNA gene in the 0–15 cm soil layer. The soil microbial communities were more similar in response to plant input than to soil management. The soil microbial communities under C4 plants shifted to a more diverse community than those under C3 plants, and the relative abundance of Proteobacteria increased while that of Cytophaga–Flavobacterium and Actinobacteria decreased. Net C accumulation was significantly correlated with the relative abundance of Proteobacteria and the ratio of Cytophaga–Flavobacterium to Actinobacteria. Our results suggest that the short-term N and plant input to soil has a strong positive effect on C accumulation and sequestration. The change in soil microbial community composition may also contribute to C sequestration in the soil, possibly through the regulation of soil C and N cycles.

The study was conducted in the field experiment at the experimental farm of the University of the Free State, Bloemfontein, South Africa. Biochar was produced from local crop residues (maize straw and sugar cane leaves) using slow pyrolysis method at 550 °C. The biochar was characterized for pH, cation exchange capacity, and surface area. The biochar was mixed into the soil at 1% (w/w) and the manure was applied at 1 t ha−1. The following year, maize was planted in all the treatments. Soil samples were collected before the application of biochar and manure (0–20 cm soil depth) and after 12 months (0–20 cm soil depth), and analyzed for pH, available P, potassium (K), phosphorus (P), electrical conductivity, microbial carbon, nitrogen and dehydrogenase (DH) activity, and the microbial biomass was also estimated. The results showed that the biochar application increased the soil pH value, and the cation exchange capacity, and the surface area of the soil. Application of biochar alone or combined with the compost and crop residues increased the soil microbial carbon (Cmic) and nitrogen (Nmic) content, and the activity of DH enzyme, and available soil P and K content. The application of biochar with manure or alone resulted in higher maize yield (9.1 and 8.3 t ha−1), and was significantly higher than the control (4.5 t ha−1) and the soil plus 1% compost (6.2 t ha−1). The trend was similar for 1000-grain weight. The results suggest that the application of 1% biochar (from slow pyrolysis of maize straw and sugar cane leaves) with or without 1% compost to the soil could be an effective and economically viable option to improve soil quality and crop yield.

This is likely due to the high C:N ratios in the biochar (which was similar for all types of biochar used here) leading to immobilization of N in the soil. The microbial biomass in the soil is largely composed of C and N, so the addition of C (biochar) leading to increased microbial growth will lead to increased respiration. However, the addition of compost (which has a 20:1 C:N) or composted rice husks (which have a 50:1 C:N ratio) leads to a release of N which can be used by the microbes, leading to increased plant growth through the increased supply of N. The biochar amendments lead to a reduction in the N2 fixation (Fig. 3c) likely due to an increased competition for N, as well as a reduction in the number of rhizobia in the soil (Supplementary Fig. 7). This reduction in N2 fixation may lead to an increase in the amount of N available to the plants, however, the C:N ratio of the plant tissue did not change in response to the different amendments (Supplementary Fig. 8), likely due to the fact that the plants were N limited and all amendments were preventing further N loss due to leaching or volatilization. The higher respiration rates in the treatments receiving amendments leads to a higher C sequestration in the soil, since the C added to the soil through amendments is not lost, but sequestered below ground.

This is consistent with the observation of other researchers such as De Lucia et al. (2011) who found increased soil respiration following biochar addition. This implies an increase in microbial activity and biomass which is supported by our findings. Our results are also in agreement with those of Steenweg et al. (2015), who found that compost addition increased microbial biomass and basal respiration. However, in contrast to our findings, they found that biochar addition did not significantly affect microbial biomass or basal respiration. This difference could be attributed to the type of biochar used in their study, as their biochar was produced from sugar maple wood, as opposed to the biochar used in our study which was produced from ground, mixed waste food. Therefore, the properties of the two types of biochar used in the two studies could be responsible for the difference in the effects observed. This is because the properties of biochar such as surface area, pore size distribution, and pH can vary depending on the feedstock and production conditions.

The study, published today in Biomed Central’s open access journal Acta Veterinaria Scandinavica, shows that biochar and compost added to soil significantly increased crop yield, nitrogen content in leaves and plant height.

Dr Elinor Burkitt-Gray, who conducted the research while at the University of Pretoria, said: “Biochar is a novel way to improve soil health and is part of the ‘4 per cent solution’ to climate change. The 4 per cent solution is a farming approach that incorporates a small amount of biochar into the soil, along with three other simple and inexpensive amendments that are appropriate for local conditions, into an overall system for sustainable agricultural production.

“Our study shows that biochar and compost are both essential for the success of the 4 per cent solution in terms of crop yield and other measures of plant health. Compost is cheap and easy to produce, but its effects are relatively short-lived. In contrast, biochar has long-lasting effects, but is more difficult to produce and is therefore more expensive. Our research suggests that the benefits of biochar for plant growth are at least ten years.”

To conduct the research, Burkitt-Gray set up 32 experimental plots and half of them received 4% biochar, half of those received 4% compost, and half of those received both 4% biochar and 4% compost. The plots were established in February 2009 and data was collected from February 2009 to October 2010. The study was conducted at the Mpoeng Experimental Station in the South Africa’s eastern Free State province.

She added: “The biochar used in the study was produced from a range of plant materials, including wood waste from a local timber mill and local dairy manure. The biochar was produced using a slow, thermal ‘pyrolysis’ method, which is known to produce a high-quality biochar with a porous structure that allows plants to readily access nutrients.

“Compost was produced from local dairy manure and grass clippings. It was high in carbon (58%) and had a wide range of nutrients including nitrogen (0.7%) and phosphorous (0.6%), which is high for compost. The high carbon content means it will not deplete the soil of its own nitrogen, making it an ideal addition to the soil.

The study also found that the addition of biochar to soil increases the number of beneficial microorganisms in the soil, further improving the soil's fertility.

The study, published in Agronomy for Sustainable Development, is the first to document the effects of long-term use of biochar in African soil. The findings suggest that biochar can be an important tool in improving soil health in Africa.

Previous studies have shown that biochar can improve soil fertility and crop yields. However, it is not clear whether these benefits persist over time. This study addresses this knowledge gap by examining the long-term effects of biochar on soil quality and fertility in Kenya.

The study used field experiments and soil analyses to assess the impact of biochar on soil quality. The researchers added biochar to soil at different rates and monitored the soil quality over a period of four years.

The results showed that the addition of biochar improved soil quality measures such as soil organic matter, available nutrients, and microbial activity. The improved soil quality was consistent across all biochar treatment rates.

The study also found that the addition of biochar increased the number of beneficial microorganisms in the soil. These microorganisms play an important role in improving soil fertility and crop health.

The increased microbial activity further improved soil fertility by making more nutrients available to plants. The study also found that the addition of biochar helped to reduce soil acidity, which is a common problem in African soils.

The findings of this study suggest that biochar can be an important tool in improving soil health in Africa. However, further research is needed to better understand the long-term effects of biochar on soil and to determine the most effective application methods.

samples.ref: Ye nngwe ya mathata a magologolo ao a lebaganego le tšweletšo ya dibjalo go borwa bja kontinente ya Afrika ke go phuhlama ga go nona ga mabu.

This is a complex problem with many different causes, and it is difficult to get a precise idea of the extent of the problem. In order to find out more about the extent of the problem and the factors that may be causing it, we did a literature survey to find previous studies that measured soil fertility in different African countries and regions. 

We found 95 studies that measured soil fertility (total nitrogen, available phosphorus and/or exchangeable potassium) in the top 20cm of the soil. The studies were conducted in 24 countries in sub-Saharan Africa. Most of the studies only measured soil fertility once at different locations within a country and were therefore not repeated measurements at the same sites. The few studies that measured soil fertility more than once, measured it in only two or three times. There were also no long-term studies (more than 5 years) in which soil fertility was measured at regular intervals. 

The few studies that provided data for different land uses (land use data was available for 41 studies), we used to calculate the change in soil fertility under different land uses (arable land, pasture, forest, fallow and woodland). From those 41 studies, we found that in 12 studies soil fertility was higher under arable land than under other land uses. In 25 studies, there was no difference in soil fertility between arable land and the other land uses. In 4 studies, soil fertility was higher under land uses such as pasture, fallow or woodland than under arable land. 

From the 95 studies we found, 53 measured soil fertility in the top 20cm of the soil, while 42 measured it in three depths (0-20cm, 20-40cm and 40-60cm). Only five of these 42 studies that measured soil fertility in three depths, measured soil fertility under different land uses in the same depths. From those five studies we found that available phosphorus increased with depth in all land uses, while total nitrogen and exchangeable potassium either decreased or did not change with depth. 

Most of the studies (78) used soil sampling designs where soil was only collected from different locations at different sites. Only 17 studies used a pit or trench that was dug and described the horizontal and vertical variation of the soil within that pit or trench. Of those 17 studies, 13 described the horizontal variation of the soil, 3 described the vertical variation and only 1 study described both the horizontal and vertical variation of the soil within the pit or trench

But the effects of biochar on the soil microbiome are not well understood. Now, publishing in ACS’ Environmental Science & Technology, scientists have shown that adding biochar to different types of soil changes the structure of the bacterial communities that live there, increasing the evenness of their make-up while reducing the total number of species present.

The soil microbiome is a complex, tightly knit community of microorganisms that can affect how carbon from biochar is released into the environment. So, Guipie et al. studied how the addition of biochar to different types of soil affected the structure of this community. The team added biochar to samples of either an agricultural loam, an agricultural sandy loam or a grassland soil and left it for 24 days. Then, they analyzed the samples for their bacterial content.

The researchers found that the addition of biochar increased the evenness of the number of different bacterial species present in all types of soil. This was accompanied by a reduction in the total number of species present. The soil type affected the changes in the communities’ structure, as well as how the biochar modified the environment. For example, the team found that biochar increased nitrogen levels in all types of soil. But only in the agricultural soils did it decrease levels of phosphorus. Overall, the work gives a better understanding of how the addition of biochar to soil can change the environment for the microorganisms living there, which could aid efforts to improve soil health and fertility.

Reference:
Guipie, B., Li, Q., Zhao, F., Rousk, J., Cheng, H. Biochar Amendment Alter the Structure of Soil Bacterial Communities across Different Soil Types, Environ. Sci. Technol., 2021.

Biochar can be used as a soil additive to improve soil fertility and crop yields. It can also be used to sequester carbon and mitigate climate change.

The term “biochar” was first coined in 2009, but the concept of using charcoal as a soil additive is not new. The use of charcoal as a soil additive is believed to date back thousands of years, to pre-Columbian times in South America. They tested the biochars as soil amendments in two field experiments: one in a rainfall site in western Kenya and the other in a drought-prone site in eastern Kenya.

The researchers evaluated the effect of biochar dose on soil properties and plant growth in a pot trial conducted in a rainfall site in western Kenya. They also monitored the effect of biochar application on soil properties and crop yield in two consecutive seasons in the field experiments conducted in rainfall and drought-prone sites in Kenya.

The results showed that the corn cob biochar improved soil pH, electrical conductivity, and water holding capacity, as well as C, H, O, and N content. The corn cob and rice husk biochars increased available potassium (K) but decreased available phosphorus (P).

In a rainfall site in western Kenya, the corn cob biochar increased maize leaf area but decreased the number of maize ears per plant. However, in a drought-prone site in eastern Kenya, the corn cob biochar reduced maize leaf area, number of ears per plant, and kernel weight, resulting in lower grain yield, but increased the number of cobs per plant.

The coconut biochar improved soil physical properties and K availability in the drought-prone site in eastern Kenya.

The results from this study suggest that the corn cob and coconut biochars can serve as potential soil amendments to improve soil quality and crop productivity in smallholder farming systems in tropical environments.

The first part of my thesis deals with the analysis of the fibrin fibre network in rheumatoid arthritis (RA) using different methods. The special fibre structure in RA has long been known but has recently been revitalized due to new technical possibilities. I have studied whether the atypical fibre structure is due to a) post-translational modifications of fibrinogen leading to altered fibrin polymerisation or b) an altered interaction between fibrinogen and the fibrinolytic system. I also studied the relation between the atypical fibres and a) the inflammatory reaction in RA and b) the increased thrombomodulin (TM) activity in RA. Concerning a) I could show with Western Blotting that the atypical fibres contain more high molecular weight fibrinogen. This could be due to acylation or similar modifications. With immunofluorescence and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) I studied the relation between the atypical fibres and the fibrinolytic system. The results from these studies point towards an altered interaction between the atypical fibres and the fibrinolytic system. Concerning b), there was a significant negative correlation between the amount of atypical fibres and C-reactive protein (CRP), whereas there was a significant positive correlation between the amount of atypical fibres and TM. The increased TM activity could be an effect of the atypical fibres, or of the inflammatory reaction, or both.

The second part of the thesis deals with the anti-fibrinogen antibodies in RA. There was a highly significant (p<0.001) positive correlation between the amount of anti-fibrinogen antibodies and the amount of atypical fibres.   • There is an ongoing search for biomarkers in rheumatoid arthritis (RA), in order to improve early diagnosis and treatment of affected individuals.
  • We measured the circulating levels of five biomarkers; C-reactive protein (CRP), serum amyloid A (SAA), interleukin-6 (IL-6), tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α) and intercellular adhesion molecule 1 (ICAM-1) in 38 RA patients and 38 healthy controls.
  • The levels of SAA, CRP and ICAM-1 but not TNF-α, were significantly elevated in RA patients.
  • The circulating levels of SAA and CRP were highly correlated with each other as well as with the levels of ICAM-1, TNF-α and IL-6, while no correlation was found between the levels of SAA and CRP on the one hand and the ESR on the other hand.
  • In RA, the levels of these biomarkers may be useful for estimation of the inflammatory load and disease activity.

In the early stages of RA, when the disease is active, patients have increased levels of procoagulant factors and decreased levels of anticoagulant factors, leading to a procoagulant state. This finding is in contrast to what is typically seen with other inflammatory conditions, such as diabetes, where a hypercoagulable state is not typically seen. In patients with active RA, the proinflammatory state may overwhelm the compensatory coagulation changes associated with chronic inflammation. The proinflammatory cytokines, IL-1 and TNF-α, appear to be the major culprits for initiating the procoagulant change in RA, although the precise mechanisms are not known. Moreover, the binding of FcγRIIa by immune complexes is also important in the generation of a procoagulant state. Thus, it is possible that the effects of immune complex binding of FcγRIIa and the effects of the proinflammatory cytokines are synergistic. This would imply that the coagulation system may serve as a target for therapeutic intervention in RA, and indeed, there are data to suggest that specific interventions in coagulation might be of benefit in RA.

We hypothesized that the altered fibrin structure would be associated with the presence of anti-citrullinated protein antibodies (ACPA) and rheumatoid factor (RF) in RA patients. A total of 23 paired plasma and synovial fluid samples were analyzed for fibrin D-dimer levels by ELISA, and assessed for the presence of ACPA and RF. Fibrin genotypes were determined by RT-PCR and allele-specific restriction enzyme digestion. Significant higher plasma and synovial fluid D-dimer levels were observed in patients with ACPA+ and/or RF+, compared to ACPA- and RF- (p=0.01 and p=0.03, respectively). Similarly, plasma but not synovial fluid D-dimer levels were significantly higher in patients with the GG fibrin 3,770C> G genotype compared to those with the GC or CC genotypes (p=0.02). There was a trend for increasing D-dimer levels in plasma with increasing number of autoimmune related genetic risk factors (p=0.04). Our results suggest that altered fibrin structure associated with autoimmunity may play a role as a novel thrombophilic risk factor in RA.

Published: Tuesday, May 19, 2009 - 16:19 in Medicine & Health

A higher risk of heart attack and stroke in people with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) may be due to the blood clots that are characteristic of this and other autoimmune diseases, according to a new study.

The study showed that patients with RA were nearly three times more likely than healthy controls to have blood clots in their legs, even though their legs were 30 percent less active than those of the healthy controls.

The study also points to potential new ways to reduce the high risk of heart attack and stroke in patients with RA and other autoimmune diseases, by targeting blood clotting factors.

"Although the exact mechanisms are not yet known, we believe that the blood clots that form in the small blood vessels of the legs are responsible for the accelerated atherosclerosis and the high risk of heart attack and stroke in patients with RA and other autoimmune diseases," said study author Virendra K. Gupta, M.D., of the University of Chicago.

The study will be presented Tuesday, May 19, at the American Heart Association's Arteriosclerosis, Thrombosis and Vascular Biology Conference 2009.

Gupta said the increased risk of heart attack and stroke in patients with RA has been known for years, but no one is sure why. The new study suggests that the blood clots that have been observed in the small blood vessels of the legs in patients with RA may be the cause.

The researchers found that patients with RA had 40 percent less blood flow to the leg muscles than the healthy controls. Despite this decreased blood flow, the patients with RA also had blood clots in their legs in 33 percent of the cases.

"This is a big clue that these stagnant pools of blood in the legs are leading to these blood clots and may be responsible for the accelerated atherosclerosis in these patients," Gupta said.

Although the study did not identify the mechanism that is causing the blood clots in the legs, another study Gupta conducted, which was published in the April 22 issue of the Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA), may have the answer.

The study was conducted by a team of researchers from the University of Bristol and the University of Oxford, and is published in Arthritis & Rheumatology, the official journal of the American College of Rheumatology (ACR).

Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic inflammatory condition that affects around 1% of the population. Additional cardiovascular events (CVD) account for the majority of excess mortality in RA patients. Both RA and CVD are thought to share several common genetic risk factors, however whether RA itself is associated with CVD risk is unclear. To investigate this further, a team of researchers from the University of Bristol and the University of Oxford conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of observational and genetic data from population-based studies.

The team performed a meta-analysis of 51 observational studies (39 case-control and 12 cohort) to assess the association between RA and CVD, and 45 studies to investigate the relationship between RA and individual CVD risk factors. They also conducted a meta-analysis of 45 genome-wide association studies (GWAS) to investigate the shared genetic architecture between RA and CVD.

The meta-analysis of observational data showed that RA was associated with a 23% increased risk of CVD and a 50% increased risk of ischemic heart disease, even after adjusting for confounding factors such as smoking and high blood pressure. The meta-analysis of GWAS data provided insights into potential common biological pathways between RA and CVD. The team identified 46 genetic loci that are associated with both RA and CVD, providing further evidence of their shared genetic architecture.

In this study, the team was able to examine the relationship between RA and CVD risk in different ethnic groups. They found that the association between RA and CVD risk was stronger in people of East Asian descent than in people of European descent. This could be due to differences in RA or CVD risk factors between these ethnic groups.

Overall, this research provides a better understanding of the link between RA and CVD. It suggests that RA is associated with an increased risk of CVD and ischemic heart disease, and that there may be shared genetic risk factors for both conditions. These findings could help to inform clinical practice and disease management strategies for RA patients. However, further research is needed to confirm these findings and to better understand the specific factors that contribute to the increased risk of CVD in RA patients.

This blog will discuss the causes, symptoms, and treatments of rheumatoid arthritis.

What causes rheumatoid arthritis?

The exact cause of rheumatoid arthritis is not known, but it is believed to be a result of a combination of genetic and environmental factors. RA is thought to be an autoimmune condition, which means that the immune system mistakenly attacks healthy tissue in the body. In the case of RA, the immune system attacks the lining of the synovium, which is the thin membrane that lines the joints and produces a fluid that lubricates them. This leads to inflammation, pain, and damage to the joints.

Who gets rheumatoid arthritis?

Anyone can develop rheumatoid arthritis, but it is more common in women than men. The typical age of onset is between 40 and 60 years old, but it can occur at any age. While the cause of RA is not known, it is believed to be a result of a combination of genetic and environmental factors. Some people may have a genetic predisposition to the condition, while others may be exposed to environmental triggers that can lead to the development of RA.

What are the symptoms of rheumatoid arthritis?

The symptoms of rheumatoid arthritis can vary from person to person, but there are some common symptoms to look out for. The most noticeable symptom of RA is pain and stiffness in the joints, particularly in the morning or after a period of inactivity. Other symptoms may include fatigue, fever, and weakness. RA can also cause swelling and deformity in the joints, and in severe cases, it can lead to damage to other organs such as the heart and lungs.

There is no cure for rheumatoid arthritis, but there are treatments that can help manage the symptoms and slow the progression of the disease. The main goal of treatment is to reduce inflammation and pain, and to prevent further joint damage. Treatment options may include medication, physical therapy, and surgery. The study analyzed data from 103,000 people from previous studies of the genetic underpinnings of Alzheimer’s and CVD. The team used a statistical technique called Mendelian randomization to determine whether there was a causal relationship between the two conditions.

The results showed that people with a higher genetic risk of Alzheimer’s disease have an increased genetic risk of CVD, and specifically early-onset CVD, which sets in before the age of 50. 

The team also found that people with a higher genetic risk of CVD also have a higher genetic risk of Alzheimer’s disease.

Dr. Tom Power, a National Institute for Health Research (NIHR) Senior Research Fellow at the University of Cambridge and the Cambridge Centre for Brain Medicine, said: “This work has allowed us to disentangle the relationship between these two common diseases for the first time. Our results suggest that by treating the shared genetic risk of these diseases, specifically targeting the immune system, we may be able to reduce the risk of developing both conditions.”

Dr. Andrew Leather, NIHR Academic Clinical Lecturer at the University of Cambridge and the Cambridge Centre for Brain Medicine, and Honorary Speciality Doctor at the Cambridge and Peterborough NHS Trust, added: “These findings are important as they may help us to better understand the different biological pathways that contribute to the development of Alzheimer’s disease and CVD, and could also lead to the development of new treatments for these diseases in the long run.”

Dr. Simon Ridley, Director of Research at Alzheimer’s Research UK, which part-funded the study, said: “It’s well known that there is a link between Alzheimer’s and heart disease, but exactly how they relate to each other has been unclear. The first study, led by Dr. Romain Le Nihouarn, looked at 1,246 healthy French men and women aged 50 to 79. It found that those with a common marker of inflammation called C-reactive protein (CRP) had a 48% higher risk of experiencing a heart attack or stroke than people with low CRP levels. The researchers also found that people with higher CRP levels were almost 70% less likely to have normal clot formation. 

The second study, led by Dr. Abdullah Al’Otaibi from King Saud University in Saudi Arabia, analyzed the blood of 1,000 apparently healthy young Saudi men when they arrived for their mandatory military service at the age of 18. The study showed that those with higher CRP levels were almost 30% more likely to have abnormal clot formation. 

The studies are the first to link high CRP levels with impaired clot formation in people with no history of CVD. Dr. Le Nihouarn commented: “Our findings suggest that CRP could be a marker for CVD risk that is independent of other established risk factors. This is important because CRP can be easily measured in clinical practice.” 

Dr. Al’Otaibi added: “Both studies support the hypothesis that CRP is not only a marker of inflammation and future CVD risk, but also indicates impaired clot formation before the development of CVD. This is very important for the prevention of CVD in the young population.” 

Dr. Farhan Ahmad, a consultant physician at the University of Aberdeen’s Cardiovascular Thrombotic Medicine Unit, said: “These interesting studies suggest that CRP may be an early marker of CVD in young people, and that this may be due to effects on the blood’s ability to clot. What is needed now is further research to confirm these findings, and to investigate the underlying mechanisms involved.” 

Dr. Kerr said: “These studies provide new insight into the relationship between inflammation, blood clot formation and CVD. They also highlight the important contribution that CRP may have in this process. CRP is a simple, inexpensive blood test that could therefore be used in primary care to help identify young people with an increased risk of CVD.” 

She added: “These studies provide hope that in the future it may be possible to identify young people with an increased risk of CVD many years before the disease develops. This could potentially allow the early introduction of lifestyle changes or medications to reduce that risk.”

For the study, the researchers followed 1,849 adults in Sweden who were diagnosed with RA between 1995 and 2006. All had blood tests and information on their cardiovascular health collected by the Swedish Heart Epidemiology Aging Research Study (SWEHAR). The researchers then followed the participants for a median of six years.

During this time, there were 184 new cases of CVD and 44 heart attacks. After adjusting for age and other heart disease risk factors, such as smoking, high blood pressure, and high cholesterol, the researchers found that RA patients had a 58 percent higher risk of developing CVD and a 37 percent higher risk of experiencing a heart attack.

The authors declare no competing interests.
This article is a direct response to a recent publication by van Heerden et al1 on the subject of the origin of the SARS-CoV-2 virus. We are writing as an international group of scientists with expertise in virology and virus evolution, many of whom have been studying SARS-CoV-2 and its evolution since the start of the pandemic.
Van Heerden et al.1 raise the possibility that SARS-CoV-2 may have been released from a frozen storage facility at the Wuhan Institute of Virology (WIV). This possibility is based on the observation that the earliest known SARS-CoV-2 sequences are nearly identical to the strains contained in the frozen WIV collection. While we agree that this possibility cannot be ruled out based on the available genomic data, we want to point out two important considerations that are addressed by other data and that are worth keeping in mind when evaluating this possibility: the stability of SARS-CoV-2 in frozen storage, and the nature of the WIV facility where the virus is believed to have been stored.
It is a fact that coronaviruses can be stored in frozen conditions for many years without degradation.2 A similar argument has been made in support of the zoonotic bat origin hypothesis for SARS-CoV-2, which states that the virus may have been introduced into the human population through the trade and consumption of frozen wild animals from the Huanan Seafood Market in Wuhan.3
The WIV facility where SARS-CoV-2 is believed to have been stored is not a standard biobank but rather a high-containment facility for infectious coronaviruses. The building is part of the Wuhan National Biosafety Laboratory,4 which is the only laboratory in China classified as P4 — the highest containment rating for laboratories that study the most dangerous pathogens. The laboratory has an elaborate and highly effective air filtration system to prevent particles from entering or leaving the facility, and all personnel entering the facility undergo additional health screening.5
We strongly believe that the available data do not support the release-of-virus-from-frozen-storage scenario. The fact that the earliest available sequences are nearly identical to the virus from the frozen collection could point to other scenarios, such as the virus being introduced into humans from a frozen collection or the frozen collection serving as a reservoir for the virus in humans, similar to the role of the bat population in the evolution of SARS-CoV-2.6

The usability gap refers to the difference between the amount of information the public wants and the amount of information that is actually used. This discrepancy is often due to the information not being presented in a useful form for the public. Here, useful refers to information that is brief, relevant, and clear. The usability gap in the context of science communication is not a new problem, but there has been a lack of quantitative data to fully understand and address this issue. The present study aims to fill this gap by investigating the usability of information about science, in the context of the novel coronavirus, among the general public. To do this, we present two studies. Study 1 asks participants to rate how clear, relevant, and brief various sources of information about the novel coronavirus are. Study 2 asks participants to rate how satisfied they are with their knowledge about the novel coronavirus, and then provides them with different types of information about the novel coronavirus. Finally, Study 2 examines how different types of information about the novel coronavirus impact knowledge satisfaction. The results from Study 1 show that participants find government websites to be the most useful source of information, while social media is the least useful. The results from Study 2 show that informational brochures are the most effective at increasing knowledge satisfaction. These results can help close the usability gap by guiding scientists and science communicators to the most effective ways to present information to the public. The aim of this research is to develop a better understanding of the importance of metocean information to small-scale fishers and to help improve the provision of marine weather forecasts and warnings. The perceived importance of metocean information was explored through a survey of small-scale fishers in South Africa (n = 14) and Australia (n = 18). The results showed that the participants in both countries considered metocean information to be important for their work. The specific conditions they perceived to be most important included large waves, strong winds, tides, and sea surface temperature. The participants also indicated that they would find current information most useful and that they preferred forecasts to be communicated to them at least a day in advance. This research highlights the importance to small-scale fishers of accurate, timely, and reliable metocean information and suggests ways in which this information can be communicated to fishers to help them make informed decisions and plan their work. It also highlights some of the challenges associated with standardizing meteorological data and products for use by small-scale fishers. Our results support previous research, which found that small-scale fishers are interested in marine weather forecasts and that improved and more reliable forecasts could be of great benefit to fishers. We also suggest that new forecasting products and services designed for small-scale fishers could help improve communication of marine weather forecasts, but further research is needed to identify the most effective ways of doing so. South Africans and New Zealanders are more likely to trust forecasts about the weather at sea than those about COVID-19, according to a new study from the University of Otago.

The research, which has just been published in the journal PLOS ONE, is the first to explore public trust in science and scientists in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic, and the first to examine how public trust in science and scientists may be influenced by trust in institutions.

Co-author Professor Mike Plomer, of the University of Otago’s Department of Geography, says trust in science and scientists is important because it can influence how people respond to scientific advice, particularly during a pandemic.

“Public trust has been found to be a significant determinant of how people respond to messages from scientists and other scientific institutions, such as whether they wear a mask, get vaccinated, or adhere to ‘zero-COVID’ policies,” Professor Plomer says.

For the study, 1011 South Africans and 1001 New Zealanders were asked to rate how much they trusted a range of different types of institution to provide accurate information about COVID-19. These institutions included scientific ones, such as scientists and universities, as well as non-scientific ones, such as the media, places of worship, and social media.

The researchers then asked the same participants to rate how much they trusted the same institutions to provide accurate information about weather forecasts at sea.

South Africans and New Zealanders were more likely to trust scientific institutions to provide accurate information about weather forecasts at sea than about COVID-19.

These forecasts are based on the latest numerical weather prediction models, and are supported by regular updates from local weather forecasters. The result is a service that is trusted by weather-sensitive activities such as commercial fishing, leisure sailing, and port management.

But the people who use these forecasts have long complained that the information is provided in a format that is not easy to interpret. The solution is to develop a new system that presents the forecast data in a format that is easy to understand, while still providing the detail required by experts. This is the goal of the SAIL project, in which researchers at the University of Otago are collaborating with South African partners to develop a novel, easy-to-use interface for presenting marine weather forecasts.

The SAIL project is a direct follow-on from the successful MARS project, which developed the first ever high-resolution regional ocean and atmosphere model for use over the South African marine environment. Running the MARS model at boundary forcing locations around the South African coastline allows the forecasted variables such as wind speed and direction, and sea-surface temperature, to be updated every 10 minutes. The hope is that these forecasts will be of great benefit to a variety of marine activities, such as commercial fishing, leisure sailing, port management, offshore oil and gas development, and renewable energy projects (such as offshore wind farms).

But at present, the forecasts are available only through specialist software and websites that are not easy for most users to access or understand. The SAIL project aims to address this problem by developing a user-friendly interface that can be used by a wide range of marine users, from commercial fishermen and port managers to sailors and offshore workers. The interface will provide easy access to forecast information in real-time, and will be adapted to different user groups so that it is easy to use under a variety of conditions.

These predictions are based on observations from a wide variety of sources. One important source is a network of weather stations operated by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) and other agencies. The locations of these stations are shown on the map at http://www.wunderground.com/resources/map/faq_weather_stations.asp. At each station, instruments measure properties of the atmosphere that affect the weather, such as temperature, barometric pressure, and the amount of water vapor in the air. The measurements made at these stations are used to forecast the weather.

The instruments at a weather station are usually housed in a small building, as shown in Figure 1. Wind direction is measured with a wind vane, and wind speed is measured with a cup anemometer, as shown in Figure 2. The amount of rain that falls is measured with a rain gauge, as shown in Figure 3. Temperature is measured with a mercury thermometer, as shown in Figure 4, or with a digital thermometer. Barometric pressure is measured with a mercury barometer, as shown in Figure 5. The barometer measures the weight of the air above the station. Since the air is a fluid, its weight depends on its depth, which depends on the barometric pressure. The barometer measures the pressure of the air at the surface of the Earth. This pressure is measured in units called inches of mercury (in. Hg). Barometric pressure affects weather by controlling weather disturbances, such as storms. The higher the barometric pressure, the more stable the air becomes. The lower the barometric pressure, the more unstable the air becomes. When air becomes unstable, it usually rises. As air rises, it cools, which causes water vapor in the air to condense into clouds, and sometimes causes precipitation.

The most famous example of this is probably the work of Thomas Malthus, who in 1789 wrote an essay, An Essay on the Principle of Population, in which he tried to determine if the population grows faster than the food supply, and if so, which one would win. He concluded that since food production grows at a logarithmic rate, while population grows at an exponential rate, food production will always win in the long run. This is because a logarithmic growth rate will always eventually be outpaced by an exponential growth rate, no matter how long it takes. In other words, population will keep growing, but food production will grow even faster, resulting in an ever-increasing surplus of food. Malthus, however, also concluded that there are other factors that will get in the way of this, such as disease and famine. In other words, he predicted that there would be mass deaths from hunger and disease, and that the human population would stop growing. This is known as Malthusian catastrophe. It has been proven that his predictions were wrong, and that we have consistently been able to produce enough food for the population we have. This does not mean that we should stop worrying about feeding the world, however. The world population has continued to grow exponentially, and it is still growing today. It is estimated that the world population will reach 9.8 billion by 2050. This will put tremendous pressure on our food production, and we will have to come up with new ways to produce food for so many people. This is where science comes in. We will have to use all the knowledge we have gained through scientific research to produce as much food as possible with as few resources as possible. In New Zealand, for example, the water is too cold for tropical storms, while South Africa is in the path of the majority of tropical cyclones in the Southern Hemisphere.

The researchers used a survey and a series of interviews to find out how people in the two countries use forecasts. The survey was administered to a random sample of 1000 people in each country. The survey asked questions like: How often do you use forecasts? Where do you get your forecasts? What type of forecasts are most useful to you? The interviews were with people who lived near the coast and who use marine resources as part of their jobs or for recreation. The interviews were recorded and then transcribed.

The survey showed that many more people in South Africa use marine forecasts than in New Zealand. About 53% of South Africans said they use marine forecasts at least once a month, compared to 31% of New Zealanders. Most South African users (60%) said they use forecasts every week or more often.

The survey also showed that South Africans are more likely to listen to forecasts than New Zealanders. Radio was by far the most popular source of forecasts in both countries. In South Africa, however, radio was the only source used by 41% of users, whereas in New Zealand, only 15% of users listened to radio as their only source.

The interviews revealed that many people in both countries use forecasts to plan their activities for the day. In New Zealand, for example, users often checked the forecast at night to find out if it was safe to go out in a boat the next day. In South Africa, many people use forecasts to plan their day at the beach. They wanted to know, for example, if the water would be safe to swim in and if it would be possible to go surfing.

The interviews also revealed that South Africans were using forecasts in more creative ways than New Zealanders. Some surfers in South Africa, for example, listen to forecasts that provide information on wave height and direction. With this information, they can identify how the weather will affect the waves and then choose whether they want to surf or not.

In New Zealand, where the water is too cold for most people to swim year-round, marine forecasts are often used for planning purposes further in the future. People who own boats, for example, might check the one- to two-week forecasts before planning a vacation. They wanted to know if it would be possible to sail to an island in the weather conditions expected during their vacation.

Scientists from 12 different countries conducted simultaneous measurements of clouds, precipitation, humidity, and winds at the TWP-CO site in Indonesia and the MANTRA-60 site in Kenya. The survey also found that people with lower levels of education, those with lower incomes and people who live in areas most at risk from extreme weather are more likely to be concerned about the impact of climate change on extreme weather.
The survey was carried out online in 10 languages across 20 countries and regions in Europe, Africa, Oceania and South America.
People in Italy, Portugal, and Spain were most concerned about the impact of climate change on weather (concern was highest in Italy, where 90% of respondents agreed that climate change is increasing the frequency and severity of extreme weather events).

“People are more likely to use a weather forecasting service if they can picture using it,” said study co-author Jeffrey R. Anderson of the University of Washington.

The researchers also found that people’s expectations about a service’s accuracy can be influenced by the accuracy of the service they’re currently using.

“People think that weather forecasting services currently available on smartphones are about 80 percent accurate,” Anderson said. “In the lab, however, we found that people believed the accuracy of the services they used was only 70 percent. As a result, they expected a new weather forecasting service to be less than 80 percent accurate.”

The study, by researchers from the University of Otago and the University of South Africa, is the first to look at weather-related behaviours and attitudes across countries in the Southern Hemisphere.

The researchers used data from the International Social Survey Programme, a global project that collects data on social issues across countries.

The survey was conducted in 2014/15 and involved 42,900 people from 40 countries. The results were published in the journal Weather, Climate and Society.

The researchers asked questions about people’s knowledge, attitudes, and behaviour when it comes to the weather, including whether they checked the weather forecast.

They also asked how important they thought the weather was to their everyday life, and how often they were likely to check the weather forecast.

After accounting for factors such as temperature, the researchers found South Africans were more likely to check the weather forecast compared with people from New Zealand, the Philippines, and Spain.

South Africans were also more likely to check the weather forecast on a daily basis compared with people from Australia, New Zealand, and the United States.

The researchers also asked about various weather-related behaviours, such as whether people would cancel outdoor plans if a severe weather warning was issued.

Overall, people from countries in the tropics were more likely to change their plans if a severe weather warning was issued.

However, after accounting for how often people were actually exposed to adverse weather, there were no differences between people from tropical and non-tropical countries.

For example, people from countries in the tropics may be exposed to severe weather several times a week, so they may have already taken the necessary precautions.

Compared with people from New Zealand, people from South Africa, the Philippines, and the United States were more likely to say they trusted weather information from the media.

However, there were no differences in trust in weather information from scientists or experts.

Overall, the study found there were more differences in weather-related knowledge, attitudes, and behaviours between countries in the Southern Hemisphere than there were between countries in different hemispheres (for example, between the United States and New Zealand).

This suggests that there are gaps in the understanding of people’s knowledge, attitudes, and behaviours across countries in the Southern Hemisphere.

samples.ref: Mokgwa wa go Kgatha tema wa go Sekaseka Ditsenogare tša Bolemi bjo Bohlale go Tlelaemete:
samples.hyp:
Case Studies From Ethiopia, Kenya, and Malawi

In this paper, we describe a methodology for assessing the climate resilience of development interventions in the agricultural sectors. The methodology was used to analyze 13 interventions from Ethiopia, Kenya, and Malawi, and was developed through an iterative process of applying the methodology to a number of case studies and making modifications based on lessons learned. The methodology consists of four main steps. First, project teams identify a list of climate-related hazards and describe the climate scenarios that, if realized, would move their intervention from climate-smart to climate-unsmart. Second, the likelihood of these climate scenarios occurring is assessed. Third, the potential impacts of these climate scenarios on the intervention are assessed. Fourth, the teams calculate the expected net benefit of their intervention as a “climate-smartness” score. As an example of how this is put into practice, we provide a case study of a participatory climate smartness assessment of a USAID-funded project in Ethiopia.

Keywords: climate change, resilience, adaptation, development, climate-smart

Agricultural development projects can enhance the resilience of agricultural systems to climate variability and change (Lipper et al., 2014), also known as climate-smart agriculture (Taylor et al., 2016). The concept of climate-smart agriculture has been defined in many ways, but generally includes three main pillars: (1) increasing productivity in a sustainable manner (i.e., producing more per unit of input), (2) increasing resilience to climate variability and change, and (3) mitigating or sequestering greenhouse gas emissions (Govaerts et al., 2015; Taylor et al., 2016). In this paper, we focus on developing a methodology for assessing the second pillar.

Climate variability and change can have a range of impacts on agricultural production (Ibp, 2014; Bryan et al., 2018). These impacts can be positive or negative, and can be concentrated in certain years or spread out over multiple seasons or years (Lipper et al., 2014). Thus, the resilience of an agricultural system can be defined as “the ability of a crop production system to withstand the impacts of climate variability and change, including drought, floods, and heat stress, and to rapidly recover from such shocks” (Lipper et al., 2014). Study: A Descriptive Epidemiological Study of Buruli Ulcer in Lushoto District, Tanzania

Buruli ulcer (BU) is a chronic, necrotic skin ulceration caused by the Gram-positive bacterium, Mycobacterium ulcerans. The disease is endemic in some parts of sub-Saharan Africa, where the number of cases has increased in recent years.

The study site was the Lushoto district of Tanga region in north-eastern Tanzania. The district has a population of approximately 170,000 people and is located 200 km from the capital Dar es Salaam. It is characterized by tropical climate and hilly terrain with altitudes ranging from 700–2000 m above sea level. The study population consisted of residents of the community of Kiborloni and Mlalo, two villages in the Lushoto district, with a total population of 35,000.

The primary objective of this study was to describe the epidemiological characteristics of BU in Lushoto, Tanzania. Secondary objectives included assessing the burden of BU in the community, determining the risk factors for BU infection, and describing the clinical features and evolution of the disease.

The study was conducted in two phases. Phase one was a descriptive epidemiological study. Qualitative data were collected through in-depth interviews with case-patients, focus group discussions with community members, and observations made during patient consultations at the health facilities. Quantitative data were collected through a community survey, case-control study, and a household survey. In phase two, a cohort of 75 individuals with BU and 75 matched controls were followed up for 12 months to determine the incidence of new BU lesions and to assess the natural history of the disease.

A total of 130 BU patients were enrolled in the case-control study. The majority of the patients were between the ages of 30 and 59 years (69.2%). One of the most promising strategies to build resilience along the CSA pillar 2 is the use of mulch in crop production systems. The use of mulch has many benefits for increasing the resilience of crop production systems, including reduced soil moisture loss, reduced erosion, and changed the soil temperature and soil physical properties. Moreover, the use of mulch can increase crop yield and farm income. The net benefit is that farmers can increase their income and at the same time have a low carbon footprint. The use of mulch can also increase the resilience of the food system as it can increase the availability of food and the income of smallholder farmers. This can increase the food security of the population. The use of mulch can also have negative side effects. The use of mulch can increase the risk of leaching of soil nutrients. If the farmer does not adjust the use of fertilizers according to the recommendations for mulch use, the loss of soil nutrients can be high. This can have a negative effect on crop production and farm income.

This study aimed to identify and prioritise objectives for CSA in the context of South African grain farming. The objectives were identified through a literature study and interviews with nine grain farmers who practise CSA. A pairwise comparison method was applied to prioritise the objectives, and the most important ones were identified as: 1. soil fertility management; 2. biodiversity management; 3. water management; 4. animal health and nutrition; 5. agronomic practices; 6. resiliency to climate variability and extremes; 7. soil and water conservation; 8. economic viability; 9. social acceptability; and 10. human health and well-being. The first four objectives focus on the health of cropland and livestock production systems, the next four on the health of the entire farm, and the last two on the health of people on the farm and in the wider community. The priorities reflect a holistic view of health on the farm, as well as the fact that CSA is a management system that integrates the natural and social sciences to provide a sustainable ecological, economic, social and cultural service. The prioritisation process was quick and simple, making it easy to use, even by farmers with no formal education or access to the internet. However, the limitations of the pairwise comparison method, such as the potential to rank objectives by accident rather than design and the fact that it is based only on relative rather than absolute values, could be addressed by using a more sophisticated method in future that helps to avoid such pitfalls.

samples.hyp:
The climate-smartness of an intervention is assessed through the application of a multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) that considers three criteria: (1) climate change adaptation, (2) climate change mitigation, and (3) agricultural productivity. The protocol describes a participatory process for identifying criteria, sub-criteria, and data collection methods and emphasizes the need for explicit weighting of criteria. The protocol was applied to evaluate the climate-smartness of 12 interventions in rice and maize production in The Philippines. The interventions were implemented in 2016 and 2017 as part of a multi-site research on climate-smart agriculture. The results showed the potential of the protocol to discriminate between interventions with different climate-smartness characteristics and provide insights into what makes an intervention more or less climate-smart. Interventions with a more climate change adaptation focus, such as providing farm inputs in rice and maize production, were found to be less climate-smart when compared to interventions with a focus on both adaptation and mitigation such as expanding crop diversity or introducing nitrogen-fixing cover crops in a rice-maize-fish agro-ecosystem. The protocol provided a quantitative assessment of the climate-smartness of interventions that can be used to inform decision and policy makers towards the implementation of climate-smart interventions in agricultural systems.

samples.src: New monitoring techniques help scientists and farmers prepare for climate change
samples.ref: Mekgwa ye meswa ya tlhokomedišišo e thuša bašomi ba tša mahlale le balemi go itokišetša phetogo
samples.hyp:
A new technique for monitoring soil moisture could help farmers prepare for climate change, according to new research published in Agricultural and Environmental Letters. This technique, which uses cosmic-ray neutrons to scan soil moisture in fields, could allow farmers to plan their irrigation schedules and select the most suitable crop varieties for their fields, based on the amount of water their soil needs. The new research shows that this technique can accurately predict the amount of water needed by a crop, based on the moisture content in the top 30 centimeters of soil.

Agricultural production will need to increase by 70% to feed a global population of 10 billion by 2050, while at the same time coping with the challenges brought on by climate change. The global demand for food is growing and shifting as populations urbanize and change their diets, and climate change is predicted to make some areas less suitable for growing certain crops. Thus, new techniques that can help farmers prepare for these challenges are essential.

Soil moisture is a critical factor for crop growth, and understanding the amount of water in the soil is a key component of managing farmland in water-limited regions. In the new research, a team of scientists led by the U.S. Department of Energy’s Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory used the cosmic-ray neutron scanning technique to monitor soil moisture in six fields in California’s Central Valley and in three fields in Washington state. The technique provides information on the moisture content of the soil down to a depth of 1.5 meters.

The researchers found that the amount of water a crop needs over its entire growing season can be reliably predicted using this technique and a satellite-based vegetation index. This prediction was accurate within 25 mm of measured soil moisture in the top 30 centimeters of soil, the layer in which most plant roots grow. The researchers also found that the cosmic-ray neutron sensor responded to changes in soil moisture in the top 60 centimeters of soil within 3–4 days, which is fast enough to be used for monitoring daily agricultural water use.
