This is thanks to a new set of tools that help measure how soil health, water management, and even crop yields are affected by climate change.

The tools were developed by scientists at the International Center for Tropical Agriculture (CIAT) and the Alliance of Global Sustainability (AGS) based at the University of Tokyo. They are now available online for free at https://climate-smart-agriculture.org/impacts

The tools help farmers, agricultural advisors, and researchers answer one simple question: “How effective are our climate-smart agriculture (CSA) options in reducing the impacts of climate change?”

The new platform allows CSA users and researchers to upload their own data and use a user-friendly interface to explore how different factors are influenced by climate smart agriculture practices.

The tool allows users to explore and visualize four key indicators: soil health, water management, crop yields, and economic resilience.

Each indicator is made up of several components. For example, soil health considers factors such as soil organic carbon, soil aggregate stability, and available soil water holding capacity. These indicators help assess how well specific CSA practices can increase soil health compared to business as usual practices. They also help identify which CSA practices are best for achieving better soil health.

Similarly, the other indicators look at how various CSA practices can help adapt to climate change.

The tool also allows users to look at the interplay between different factors. For example, it can show how better soil organic carbon (a component of soil health) can also help sequester more carbon, meaning it can help remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.

To build the platform, scientists at CIAT and AGS developed a unique dataset that includes 5000 observations from 16 sites across Tanzania. This dataset is the largest of its kind for the country and it is regularly updated with new data. It includes a range of information such as weather data, soil analysis, and crop yields.

This dataset is part of a larger effort to develop and test a universal approach for measuring the impacts of climate smart agriculture. This work is part of a broader effort to develop much-needed evidence on the effectiveness of climate smart agriculture.

“Measuring the impact of these practices has so far been difficult,” says Diogo Sinzig, one of the scientists that developed the tool. “But this tool provides an important step forward by allowing us to look at how different factors influence each other,” he adds.

The new platform is also a proof of concept that user-generated data can help inform climate smart agriculture policies and investments.

The project works at the watershed level, reforests degraded land, promotes conservation agriculture, and helps farmers access new markets.

The project is part of a larger effort by IFAD to help small-scale farmers cope with climate change while at the same time contributing to the effort to mitigate climate change.

Photo: C. Kozar, CIAT

International Climate Week is an annual event that takes place every February. The event is an opportunity to highlight the urgent need for climate action, and to showcase how climate change is already affecting our world, and what we can do about it. This year’s event ran from the 3rd to the 14th of February and had the theme of ‘Climate Smart Agriculture’.

The International Climate Week is organized by the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), the UN Development Programme (UNDP), and Climate Analytics. These organizations selected 10 countries from around the world to feature as case studies, and one of the selected countries was Colombia.

The Climate Smart Agriculture (CSA) approach is an agriculture practice that aims to increase productivity, while also building resilience to climate change. It does this through three pillars: (1) productivity, (2) sustainability, and (3) adaptation. By increasing productivity, smallholder farmers will have more food to eat, and can earn more money by selling a surplus. CSA also includes activities that help farmers better plan for the future under a changing climate. For example, having access to weather data and making decisions about when to plant based on that data. This helps farmers adapt to the changing weather patterns that they are experiencing.

The International Climate Week aims to showcase how climate change is affecting our world, and what we can do about it. Climate change is causing temperatures to rise, and weather patterns to change. This can make it difficult for farmers to decide the best time to plant their crops. If they plant too early, their crops might drown in a flood. If they plant too late, their crops won’t have enough water to grow. This can cause food shortages and even hunger. But by using the CSA approach, farmers can better adapt to the changing weather and have enough food to eat.

These changes have already led to a shorter rainy season, especially in the Arusha and Manyara regions, where farmers rely on rain-fed agriculture.

The goal of this study was to assess farmers’ perceptions of the effects of climate change on crop productivity in Arusha and Manyara regions of Tanzania.

This study used a cross-sectional survey design to collect data from 500 randomly selected households from each of the two regions. A pre-tested semi-structured questionnaire was used to collect information on household demographics, farming activities, perceptions, and measures taken to mitigate the impact of climate change on crop productivity.

Data were analyzed using both descriptive statistics to identify the characteristics of the study participants and infer their perceptions, and multivariate statistical techniques to identify factors influencing their perceptions.

A total of 17 factors were identified, 14 of which were found to have a significant influence on the perceptions of climate change. These were crop drought stress, soil erosion, heavy rainfall, high temperature, crop pests and diseases, shortage of farm labor, flooding, low soil fertility, crop yield and quality reduction, financial limitations, agricultural extension, competing land use, inadequate agricultural credit, agricultural research, and farm size.

The study results showed that as crop drought stress, heavy rainfall, high temperature, and low soil fertility increase, farmers’ perceptions of the impact of climate change on crop productivity also increase.

Farmers in the study generally agreed that climate change is happening and is reducing crop productivity, although they did not have accurate knowledge about its underlying causes. The study, therefore, recommends increasing public awareness about climate change, promoting research in the field, and providing agricultural extension services to help farmers better adapt to climate change.

The study also recommends that policies be developed to promote the use of weather-index insurance and climate-smart agriculture practices, such as crop diversification, improved soil management, and water harvesting to help farmers adapt to climate change and increase crop productivity.

A new study from Sweden shows that climate-smart agriculture can help small-scale farmers in Tanzania to adapt to climate change, increase their crop yields, and reduce greenhouse gas emissions from agricultural land. The study was led by Uppsala University’s Professor Benjamin Amey and involved researchers from the International Crops Research Institute for the Semi-Arid Tropics (ICRISAT) in Tanzania and India.

The climate in Tanzania is expected to become warmer and drier in the future. This will impact the country’s small-scale farmers, who are already operating in a low-resource context with poor access to knowledge, information, and agricultural technology. Therefore, the farmers need to be supported to adapt to these changes and implement agricultural practices that can increase food security and reduce greenhouse gas emissions from agricultural land.

In the study, the researchers focused on the Lushoto district in Tanzania’s northern Kilimanjaro region. The researchers developed an approach that involved three steps. First, they conducted 25 key informant interviews and 40 semi-structured interviews with local stakeholders to identify challenges and opportunities for climate smart agriculture in the area. Second, they used household survey data from a larger study to characterize the farmers and the context. Third, the researchers used the two datasets to apply a method called KONDA to analyze which climate smart agriculture options the farmers would likely implement in the future.

“KONDA is short for Knowledge Elicitation using Mental Imagery and Delphi Domain Analysis. The method was developed by Professor Roy Bhui at Uppsala University,” says Benjamin Amey, an Associate Professor at the Department of Peace and Conflict Research.

The project, “Adaptation in Tanzania through Scaling Up Climate-Smart Agriculture” (ATSA), is a five-year initiative that aims to improve food security and reduce greenhouse gas emissions. 

“We are working to increase climate-smart agriculture practices, and to provide decision-makers with the information they need to implement these practices,” says Dr. Margaret Hoeschle, a Cornell University scientist and the project’s principal investigator. 

Climate-smart agriculture is a broad concept that includes practices, such as conservation agriculture, precision agriculture, and agroforestry, which contribute to food security, increased farm income, and climate change adaptation and mitigation. 

To help implement these practices, the ATSA project has trained “climate-smart agriculture facilitators.” These facilitators, 33 in total, work with farmers to help them transition to climate-smart agriculture practices. 

The facilitators don’t just tell farmers about climate-smart agriculture practices; they also help create a learning environment where farmers can share their knowledge and experiences. 

“ATSA has supported 19,000 smallholder farmers in Tanzania to adopt climate-smart agriculture practices,” says Dr. Hoeschle. 

The project has also trained “upscaling facilitators,” 25 in total. Upscaling facilitators help the climate-smart agriculture facilitators do their work, and they also help other projects want to adopt the ATSA approach. 

The project has just ended its first phase and is now in the second phase. The second phase will build on the first phase and will continue to support the upscaling of climate-smart agriculture in Tanzania.

This is surprising given that alien species are often the agents of disease introduction and spread. In this study, we examine the introduction of disease organisms as invasive alien species using three case studies: the introduction of the European brown hare (Lepus europaeus) and the American brown hare (Lepus americanus) to Australia, the introduction of the Mediterranean fruit fly (Ceratitis capitata) to Africa, and the re-introduction of smallpox virus (variola virus) to Africa. We apply a newly developed framework that classifies alien species as invasive according to their negative impact on native biota and then identifies those species that are also disease agents. For the three case studies, we find that the introduction and spread of the disease were a direct consequence of the introduction and spread of the alien species, i.e., the alien species were also the disease organism. We conclude that the introduction and spread of alien species should be viewed as a potential health threat and highlight the need for closer collaboration between invasion scientists and disease scientists.

The study, published today in Nature Communications, used a combination of historical and modern data to reconstruct the impact of human activities on global ecosystems. 

“We wanted to disentangle the impact of pre-industrial humans from the effects of post-industrial modern human activities,” said Dr. Luke Baker from the University of Exeter. “To do this, we needed a global perspective as the movement of people and ideas is not restricted by national borders.”

Using historical data spanning the last 200 years, the team developed a new method to remove the contemporary noise from the data, allowing them to examine ecological changes on a global scale over the last 200 years. 

The results showed that the area occupied by wild terrestrial plants and animals, birds, and fish, has declined by 23%, 28% and 17% respectively over the last 50 years. 

The top four countries contributing to the overall loss in habitat were the USA, Brazil, Russia and China. 

The analysis also revealed that the largest decline in habitat occurred in Europe, at almost 60% since 1900. 

Co-author Professor William Sutherland, from the University of Cambridge, said: “These losses are occurring despite the implementation of many global environmental policies and many countries developing extensive systems of nature conservation. It is clear that we need to redouble our efforts to ensure that conservation science is used to its full potential.”

Dr. Baker added: “Our analysis shows that, in order to protect species and ecosystems, we need to look beyond international policy and national conservation strategies and focus on the drivers of global change, such as specific sectors of the global economy.”

in pediatric population: A modified protocol

Odontogenic Keratocyst (OKC) is a relatively rare, non-neoplastic, cystic lesion derived from the oral epithelium that can occur at any age. It shows high recurrence rate if not treated adequately. We aimed to discuss the management of OKC in pediatric population with an evidence based surgical algorithm.


Odontogenic Keratocyst (OKC) is a relatively rare, non-neoplastic, cystic lesion derived from the oral epithelium that can occur at any age. It shows high recurrence rate if not treated adequately. We aimed to discuss the management of OKC in pediatric population with an evidence based surgical algorithm.


Twenty seven patients who met the inclusion criteria and gave consent to be part of the study population were included. Inclusion criteria were age between 8 and 18 years, clinical diagnosis of OKC and radiological evidence of cystic lesion with well defined radiolucency in the region of mandibular canal. Patients with a history of orthognathic surgery, chronic steroid use, or any other condition that might effect wound healing were excluded.

Data Collection

The data was collected by reviewing medical history, clinical examination and radiographic assessment. The study was approved by the institutional review board and written informed consent was obtained from patients or guardians.

Treatment modalities

All patients were treated by the same surgical team and the treatment was performed in two phases: 
Phase I: Initial corticosteroid injection
Phase II: Surgical procedure

Surgical procedure

Intralesional corticosteroid injection was performed under general anesthesia in all patients. Surgical excision was performed under general anesthesia; the cyst was excised with a 2 mm normal mucosa margin. The surgical defect was filled with a free autogenous bone graft covered with a vascularized flap (mucoperiosteal flap).

Follow up

The follow up started one week after the surgical procedure and continued for 3, 6, 9 and 12 months. Clinical photographs were obtained and orthopantomox ray was taken during follow up appointments.

Statistical Analysis

Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS software. Qualitative data were presented as frequency tables and relative frequency. Quantitative data were presented as mean ± standard deviation or median and interquartile range, if not normal, and range for minimum and maximum values. Categorical data were analyzed using chi-square test or Fischer's exact test, when appropriate. Continuous data were compared using independent sample T

samples.src: The effective management of odontogenic keratocyst (OKC) remains a subject of interest and confusion in the Oral and Maxillofacial surgery literature.
samples.ref: Kalafo ya maleba ya odontogenic keratocyst (OKC) ke hlogopoledišano ye e gogago šedi ka mehla ebile e bakago tlhakatlhakano go dingwalo tša mabapi le karo ye e dirwago Leganong le Sefahlogong.
samples.hyp:
Although it is the most common cystic lesion of the jaw, accounting for 3% of all jaw lesions, the management of OKC is more challenging than that of other more common jaw lesions, such as dentigerous cysts and radicular cysts. While the majority of OKC behave in a benign fashion, they can be aggressive in approximately 1/3 of cases with a high rate of recurrence even after surgical treatment and pursuit of a complete surgical margin. 
The recent literature suggests several factors that may be associated with aggressive behavior of OKC. These include younger age, larger size at presentation, ankylosis of the temporomandibular joint, and the presence of multiple OKCs. While younger age and larger size at presentation are not unique to OKC and are also associated with more aggressive behavior in other odontogenic lesions such as dentigerous cysts and ameloblastomas, the association of aggressive behavior with ankylosis of the temporomandibular joint and the presence of multiple OKCs has only been described with OKC. 
The management of OKC has been described in the literature as enigmatic, with various modalities of treatment and poor reproducibility of most of these modalities. Complete surgical removal with 2 mm surgical margin is considered to be the standard of care for OKC. However, the reported recurrence rate after complete surgical removal with 2 mm surgical margin is between 46-64%. This would suggest that complete surgical removal with 2 mm margin is not adequate and a more conservative margin may need to be considered. 
The reported high recurrence rate of OKC after complete surgical removal suggests that the current diagnostic and management approach to OKC is not adequate. While some authors have suggested that complete surgical removal with 3 mm margin is the treatment of choice for OKC, given the poor reproducibility of the current diagnostic modalities and the lack of a standard surgical margin associated with low recurrence and high cure rates, a more conservative management approach may be warranted. We propose a management algorithm for OKC that takes into account the current diagnostic and surgical management approach and suggest some modifications that may be considered to improve the management of OKC.
Keywords: odontogenic keratocyst; management; algorithm

The literature describes the odontogenic keratocyst as a cystic lesion that shows aggressive behavior and has a high recurrence rate. Therefore, surgical excision is considered the best treatment option. However, the lesion shows a high rate of intralesional recurrences even after surgical margins were considered free of lesion. The reason for these recurrences is most likely multifactorial and might be related to incomplete surgical margins, tumor cells left behind, or a true recurrence of the lesion because of retained cystic fluid. In the literature, different treatment options such as intralesional bleomycin, cryosurgery, and irradiation are described with controversial results. The purpose of this review is to summarize the current treatment options and give an overview of current research to help clinicians make appropriate treatment decisions for their patients. In addition, recommendations for future studies are outlined.

The search was conducted according to a specific time frame, in order to avoid an overlapping meta-analysis. The clinical characteristics, treatment, and recurrence of odontogenic keratocyst were extracted from the studies and data were managed using the Comprehensive Meta-Analysis Version 2 software. After 19 articles were identified, only 7 met the inclusion criteria. In the selected studies, the mean age of the patients was 28.5 years old, and the male to female ratio was 1.58. Radiotherapy was identified as a significant source of misclassification in the literature; therefore, we created two separate algorithms, one for radiotherapy positive and the other for radiotherapy negative patients. The positive predictive value of radiotherapy in this series was 100%, suggesting a nearly perfect relationship between radiotherapy and aggressive behavior. Our algorithm recommended en bloc resection for radiotherapy positive patients, and selected cases of radiotherapy negative patients with clinical and radiographic evidence of aggression. Recurrence rate for patients who underwent en bloc resection was 25.0%, compared to 80.0% in patients who underwent marginal resection. Marginal resection was recommended for asymptomatic, small sized, non-aggressive odontogenic keratocyst.

samples.hyp:
TMD

A click here and a pop there, and the work is done.

Researchers have identified the biological processes behind the progression of a form of jaw disease that causes pain and disability, and have identified potential drug targets in a key enzyme to block the disease’s progression.

In a new study published online in the journal Science Signaling, researchers working in the laboratory of senior author Dr. Min Dai, associate professor at NYU Rory Meyers College of Nursing, identify the signaling pathways — a series of biochemical reactions that convert chemical signals from outside the cell into signals inside — that drive the progression of temporomandibular joint disorder, a form of arthritis in the jaw that affects about 10 million Americans. The researchers also identify the enzyme cathepsin S as a potential drug target to block the disease’s progression.

The study’s findings are significant because they reveal a new therapeutic strategy to block the disease’s progression, a process that until now has been difficult to treat. With these findings, researchers now have potential drug targets to treat the disorder, which has previously had no known treatment.

“With these findings, we have opened the door to new targets for drug development to treat this painful and disabling disease,” says study lead author Dr. Lei Li, a doctoral student in nursing at NYU Rory Meyers College of Nursing.

TMD, which is characterized by pain and limited jaw movement, is one of the most common musculoskeletal disorders. The condition gets its name from the temporomandibular joint, the hinge-like joint connecting the lower jaw to the skull, which allows humans to chew and talk. TMD sufferers often experience pain when they try to chew, and the condition can lead to difficulty speaking, disfigurement of the lower jaw, and headaches and pain in the neck and ear.

Researchers know that TMD is caused by inflammation in the joint, which is linked to tissue degeneration. Cathepsins, a type of enzyme, are known to be involved in tissue degradation. Researchers have previously suspected that cathepsins may be involved in the inflammation that leads to tissue degeneration in TMD, but no one had identified this until now. In the new study, the researchers verified that cathepsin S plays an important role in the inflammation process.

The researchers’ experiments also revealed that inhibiting cathepsin S reduces inflammation and prevents the degradation of collagen in the joints of mice, a key finding that suggests the enzyme is a potential drug target to block the disease’s progression.

The results could help doctors improve the prognosis of patients with this disease.

The disease originates in the cells of the dental root and is characterized by a cystic lesion and a tumor-like growth.
It is not very common, affecting only 0.13% of people who went to a dental clinic to treat a jaw pain.
The average age of the patients was 56 years.

The researchers, led by Prof. Nils-Cristian Gingura of the University of Puerto Rico School of Dental Medicine, first searched for case reports and case series of OKC published between 1950 and June 2021. Then, using a pro forma table designed by the International Task Force on OKC, they combined the findings of these studies to create a large dataset.

This dataset included 2,154 patients, mostly from Europe and Asia, but also from North and South America, Australia, and Africa.

The most consistent finding was that the disease was diagnosed and treated at an advanced stage, which is the reason for a poor prognosis.

To address this problem, the researchers developed a new set of criteria that doctors can use to identify patients who need further investigation. Their results showed that 1,343 patients (62%) fulfilled these criteria.

The second part of the new criteria is that the cystic lesion must be treated as a surgical procedure. The researchers then investigated the different ways in which the cystic lesion was treated and found that it was most often removed with a scalpel or laser and sometimes with the help of a biological agent.

Finally, the third and most important part of the new set of criteria is that after the removal of the cystic lesion, the patient must be treated with an odontogenic injury. This is a lesion that is caused by the root of a tooth and is characterized by a tumor-like growth.

The researchers found that 1,157 out of 1,343 patients (86%) met these criteria. They also found that the average age of these patients was 59 years, which is lower than the average age of patients who were diagnosed and treated at an advanced stage.

The authors suggest that this may be due to the fact that OKC is not a single disease, but a group of conditions that have similar symptoms.

The authors reviewed the medical literature on OKC and found 14 studies that met their criteria. Eleven studies looked at the effectiveness of oral medications, and three studies looked at the effectiveness of eye drops.

The authors found that allopurinol was the most effective oral medication. Allopurinol reduces the production of uric acid by the body. About 70% of people with OKC have high uric acid levels.

However, allopurinol can cause side effects, especially in people who have kidney disease or heart failure. The most common side effect is skin rash, and a small number of people have developed serious liver problems while taking allopurinol.

The authors also found that dipyridamole and probenecid were effective in some studies, but not in others. The results of the studies using eye drops were not consistent. More research is needed to determine which treatments are most effective for OKC.

The authors advise that people with OKC should try to control their condition with oral medications, since eye drops can cause side effects, such as high blood pressure and changes in heart rate. However, eye drops may be necessary for some people if they are not able to take oral medications or if they do not respond to oral treatment.

They used this information to identify 3 key themes: 1) the importance of early identification of patients at risk of OKC, 2) the importance of multidisciplinary teams, and 3) the importance of a positive hospital culture around OKC.


The findings of this review highlight the importance of a positive hospital culture in preventing and managing OKC. The development of such a culture is a key recommendation from our review and is in line with the new National Patient Safety Policy in Scotland, which states that organisations should work towards creating “a positive safety culture that fosters a willingness to learn from errors, reporting of errors openly, and local systems that reliably report adverse events.”


The review also highlights the importance of early multidisciplinary team involvement in managing OKC. Our review found that early multidisciplinary team meetings were important in the identification of patients at risk of OKC, and the management of these patients. Multidisciplinary team meetings were reported to improve communication, co-ordination of care, identification of patients at risk of pressure ulcers and prevention of pressure ulcers. The frequency of multidisciplinary meetings was reported as either monthly or weekly. However, it was not clear which was more effective. As such, the authors recommend monthly multidisciplinary meetings, as this avoids meeting fatigue and allows for discussion of all patients. If this is not possible, then daily meetings for patients at high risk of developing OKC may be beneficial.


This review found that prevention of OKC was most effective when healthcare professionals had a positive culture of patient care. This was defined as a culture where healthcare professionals felt empowered to make decisions in the best interest of the patient, and to provide the highest standard of care possible. This included a strong emphasis on evidence-based practice, and a focus on shared decision making and goal setting with patients. The authors suggest that implementing strategies, which promote a positive culture, such as bundles and checklists, is not enough on its own to prevent OKC. Instead, these strategies should be implemented as part of a wider cultural change that promotes a positive and supportive team environment and learning from errors, in order to improve safety and quality of patient care.

Keywords: SARS-CoV-2; SARSr-CoV; MERS-CoV; vaccine; molecular epitope; artificial intelligence; machine learning.

The current COVID-19 pandemic is caused by a β-coronavirus named SARS-CoV-2. At present, there is no available vaccine against this virus. Here, we have predicted the molecular epitopes of SARS-CoV-2, MERS-CoV and SARSr-CoV using the method of molecular epitope prediction, human HLA class I and class II binding, and human immune repertoire. The binding affinity of the predicted epitopes was validated using a machine learning approach. To support the selection of candidate epitopes for vaccine design, we compared the human immune repertoire coverage of the three viruses. This analysis can be used to select the most promising candidate epitopes for vaccine design. Our results provide a comprehensive set of candidate epitopes that cover the majority of the human immune repertoire and have a high binding affinity for the development of a synthetic multivalent vaccine against SARS-CoV-2, MERS-CoV and SARSr-CoV.

The human HLA-A02 molecule was used as the restriction allele. The binding repertoires of 124 HCoV-NCP epitopes to HLA-A02 were predicted by using a combination of in silico stabilization energy prediction, peptide binding pocket volume analysis, and binding affinity estimation by a neural network. The in silico stabilization energy of the peptide-HLA complex was estimated by using a neural network that was trained by a set of 24,126 binding and 24,127 non-binding peptide sequences. The binding affinity of each peptide to HLA-A02 was estimated by a backpropagation neural network trained by the binding affinities (IC50 values) of 204 HLA-A02-binding peptides. The binding pocket volume of each peptide was calculated by a computer program that we have previously established. Based on these three criteria, 43 HCoV-NCP peptides were determined as potential HLA-A02-restricted epitopes, among which are 21 M, 11 J2, 10 J1, and 1 J3 epitopes. Covering all 124 epitopes, 102 of them were obtained from the M protein, 11 from the S protein, 10 from the N protein, 1 from the ORF3a protein.

samples.ref: Didirišwa le Mokgwa
samples.hyp:
A total of 10 published articles were identified from an electronic search of PubMed using the search terms “neither/nor” and “polysomnography” in various combinations. These articles were selected to represent publications from the past 65 years that evaluated the use of polysomnography in patients with narcolepsy.

Results
Of the 10 selected articles, 6 demonstrated the use of polysomnography in the evaluation of patients with narcolepsy. All 6 articles published between 1956 and 2009 described polysomnography as a useful tool in the diagnosis of narcolepsy. In the past 10 years, 4 articles were published that evaluated new polysomnography scoring criteria for the diagnosis of narcolepsy. The ability of polysomnography to detect sleep-related motor events in patients with narcolepsy was also examined in 3 of the selected articles. Two of these articles evaluated the efficacy of different polysomnography montages in the detection of sleep-related motor events in patients with narcolepsy. The apnea-hypopnea index and the number of arousals were demonstrated to be lower in patients with narcolepsy than in normal controls. The REM sleep time was significantly increased in patients with narcolepsy when compared with controls. Video polysomnography was reported to be useful in the diagnosis of narcolepsy in 1 of the selected articles. No articles were found to examine the usefulness of polysomnography in the evaluation of idiopathic hypersomnia.

and treatments

The first step in developing treatments and vaccines against a novel virus is to understand its genetic instructions. But with a virus like SARS-CoV-2 — which has only been around for a year — it can be hard to do this, since there’s not enough time to study it in large numbers of people. Instead, scientists can look at how it’s related to other viruses, like SARS-CoV-1, which caused the outbreak in 2003, and MERS, which emerged in 2012. These viruses all came from the same family tree: a group of viruses called beta-coronaviruses, or betacoronaviruses. By comparing the genes of these three viruses, scientists can get an idea of what the SARS-CoV-2 genome looks like. This comparison is called a phylogenetic analysis.

Phylogenetic analyses can help scientists do two things: they can estimate when and where the virus may have first emerged, and they can help scientists zero in on parts of the virus that could be especially important for developing treatments and vaccines. That’s because different viruses within a family have some parts of their genomes in common. For example, the SARS-CoV-1 and SARS-CoV-2 viruses both have three spike proteins, called S, M, and N. These proteins help the virus attach to human cells, so targeting them with a treatment or a vaccine could block infection. By comparing the genes that code for these proteins in the three viruses, scientists can look for regions where the viruses are most different. These regions are strong candidates for vaccine development and testing. They are also targets for treatment development, since blocking them could prevent the virus from infecting cells.

This study aimed to summarize the current understanding of the prevalence, mechanisms, and management of arrhythmias in COVID-19 patients. A systematic search was conducted in seven databases until March 31, 2020, with an update until July 31, 2020. The study selection was based on the inclusion and exclusion criteria. Quality assessment and data extraction were performed for all included studies. A total of 49 articles were included in this study, with 35, 30, 23, and 21 articles before, at, after discharge, and in mortal patients, respectively. The prevalence of arrhythmia was 30.2% (95% confidence interval (CI): 20.9-39.5%). Supraventricular rhythm disorders were the most common arrhythmias, while atrial fibrillation was the most prevalent. Brugada syndrome and long QT syndrome were also relatively common. In patients who received mechanical ventilation, the prevalence of arrhythmia was higher than that in patients who did not receive mechanical ventilation. Cardiac death was the main cause of mortality in patients with arrhythmia. Antiarrhythmic drugs should be used as a last choice due to their potential proarrhythmic effects. Early initiation of antiarrhythmic drugs may increase the risk of new-onset atrial fibrillation. Glucocorticoids and ACEI/ARB may increase the risk of arrhythmia. This will be done by translating the current understanding of the pathophysiology of COVID-19 into a potential diagnostic algorithm that can be used to guide the management of these patients.

The pathophysiology of COVID-19 has been extensively described as a multi-organ disease with a strong inflammatory component and potential for a hypercoagulable state. The most commonly described manifestation is respiratory in nature, however, a wide variety of cardiac complications have been reported, ranging from arrhythmias to acute coronary syndrome and even heart failure. The exact incidence of these cardiac complications is unknown, but it has been estimated that up to 2% of patients with COVID-19 may develop acute coronary syndrome, and that 20-30% may develop arrhythmias. Arrhythmias described in these patients include supraventricular rhythms (SVT), ventricular tachycardia (VT), and ventricular fibrillation (VF), with the former being the most common. These arrhythmias may occur in the context of severe COVID-19 infection, or acute coronary syndrome, and can lead to patients collapsing and sudden cardiac death. It has been postulated that the inflammatory component and the hypercoagulable state associated with COVID-19 may explain the occurrence of these arrhythmias. However, the underlying mechanism remains unknown, and the question whether the incidence of these arrhythmias is higher than expected in a young population remains unanswered.

We aimed to develop and validate a deep learning system for detecting and grading the severity of atrial fibrillation (AF) using short single-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) recordings. A deep learning model was trained and validated on generalizable 2-min ECG recordings from 220,025 patients (99,949 with AF) from 10 countries for detecting AF, and an additional 20,648 patients from 6 countries for determining AF burden and its severity. Performance was evaluated internally on unseen notes from the same cohorts and externally on 25,448 patients (13,345 with AF) from 7 countries in two independent datasets. The deep learning model performed better than physicians (sensitivity 0·98, specificity 0·79) in detecting AF, and identified patients with high AF burden in patients with normal rhythm (C-statistic 0·81). The model also differentiated between AF burden scores of patients receiving antiarrhythmic therapy (p<0·0001). The model is easily integrated into mobile technology for real-time AF detection. Our deep learning model has the potential to be a simple and inexpensive tool for detection and guidance of therapy in resource-limited settings.

The condition is not unique to the virus, but is more common in the elderly and those with existing heart conditions. 

It can be fatal if not treated, but there are ways to stop it before it becomes life-threatening. 

Dr. Luis Capriles is an electrophysiologist at the University of Utah Hospital, and he says the pandemic has caused a 20 to 30 percent increase in patients with these conditions. 

“Patients that have these arrhythmias, they’re coming in with shortness of breath, palpitations, sometimes they have no symptoms, but they’re coming in because they feel like their heart is not working right,” Capriles said. 

Capriles says patients who have a history of heart issues, chest pain, or heart failure are the most likely to develop these irregular heartbeats. 

He says the best way to prevent it is by taking care of your current health conditions. 

“If you have underlying heart disease, lung disease, or diabetes, really try to optimize those conditions before you get sick,” Capriles said. 

Capriles says patients who do end up in the ICU with Covid-19 are often put on ventilators, which puts major stress on the heart. 

“When the patient is really, really sick, they’re going to need more support and that’s when the ventilator can cause some of these arrhythmias because the heart is so sick,” he said.  

Capriles says the most common treatment is cardioversion, which uses an electrical impulse to help the heart return to a normal rhythm. 

If that doesn’t work, the next step is implanting a device that can send shocks to the heart to help it maintain a normal beat. 

In severe cases, the patient needs to be hospitalized so doctors can closely monitor their condition and give them medications. 

Capriles says about 10 to 15 percent of patients who get Covid-19 and develop arrhythmia will die. 

While this sounds like a high number, Capriles says it’s important to keep in mind most people with the virus will not develop the condition.

The most common arrhythmia is atrial fibrillation, which affects about 33 million Americans. 

Atrial fibrillation is when the two upper chambers of the heart beat rapidly and irregularly. 

The irregular beat can cause blood to pool and form clots, which can then cause a stroke. 

About 15% to 20% of strokes are a result of atrial fibrillation. 

The next most common arrhythmia is sinus node dysfunction, which is when the heart’s natural pacemaker, the sinus node, doesn’t work properly. 

This can cause the heart rate to be too fast, too slow, or to have an irregular rhythm. 

The third most common arrhythmia is ventricular arrhythmia, which is when the heart’s lower chambers, the ventricles, beat rapidly and irregularly. 

This is more serious and can cause the heart to stop beating. 

Less common arrhythmias include premature contractions of the heart, heart block, and Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome. 

These arrhythmias can be caused by certain medical conditions, lifestyle choices, or medications. 

Some arrhythmias have no known cause. 

Arrhythmias are diagnosed through a physical exam, medical history, and electrocardiogram. 

Treatment depends on the type of arrhythmia and symptoms. 

Lifestyle changes, medications, or cardiac ablation can be effective treatments. 

In some cases, implanting a cardioverter defibrillator can be recommended to treat and monitor ventricular arrhythmias. 

A cardioverter defibrillator is a small device that you wear over your heart. 

It monitors heart rhythms and can automatically shock your heart back into a normal rhythm if it senses a life-threatening arrhythmia. 

Research is being done to develop new treatments for arrhythmias, including devices that can be implanted under the skin and generate electric pulses to treat abnormal rhythms.

samples.src: Viewpoints of Other Scientists on Migration, Mental Health and PTSD:
samples.ref: Maikutlo a Ditsebi tše dingwe tša Saentshe mabapi le Go khuduga, Go phelega gabotse Monaganong le PTSD:
samples.hyp:
A Qualitative Analysis

Author(s): S. Abu Qader, A. Al Zoman, S. Abdul Jabar, S. Abu Qader, A. Al Zoman, S. Abdul Jabar

Abstract: INTRODUCTION: Cross-border migration is a global phenomenon that has increased significantly over the past several decades. It has major implications for the health of migrants as well as their families and communities. The aim of this study was to describe and reflect on the views of other scientists on migration, mental health, and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). METHODS: This is a qualitative study that used a content and data-driven approach. We searched the databases for relevant articles on migration, mental health, and PTSD published between 2000 and 2018. We analyzed the data using an inductive approach to identify themes and sub-themes. RESULTS: We included 30 articles in this study. Most of the included articles were published in 2017 and 2018. Nine articles were related to mental health problems, 10 articles were related to PTSD, and 11 articles were related to the impact of migration on the mental health of children. CONCLUSIONS: Most of the included articles focused on the impact of migration on the mental health of children, adolescents, and women, and the late consequences of PTSD. Trauma-informed services for migrants need to be a key priority for policy-makers and service providers to provide more efficient services.

Keywords: migration; mental health; post-traumatic stress disorder; children

samples.ref: Bontši bja dinyakišišo di šišinya gore mabaka a go hlola kgatelelo ya monagano a pele ga go khuduga le ka morago ga go khuduga a ama go phelega gabotse ga monagano le PTSD tša bafaladi le batšwantle.
samples.hyp:
However, a few studies have suggested that post-migration stressors have a stronger effect on the mental health of migrants and refugees. The current study aimed to investigate the relative effect of pre- and post-migration stressors on the mental health of a sample of Arab migrants in the United States (N = 226). The sample's mental health was measured by the Symptom Checklist-90-Revised (SCL-90-R), and migration stressors were measured by the Armas Migration Stress Scale. The results of multiple regression analyses indicated a significant effect of pre- and post-migration stressors on the mental health of the sample. In a step beyond previous studies, the results of this study also indicated that post-migration stressors had a significantly stronger effect on the sample's mental health. The findings of the current study contribute to the growing body of research on the mental health of migrants and refugees in the United States and provide further support for the use of trauma-informed interventions for the treatment of mental health conditions among migrants and refugees.

Keywords: Arab migrants; mental health; post-migration stressors; pre-migration stressors; PTSD; SCL-90-R; United States

In Libya, a common transit country, there are no mental health services available for migrants. Therefore, there is an urgent need to develop and improve mental health promotion and intervention programmes for migrants along the migration route from Libya to Europe. This thesis aims to gain a deeper understanding of the needs of migrants regarding mental health promotion and intervention from the migrants’ perspective in order to develop a theory-based mental health promotion programme in the future. A mixed-methods research approach was used to examine the needs of migrants in two phases. In phase 1, a cross-sectional study was conducted to assess the mental health status of migrants in two different settings in Libya. In phase 2, a qualitative study was conducted to gain a deeper understanding of the migrants’ needs and experiences regarding mental health promotion and intervention along their migration route from Libya to Italy. In the first study, 174 Sub-Saharan migrants were included. The study revealed a high prevalence of psychiatric disorders, namely mood disorders, followed by anxiety disorders. The migrants in the Libyan community had a higher prevalence of psychiatric disorders compared to those in the detention centre. The study also revealed a significant association between length of stay and psychological distress, detention centre stay and post-traumatic stress disorder. In the second study, in-depth interviews were conducted with 31 migrants. Most of the migrants had left their countries due to war or social unrest. The migrants had experienced a range of traumatic events in their countries of origin, during their journey, and in the transit country of Libya. The migrants had little social support in the transit country and their mental health was negatively impacted by their traumatic experiences. Therefore, there is an urgent need to develop and improve mental health promotion and intervention programmes for migrants along the migration route.

These psychological issues are among the most important contributors of the global burden of disease, and are considered as leading causes of disability adjusted life years (DALYs) lost worldwide. Moreover, depression and anxiety are also among the most common reasons for early retirement and disability benefits in Europe. 
The high prevalence rates of mental health problems have been confirmed in the African context as well. In South Africa, a study among 15,000 participants reported lifetime prevalence rates of 19.8% for depression, 22.9% for anxiety disorders and 4.5% for PTSD. Similarly, a study from Kenya found lifetime prevalence rates of 12.9% for major depression, and a study from Tanzania reported a prevalence of 20% for anxiety disorders. 
Despite the high disease burden, the low proportion of individuals with mental health disorders who actually receive treatment, is a major problem in both high- and low- and middle-income countries. In Africa, the proportion of individuals with a mental disorder who report having used mental health services during the past 12 months or who would be willing to seek such services if needed is around 1–3%. 
The underutilization of mental health services can be related to various barriers, including stigma, lack of services, financial barriers, lack of skilled human resources, and inadequate training opportunities for the available health workers. 
Stigma and discrimination associated with mental disorders can have a severe impact on the lives of individuals who have, or who are at risk of developing mental health problems. 
Mental health stigma can result in the avoidance and exclusion of people with mental health problems from social activities and in the withdrawal of social support. 
Stigma can also have a more direct impact on individuals with mental health problems, e.g. by affecting their social relationships and living conditions, by discouraging them from seeking treatment or by directly contributing to the development of more serious mental health problems. 
The high level of stigma associated with mental health problems might be one reason why the majority of individuals do not seek professional help for their mental health problems, even when they experience severe symptoms. 
In order to reduce the stigma associated with mental health problems, educational programs are considered as the most important intervention to change help-seeking behavior. 
In this context, the Internet provides an alternative source of information for the general public and can be used to increase mental health literacy and to reduce stigma associated with mental health problems. 
A number of studies have reported positive effects of online interventions on symptoms of depression and anxiety.

For the first time, the researchers have been able to describe the entire journey that a refugee goes through, from his or her country of origin, through a transit country to the host country. The researchers have developed a model which provides an explanation for previous research results. The researchers publish their findings in the scientific journal Social Science & Medicine.

Refugees experience a series of losses and disconnections as a result of forced migration. The model that the researchers have developed describes the different stages of a refugee’s journey. The first stage is the situation in a refugee’s country of origin. The second stage is a period of disconnection from family, community and place. The third stage is related to the journey itself. The fourth stage is the point in time when refugees are allowed to stay in the host country. The fifth stage is the moment of potential reconnection with family, community and place. The researchers have been able to collect data for each of these stages in the countries Afghanistan, Iran, Iraq, Syria, Turkey and the Netherlands.

The researchers have been able to explain previous research results using their model. For example, they were able to show that the number of losses and disconnections that refugees experience is directly related to the mental health upon arrival in the host country. The more losses and disconnections refugees have experienced, the worse their mental health. However, this relationship is not as strong in the case of voluntary migration. This could mean that refugees who settle in a new country after leaving their country of origin by their own free will experience fewer mental health problems than refugees who were forced to leave their country and/or who have experienced more losses and disconnections.

These conditions can be caused by or worsened by various factors, such as:

  • Experiencing or witnessing traumatic events, such as violence, war, or natural disasters, either in their country of origin or along their migratory route
  • Loss, such as the loss of family, friends, material possessions, or their sense of safety and security
  • Uncertainty about the future and powerlessness to change their circumstances
  • Adjustment difficulties in the host country, such as language difficulties, lack of social connections, limited access to education and healthcare, and discrimination
  • In addition, the specific circumstances of women migrants and refugees may increase their risk of developing these conditions even further. 
  • For instance, they are at a higher risk of experiencing gender-based violence, such as sexual harassment, assault, and trafficking, as well as specific health risks, such as mother and child health problems.
  • Unaccompanied minors face even greater difficulties. In addition to the above factors, they have to deal with the loss of a parent or guardian, which can lead to feelings of abandonment.
  • Finally, a lack of social connections can have a major impact on mental health. Migrants and refugees are at a particularly high risk of social isolation.

samples.src: Presence and Persistence of Amblyomma Hebraeum Augments the Burden of Heartwater in the Southern District of Botswana
samples.ref: Go hwetšagala le go Ngangabala ga Amblyomma Hebraeum go Oketša Mathata a Bolwetši bja leruo ka Bohlabela bja Distriki ya Botswana
samples.hyp:
Heartwater is caused by the protozoan parasite, Cardia Olympica, which is transmitted by the brown dog tick, Amblyomma hebraeum. The brown dog tick is a three-host tick; it spends the first and the second life stages on the dog as the host and the rest of the life stages on small and large wild animals respectively. The tick ingests the parasite when it feeds on an infected host. The parasite transforms into an infective sexual stage in the tick and is transmitted to a new host when the tick feeds again. The life cycle is completed when the infective tick is ingested by a dog or small and large wild animals. To determine the prevalence and intensity of infection of both the parasite and the tick in the southern district of Botswana, 106 dogs were sampled from three districts in the south-central region of the country. Blood was collected from each dog and examined for the presence of Cardia Olympica using indirect fluorescent antibody test. Ticks were counted and identified from each dog. The results indicated a parasite prevalence of 18.9% and an average intensity of 15.2±3.3kmpf (Kato-Katella MPF). Of the 106 dogs sampled, 20 were positive for the presence of Cardia Olympica with 13 of the 20 having a mixed infection with Trypanosoma brucei variant Treuza. The mixed infection did not prevent the development of an antibody response to Cardia Olympica. The tick, Amblyomma hebraeum was found on all the dogs sampled with a mean of 3.09±1.80 ticks per dog. The presence and persistence of the tick, Amblyomma hebraeum augments the burden of heartwater in the southern district of Botswana.

Mortality rates of livestock in subsistence farming are high due to lack of or poor quality of veterinary medicines, poor feeding and nutrition, diseases associated with poor sanitation and unclean living conditions, parasite infestation and injuries caused by poor fencing. These factors are not peculiar to small stock but also affect commercial livestock production. However, the effect is more pronounced in the former than the latter. The high mortality rate results in less meat, milk, manure, draft power and hide for human use. Small stock farmers are thus unable to fully meet their own nutritional needs, let alone have surpluses for sale. The low production and mortality of livestock in subsistence farming form a major constraint to the attainment of food security in the country. The situation is further exacerbated by the high population growth rate, particularly in the urban areas where the demand for food is high. The high population growth rate results in increased pressure on available arable land for food production, resulting in subsistence farmers engaging in land fragmentation. As a result, available land for crop production becomes smaller, resulting in low yields. As land size per farming household decreases due to population pressure, the need for alternative sources of income to complement food production increases. Due to low crop yields, commercial off-farm employment or business opportunities are limited, further limiting the household income and hampering the ability of farming households to meet their nutritional needs. This situation is more acute among small stock farmers than among crop farmers. The low income and the need to meet their own nutritional needs force small stock farmers to rely on their own livestock rather than purchase food from commercial markets. The result is that small stock farmers produce food for their own consumption but do not have any food surpluses for sale. The major source of income for small stock farmers is the sale of livestock, particularly to urban markets where the demand for small stock is high. However, the mortality rate among the livestock kept by small stock farmers is high, resulting in the farmers’ being unable to sell their livestock at a frequency that will meet the demand from urban markets and also result in low incomes from the sale of livestock. The low incomes, coupled with the need to meet their own nutritional needs, further limits the ability of small stock farmers to purchase food from commercial markets. The situation is a major constraint to the attainment of food security for small stock farmers. The low production and mortality of livestock in subsistence farming of small stock is, therefore, a major constraint to the attainment of food security in the country.

Heartwater is caused by the protozoan parasite Cardia olstoni, transmitted by the brown ear tick, Amblyomma variegatum. The study was a retrospective study using tick and cardiac puncture records of cattle from 1996 to 2018. The records were obtained from the surveillance reports and the national cattle herd health database. The number of ticks and the percentage positive for heartwater were determined for each year. The annual percent positivity was calculated and mapped. The study found that out of 66,395 ticks tested, 2,162 (3.27%) were positive for heartwater. The infection prevalence showed an increasing trend from 1.4% in 1996 to 6.0% in 2018. The map showed that the positivity was more prominent in the North-Western part of the country and less in the South-Eastern part. There was a significant correlation between the number of ticks and the positivity for heartwater (p < 0.01; r = 0.849). The high heartwater positivity in the North-Western part of the country could be a result of low vector control program in that part of the country.

The aim of this study was to determine the prevalence of A. hebraeum in the Southern District of Botswana. A total of 1,155 cattle from 13 villages were examined for the presence of A. hebraeum. The villages were located in the North-Eastern (5), Kweneng (5) and Southern (3) Districts of Botswana. The prevalence of A. hebraeum was determined by counting the number of adult ticks and the percentage of infested cattle. The prevalence of A. hebraeum in the three districts was 26.5% (Kweneng), 5.0% (North-Eastern) and 100% (Southern). Cattle in the Southern District were significantly (P<0.05) more infested with A. hebraeum than those in the North-Eastern and Kweneng Districts. These results suggest that A. hebraeum is a serious constraint to livestock production in the Southern District of Botswana. Further research on the distribution of A. hebraeum in Botswana is required to determine the prevalence of A. hebraeum in other districts in Botswana and to determine the geographical range of this tick in the country.

samples.hyp:
Gaborone, Botswana, 23rd of February 2021 – The number of ticks in the southern districts of Botswana is higher than normal and is expected to increase in the coming rainy season, according to the Department of Veterinary Services (DVS) in the Ministry of Agricultural Development and Food Security.

The DVS is concerned about the rise in the number of ticks in the Ghanzi, Kgalagadi, and Ngami areas. “The number of ticks in the southern districts of Botswana is higher than normal and is expected to increase in the coming rainy season,” said Dr Micus Chimbombi, Director of Veterinary Services.

The increase in the number of ticks is worrying because it may lead to an increase in the incidence of heartwater, a fatal disease transmitted by ticks.

According to Dr Chimbombi, the number of reports of heartwater has increased from 31 in the 2019/2020 reporting season to 82 in the current 2020/2021 season.

Heartwater is a fatal disease that affects animals, caused by a parasite that is transmitted by the brown dog tick.

The disease is characterized by a fever in animals, followed by a tick-bite, which makes them lick or bite themselves.

This is usually followed by the animal becoming lethargic, losing appetite, and then eventually dying.

The disease can be treated with antibiotics, but if not treated in time, it can be fatal.

Dr Chimbombi has called on livestock farmers in the southern districts of Botswana to take precautions to protect their animals from ticks.

Heartwater is caused by the protozoan parasite, Cardiaboldes elognatus, which is transmitted by the brown ear tick, Amblyomma variegatum. We surveyed 1,440 farms in the Tuli Block study area to determine the prevalence of ticks and heartwater. We tested cattle for heartwater using the Carbo-Red method and, for confirmation, a polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assay was also conducted on serum samples from selected positive animals. A total of 458 farms (31.6%) had at least one tick species present. The prevalence of ticks was significantly higher in the Ngwaketse District (41.4%) than in the Mahalapye (22.9%) and Ramotswa (21.8%) Districts. A. variegatum was the most prevalent tick species in all districts, followed by Rhipicephalus evertsi and Rhipicephalus muhsamae. The prevalence of heartwater infection was 2.6% with 37 positive out of 1,440 animals tested. PCR screening of serum samples confirmed that 34 of these 37 animals were infected. There was no significant association between the prevalence of ticks and heartwater (χ2 = 0.05, p = 0.81). The results highlight the widespread nature of ticks and heartwater in Botswana, a disease that poses a significant threat to the national cattle industry. Our findings also suggest that the current control methods for ticks and trypanosomiasis in Botswana might be ineffective and should be reviewed.

Heartwater occurs when the parasite that causes the disease (D. virpinus) migrates to the brain. This causes the animal to become restless, and it will often die within 24 hours. There is no known treatment for the disease.

The disease is transmitted by a tick (A. cookei), which is found in the southern part of Botswana. The tick picks up the parasite when it bites an infected animal, and then transfers the parasite to an uninfected animal when it bites again. A cow can be infected by as many as 50 ticks. The ticks are very small (about the size of a sesame seed), so they are difficult to see. A veterinarian can usually diagnose the disease if an animal has been in an area where the disease is known to occur. He will test for the presence of the parasite in the animal’s blood. If the animal has died of heartwater, the veterinarian will find characteristic lesions in the brain.

The disease can also be transmitted if an uninfected animal eats the heart, lungs, or liver of an animal that has died of heartwater. Therefore, it is important that butchers and cooks know to handle and prepare these organs with care.

The researchers then tested the effectiveness of different temperatures on tick survival. They exposed ticks to 37.5°C, 40°C and 42.42°C, temperatures they would experience at different times of the day or during heat waves, and found that all the tick life stages and both species were sensitive to heat. At 42.42°C, for example, mortality was high after just one hour of exposure for all tick stages. The researchers also tested how different temperatures influence the feeding behaviour of the ticks. They found that at 37.5°C, the majority of adult ticks dropped off after taking three blood meals, whereas at 40°C, the majority of adult ticks dropped off after taking one blood meal. No ticks survived at 42.42°C. The researchers stress that the high temperatures they used in their study are rare in Nigeria, but heat waves are increasing in frequency. They suggest that their findings suggest that high temperatures may help to reduce the risk of heartwater in areas where the disease is endemic, but further research is needed to confirm this.

The study, “Spatial distribution and eco-epidemiological determinants of heartwater in Nigeria,” was published in Parasites & Vectors.

Heartwater is a widespread and devastating cattle disease caused by the parasitic bacteria, Ricksettisia ricktsii, which is transmitted to animals by the brown ear tick, Rhipicephalus decoloratus.

It is one of the most important causes of cattle mortality and morbidity in Western and Central Africa, resulting in significant economic losses for farmers and the livestock industry.

Nigeria has the largest population of cattle in Africa and the greatest diversity and density of tick species, making it the epicenter of heartwater. However, little is known about the distribution and eco-epidemiological factors associated with the disease.

In the new work, researchers from the International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI), the Nigerian Institute of Leather and Science Technology (NILEST), and Texas A&M University mapped the spatial distribution of heartwater in Nigeria and investigated its eco-epidemiological determinants.

They collected tick and heartwater data from the literature and from experts, as well as cattle and farmer demographic data from a livestock survey. With this, they modeled the spatial distribution of heartwater and assessed the effect of environmental and demographic risk factors on tick infestation and heartwater prevalence in cattle.

The models showed that heartwater is unevenly distributed in Nigeria, with the southern part of the country having the highest prevalence. The researchers also found that vegetation type, rainfall, distance to rivers and rangelands, and human population density are associated with the distribution and prevalence of heartwater.

The findings suggest that climate change and land use changes are likely to increase the distribution and prevalence of heartwater in Nigeria, the researchers say.

“Climate change is predicted to increase the suitability of the tick’s habitat, which could result in an increase in tick populations.

“Additionally, land conversion to crop production, increasing farming activities, and deforestation may have a negative effect on vegetation, which is an important factor that influences the tick’s life cycle and feeding behavior, and could potentially lead to an increase in heartwater prevalence,” the team notes.

samples.hyp:
Point of care testing (POCT) is a growing field in the field of diagnostic testing. POCTs have the potential to improve patient care and health outcomes by allowing rapid testing outside of a traditional laboratory setting. However, there are barriers to the implementation and use of POCTs in certain regions, including India and South Africa. This article will discuss some of the barriers to POCT implementation in these countries and possible solutions to overcome them.

One of the main barriers to POCT implementation in India is the lack of awareness among healthcare providers. Many physicians and other healthcare providers are not familiar with POCT devices and their capabilities. This lack of awareness can lead to a reluctance to adopt new technology, as well as a lack of confidence in the accuracy of POCT results. To overcome this barrier, educational programs and training sessions can be conducted to increase awareness and understanding of POCTs among healthcare providers.

Another barrier to POCT implementation in India is the high cost of POCT devices and reagents. POCT devices can be expensive, and many healthcare facilities in India have limited budgets. To overcome this barrier, manufacturers can develop low-cost POCT devices, and governments can provide financial incentives for the purchase of POCT devices.

In South Africa, one of the main barriers to POCT implementation is the lack of infrastructure in some areas. Many remote and rural areas do not have access to electricity or reliable internet connectivity, which are necessary for some POCT devices. To overcome this barrier, POCT devices that are portable and do not require electricity or internet connectivity can be developed. Additionally, infrastructure development initiatives can be implemented to improve access to basic amenities in remote and rural areas.

In conclusion, there are several barriers to the implementation and use of POCTs in India and South Africa. However, these barriers can be overcome by addressing issues related to awareness, cost, and infrastructure. By doing so, the benefits of POCTs can be realized, leading to improved patient care and health outcomes in these regions.

The research was conducted in 2018–19 as part of a larger project on POC testing in low- and middle-income countries. The qualitative research comprised 21 in-depth individual interviews and 11 focus group discussions with key stakeholders in the public health value chain: laboratory technicians and doctors (n = 10), patients (n = 6), community health workers (n = 3), district health managers (n = 2), and diagnostic kit manufacturers and distributors (n = 3). In India, interviews and discussions were conducted in Tamil Nadu and Maharashtra, in South Africa in the Western Cape. Purposive and snowball sampling were used to select participants. Data analysis followed an inductive approach, with coding of transcribed interviews and group discussions based on the constant comparison method (Glaser, 1965).

The project combined ethnography with epidemiology and biology to understand how different actors in different sites understand, think about, and live with HIV, TB and malaria diagnostic uncertainty. The project aimed to achieve fine-grained, empirically-rich descriptions of diagnostic practices that would advance social-scientific understanding of these practices and contribute to the emerging field of diagnostic studies. The project also aimed to develop a new transnational and multi-method diagnostic lens that could be used to better understand how diagnoses are made in other disease contexts and countries. The research questions were:
  • How are diagnostic practices for malaria, TB and HIV imagined, remembered, and anticipated in South Africa and India?
  • What social and material world-shaping forces produce, stabilize, and transform diagnostic practices for malaria, TB and HIV in South Africa and India?
  • What can the diagnostic practices for malaria, TB and HIV in South Africa and India tell us about the relationship between diagnosis, disease, and social life more generally?

In South Africa, the National Health Laboratory Service (NHLS) is a single, centralized testing service that serves all public hospitals and provides testing services to private hospitals as well. This allows for economies of scale that make it feasible for the NHLS to invest in the development of testing infrastructure for diagnostic tests that are not currently available commercially. The NHLS has a proven track record of doing this for a large number of non-commercially available tests that are not currently on the WHO list of essential medicines. It is this ability to invest in the development of testing infrastructure that allows the NHLS to offer CD4 testing on a POC basis at every public hospital in South Africa. It also means that any new diagnostic test that is not available commercially, but that is made available through the NHLS, automatically becomes available at every public hospital in the country without the need for additional investment. In Nigeria, on the other hand, there is no single, centralized testing service. Instead, each hospital is responsible for providing testing to its patients. This makes it very difficult for any hospital to invest in testing infrastructure for diagnostic tests that are not commercially available, and virtually impossible to do so for tests that are not available in the country. This is why there is no diagnostic POC testing in Nigeria that is more complex than malaria testing. The only diagnostic tests that are available on a POC basis in Nigeria are those that are simple, cheap, and don’t require any equipment beyond what is already being used in the hospital’s clinical workflow. As a result, the diagnostic POC testing ecosystem in Nigeria is very different from that in South Africa.

samples.ref: Teko ya mafelong a tlhokomelo ka Afrika Borwa le India e ditela tlhokomelo ya maphelo
samples.hyp:
Published on

The quality of point-of-care testing (POCT) in South Africa and India is poor, according to a recent report published in the African Journal of Laboratory Medicine.

POCT is defined as diagnostic testing that can be performed at or near the site of patient care in a variety of clinical settings to support clinical management and treatment decisions.

The authors of the report state that POCT is becoming increasingly important in healthcare, particularly in developing countries, as it aims to improve clinical outcomes by enabling healthcare providers to rapidly obtain critical test results.

However, while POCT can provide several benefits, including cost-effectiveness, improved clinical outcomes, and reduced transport of blood and other specimens to a central laboratory, implementation of the testing is challenging.

The authors conducted a cross-sectional study with data collected between October 2017 and December 2019 from three public hospitals in South Africa and three private hospitals in India.

A total of 262 POCT devices from 14 manufacturers were included in the study. The authors found that more than one-third (36.6%) of the devices were at least five years old when the study began, and 12.2% of devices had unknown ages.

The authors also found that 24.6% of the devices were not serviced, which may result in poor performance and decreased accuracy.

The authors state that they found no association between age and service of the devices and the number of quality indicators.

However, they did find an association between poor quality and the lack of servicing of POCT devices. The authors indicate that this finding is a cause for concern, as it raises questions about the clinical and public health implications of poor POCT quality and lack of servicing.

“Point-of-care testing is becoming increasingly important in healthcare, particularly in developing countries, as it aims to improve clinical outcomes by enabling healthcare providers to rapidly obtain critical test results,” write the authors.

“However, while POCT can provide several benefits, including cost-effectiveness, improved clinical outcomes, and reduced transport of blood and other specimens to a central laboratory, implementation of the testing is challenging,” they conclude.

Source: African Journal of Laboratory Medicine

The primary advantage of POC testing is that it reduces the time between testing and the result of the test, as well as the number of steps involved in testing. This reduces the chance that the test will be done incorrectly or that the results will not be available to the healthcare professional who is caring for the patient. POC tests are also less expensive and quicker than sending samples to a laboratory. The main disadvantage of POC testing is that it requires the healthcare professional to have special training in how to perform the test. The test results may also be less accurate than laboratory tests. However, the difference is usually not great, especially for common diseases. The most common types of POC tests are urine tests, blood tests, and rapid diagnostic tests. Urine tests are used to check for things like sugar, protein, and ketones in the urine. Blood tests are used to check for a variety of things, including blood sugar, hemoglobin, and certain cell counts. Rapid diagnostic tests include things like rapid strep tests, which check for the bacteria that cause strep throat, and malaria tests, which check for the parasite that causes malaria. POC tests can be particularly useful in places where laboratory resources are limited or where it is important to get results quickly, like in emergency situations. For example, a POC test could be used to check for infection during surgery, or to check for certain conditions during an emergency department visit. POC tests have become increasingly common in recent years, as they have become more accurate and as the technology required to perform them has become more affordable and easier to use. However, it is important to note that not all POC tests are created equal, and it is important to use POC tests that have been validated and that are appropriate for the specific condition being tested for.
