These delays are not uncommon in South Africa, where a 2018 study by the Human Sciences Research Council (HSRC) found that between 15 and 20% of patients with cancer are diagnosed at a late stage when treatment is less likely to be successful.
This is a major problem worldwide, with late diagnosis of cancer generally considered to be a consequence of poor access to healthcare or ineffective screening programmes. 
But the situation in South Africa may be more complicated, says Mbulawa, who led the research.
The study suggests that a third of cancer patients in the public health sector don’t have health insurance, and 14% don’t have a fixed address, which makes it difficult for them to access care.
“Even if you have the best screening programmes in the world, if you don’t have a proper diagnostic system in place, it doesn’t matter,” says Mbulawa.
The research team is now working with the University of Cape Town (UCT) and the National Health Laboratory Service (NHLS) to improve the diagnostic process.
This includes using artificial intelligence (AI) to design a second phase of the study that will involve the review and analysis of pathology reports. 
The goal is to use the reviews to create a database of the most common diagnostic errors and the factors that may be contributing to them.
The team then hopes to implement interventions that could help reduce the errors.
For example, based on the results of the current study, the team plans to develop an educational program for pathologists to help them spot quality issues in their reports.
They are also working on an online tool that will help identify the root causes of sample-related delays.
Mbulawa says that while the current study was small, the team was surprised by the number and impact of the diagnostic errors it uncovered.
“Even though the study was done in one hospital, we expect these findings to reflect what is happening in other hospitals in South Africa,” she says.
“[We found] a significant number of cases where patients were sent home without a proper diagnosis, and that has serious implications for public health.”
The team presented their preliminary findings at the 2019 World Conference on Lung Cancer, which took place in Barcelona in December.
They will present their final results at the International Conference on Cancer in Africa, which is due to take place in Nairobi in February.

The researchers said the study was an opportunity to hear firsthand from the people who would be expected to use the new medicine. 

“We often hear about the need for more patient-centred care, but it’s easy to forget that patients are people with other commitments and responsibilities outside of healthcare,” Dr. Kirsten Cigogo, an endocrinologist at the University of Cape Town (UCT) and one of the study’s co-ordinators, said in a statement. 

The researchers said the study team included nurses, community health workers, and other healthcare professionals to ensure the study reflected the diverse backgrounds of the patients. 

The researchers said there was a “striking mismatch” between the ideal patient, as depicted in health care materials, and the “real patients” who actually use the system. 

The study said there was a focus on individual responsibility, with discussions of healthy eating, exercise, and medication adherence, without recognizing that patients had limited time, money, and social and family support. 

“While it is reasonable to want to empower patients to manage their diabetes, it is not reasonable to expect this in the context of overwhelming and unachievable demands,” the statement said. 

The study said there was a lack of discussion about the role of health systems in supporting patient management, with a focus on individual responsibility. 

“There was also limited recognition of the broader social determinants of health, such as poverty and unemployment, which are outside of patients’ control and have been clearly linked to poorer health outcomes,” the statement said. 

The study said the concept of patient-centred care is multi-faceted and cannot be reduced to an individual level. 

The researchers said the study showed that health care providers need to have better alignment with patients to ensure the patients are engaged and able to carry out their healthcare responsibilities. 

The study said to address this, the focus must shift away from patients having to manage their diabetes on their own to a more collaborative care model, which acknowledges that diabetes management requires support from the health system. 

“Health systems need to be designed to support patients to manage their health in meaningful ways,” the statement said. 

The study was a collaboration between researchers from UCT, Stellenbosch University, the University of the Western Cape, and the University of KwaZulu-Natal. 

The study was published in the journal BMC Health Services Research.

samples.hyp:
: A methodological review

Journal article Full text not available from Ebscohost


  • Background: The lack of internationally accepted definitions of critical illness and critical care hinders global comparison of patient outcomes, health care resource allocation and education. Concept analysis is a method used to clarify the meaning of a concept by identifying and defining its empirical referents, related ideas, attributes, examples, and cases.
  • Objectives: The objective of this review was to explore the use of concept analysis to develop definitions of critical illness and critical care.
  • Methods: A systematic search of four healthcare-related databases was performed. Studies were selected if they described the use of concept analysis to define critical illness or critical care. Two authors independently and systematically extracted data from the selected studies and assessed the methodological quality using the Walker and Avant concept analysis methodological criteria.
  • Results: Of the 1394 studies identified, 11 met the inclusion criteria. Year of publication ranged from 1989 to 2012, and three of the studies were conducted in Canada. Empirical referents included patient descriptions, clinical manifestations, and laboratory and physiological measurements. Attributes included levels of care and specific diseases or populations. Related ideas included terms like “severe disease,” “intensive,” and “high risk.”
  • Conclusions: Although methodological rigor was weak in the selected studies, the results provide some common understanding of critical illness and critical care. A multidisciplinary approach should be used to conduct new concept analyses to develop consensus definitions that can be tested for reliability. This review provides a methodological overview and a summary of the results of these 11 studies to advance the knowledge needed to develop such definitions.

A conceptual analysis was conducted of 44 relevant articles, which identified six categories of attributes: (1) illness acuity; (2) resource intensity; (3) clinical specialty; (4) reversibility; (5) need for subspecialty care; and (6) influence of local health system context. Most definitions of critical illness focus on acute life-threatening illness, but there is no consensus on how acute or life-threatening it should be. Although intensive care is the paradigm for critical care, there is a lack of consensus regarding the critical care setting, the types of clinicians and the types of treatments that should be provided. Reversibility is also not clearly defined. We propose that critical illness is a disease or confonding state in which there is a life-threatening, usually acute, insult to the system that requires intensive monitoring and/or therapy that is beyond the scope of basic clinical management. In this context, the term “severe” is preferred to “critical” to describe the acuity of illness.

samples.src: Our proposed definition of critical illness is, “a state of ill health with vital organ dysfunction, a high risk of imminent death if care is not provided and the potential for reversibility”.
samples.ref: Tšhišinyo ya rena ya tlhalošo ya bolwetši bja go bakwa le badimo ke, “seemo sa go lwala mmeleng moo o itemogelago go se šome ga setho se bohlokwa sa mmele, kotsi ya godimo ya go welwa ke lehu ge o sa fiwe tlhokomelo le kgonagalo ya go phologa”.
samples.hyp:
We propose a definition based on the three cardinal features of sepsis, namely infection, organ dysfunction and high mortality. Traditionally, critical illness has been defined by the presence of acute life-threatening organ dysfunction. While this definition remains useful for epidemiological studies, it is limited in clinical practice. The potential for reversibility has not been incorporated into current definitions of critical illness. We propose to adopt the term “reversibility” as it has been widely used in the context of sepsis. The concept of reversibility has important implications in critical illness. Clinically, it has important implications in terms of patient selection for clinical trials and allocation of scarce resources. Reversibility has important implications in terms of patient and family education. Research implications include the need to identify predictors of non-reversibility early in the course of the disease in order to offer palliative care. Finally, reversibility has important implications in terms of resource allocation. ICU beds, mechanical ventilators and other resources are in short supply in resource-limited settings. Early identification of patients who are unlikely to recover or reverse their illness will allow for the allocation of scarce resources to patients who are more likely to recover.

samples.hyp: Historically, the term "critical" in critical illness and critical care referred to the life-threatening nature of illness and the need for immediate and intense care to support life and organ function. In the early days of critical care, the primary separation of patients into "critical" and "noncritical" was based on whether a patient received general anesthetic versus local anesthetic, had a surgical versus medical illness, or required a surgical procedure. As the field of critical care medicine has matured and expanded, the terms critical illness and critical care have evolved to apply to any illness or care that is both acute (sudden in onset) and requires highly specialized organ support that only trained and experienced clinicians can provide. Thus, there are patients who appear "critically ill" who have a good likelihood of survival even without organ support, and there are patients who are "critically ill" and receive organ support but have a poor likelihood of survival. The term "intensive" in intensive care unit (ICU) refers to both the concept of critical illness and the highly specialized and immediate care that is provided to these patients. The focus of intensive care is to support the body's natural healing process, to treat primary diseases that cause organ dysfunction, and to prevent complications of critical illness. The terms critical illness and critical care are not synonymous with intensive care unit (ICU) or intensive care. Any patient can receive critical care without admission to an ICU, and not all patients in ICU receive critical care. Examples of critical care provided outside of ICU include emergency department care for patients with cardiac arrest, postanesthesia care for patients who undergo minor surgical procedures, and medical toxicology for patients with life-threatening poisonings. Examples of patients receiving critical care outside of ICU include a patient with subarachnoid hemorrhage who is stable and not actively bleeding and a patient with septic shock who is hemodynamically stable and not requiring pressors. Not all patients who are "critically ill" require ICU admission. ICU admission criteria, which evolved from the separation of patients receiving general versus local anesthetic, vary among ICUs and include the need for life support, monitoring, nursing care, and treatments that only ICU personnel can provide. Common reasons for admission to an ICU include acute respiratory failure, septic shock, massive pulmonary embolism and hemorrhage, status epilepticus, acute abdominal conditions, acute renal failure, and acute head trauma. samples.src: Strengths and Limitations of the Study
samples.ref: Maatla le Ditšhitišo tša Dinyakišišo
samples.hyp:
The strengths of this study include the large simple random sample, the participation of all 47 counties in Maryland, the comprehensive assessment of substance use disorders, the detailed assessment of suicide attempt history, the ability to examine associations between multiple risk and protective factors, and the novelty of the study. Also, the study sample was recruited from inpatient and outpatient settings, increasing the n and the variability in the sample. However, participants were recruited only from one hospital system in one state, limiting the generalizability of the findings to other populations. The cross-sectional design precludes causal inferences. Reliance on patient report of both outcomes (suicide attempt) and risk/protective factors limits knowledge about milder suicidal behaviors and underreports the frequency of substance use disorders and other risk factors because of underreporting, misperception, and recall bias.10 The assessment of psychopathology was performed only with the semi structured K-SADS interview and not with other well-validated measures such as the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-IV (SCID) or the Composite International Diagnostic Interview (CID). Although the K-SADS has been shown to have good test–retest reliability for major affective disorders and tic disorders,11 test–retest reliability for other K-SADS diagnoses (eg, anxiety disorders, ADD/H) is not established, and there is no information available on the test–retest reliability of specific K-SADS diagnoses in adolescents with comorbid psychopathology. In addition, K-SADS–based diagnoses have not been validated with other standard diagnostic interviews in adolescent populations. The K-SADS was developed and tested in research settings and has not been back-translated and tested for clinical utility in research or clinical settings in non–English-speaking populations. Finally, this was not a nationally representative sample, and therefore, the findings may not generalize to other populations; however, the sample was recruited from a mix of urban, suburban, and rural hospitals throughout the state of Maryland, increasing the variability in the sample and enhancing the generalizability of the findings.

A new study co-authored by researchers from the University of Washington School of Medicine has re-defined the meaning of “critically ill” patients and their care, and found that the number of patients who could be affected is higher than previously thought.

The study was published today in JAMA Network Open.

The research group, led by senior author Dr. Deborah M. Anand, professor of pediatrics at UW School of Medicine and chief of the Division of Bioethics in the UW School of Medicine Department of Pediatrics, set out to explore the history of the care of critically ill patients, and to determine how the definition of “critically ill” has changed over time.

The researchers found that the definition of “critically ill” has changed from one of acute organ dysfunction to one of acute hypoxic respiratory failure. This change has led to the exclusion of patients with chronic conditions who have a high risk of death, such as those with cancer, advanced heart or kidney disease, or advanced cirrhosis of the liver. As a result, these patients are ineligible to participate in clinical trials, and they may not receive the same level of research and investigational treatments as patients with an acute condition.

“Our study shows that if you look at cancer patients or patients with end-stage heart, kidney or liver disease, they are not considered ‘critically ill’ even though they have a high risk of death,” Anand said. “They tend to be excluded from clinical trials, and they may not get the same level of experimental treatments that other patients may receive.”

Anand said the study results could lead to changes in how patients with long-term illnesses are included in clinical trials, which examine the safety and effectiveness of new treatments and therapies.

Anand and her co-authors also propose a working definition of “critically ill” that would allow patients with a higher risk of death to be included in research studies. Currently, patients are only eligible to be included in clinical trials if they have an acute illness that is expected to get worse within 30 days.

Under the working definition proposed by the authors, patients with any chronic condition who have a high risk of dying within 90 days would be eligible.

The new definition would include approximately 1.6 million patients annually, based on data from 2012. This is approximately 10 times the number of patients who were enrolled in ICU trials that year. The majority of these patients are aged 65 years and older, and more than half have cancer.

Dr. Jeffrey Lipman from the University of Melbourne in Australia and his colleagues agree. 

“We feel that this has limited the ability of the field to grow and to attract attention to the problems that we have, because it is perceived to be a small field,” Lipman says. “We need to sell better the importance of what we do.” 

Lipman and his colleagues detail the problems facing the critical care field in an editorial published in the Intensive Care Medicine journal. 

The team, which includes researchers from the U.S., Australia, Japan, and the Netherlands, also point out that the current definition excludes post-intensive care unit (ICU) mortality and recovery. They also say the definition fails to reflect the complexity of patient acuity and the fact that critical care is a service, not a patient population. 

Lipman says the new definition they suggest aims to capture these aspects and better reflect the global burden of critical illness. 

“We’ve called it a ‘spectrum’ of illness,” Lipman says. “It can range from a person who is extremely unwell and requires a few days of support in an ICU to a person who requires support for weeks or months, or even a whole year.” 

The new definition also allows for the addition of a number—such as 5% or 10%—indicating the chance of death for a patient with critical illness. 

“People with a 5% chance of dying within 30 days of a major surgical procedure or within 28 days of being hospitalized for a severe infection would not be considered to have a ‘critical illness,’” Lipman says. 

The researchers hope that by revising the definition of critical illness, researchers around the world will be encouraged to do more research in this area. 

“With a better definition, we can then prioritize the conditions that we study, we can prioritize the interventions that we test, and we can better allocate the resources that are available to us,” Lipman says.

The researchers then did a systematic review to find out how critical care was defined in the studies they found in their literature search. They did a search in MEDLINE, EMBASE, and CINAHL for studies that described how critical care was defined at the bedside, and found 13 studies that met their inclusion criteria. Most of the studies were done in an intensive care unit, but three described how critical care was defined at the time of admission to the hospital. The unit of analysis was mostly one patient, but two studies described how critical care was defined for an entire family. 

The researchers found that most studies (n=9) defined critical care for individual patients using the presence or absence of life-sustaining treatments such as mechanical ventilation or vasopressors. Four of the studies used the presence or absence of these treatments as the main feature of critical care, while the other five also included the patient’s level of consciousness or other organ dysfunction. 

Three studies (n=3) defined critical care based on the highest level of care a patient received. In two of the studies, the researchers followed patients through the different units in the hospital and considered critical care as any level of care below the highest level of care the patient received. In the third study, critical care was defined as the level of care the patient received at the time of the survey, which may have been different from the highest level of care the patient received. 

The two studies that described how critical care was defined for an entire family defined it based on the presence or absence of a family member at the patient’s bedside. 

The researchers then identified five key messages from their review. 

First, there is a need to standardize the definition of critical care. Having a common definition of critical care helps with data collection, analysis, and comparison of studies describing the epidemiology, costs, outcomes, and burden of critical illness. 

Second, studies should be specific about the unit of analysis (e.g., individual patient, family) and the outcome of interest (e.g., critical care as a process, critical care as a result). This will help future researchers be explicit in their definitions and select the most appropriate patients for their study. 

Third, critical care should be defined as a continuum of care from the time of presentation to the time of death or recovery. This will ensure that all the care provided during a critical illness is captured in studies. 

Fourth, critical care should be defined using a common set of organ failures or life-sustaining treatments.

Abstract
Background The obligate intracellular parasite Plasmodium infects liver cells of its mammalian hosts to initiate a new asexual blood stage infection. Successful liver-stage infection requires reorganization of the host endomembrane system to permit parasite development. Microtubules (MTs) are essential components of the endomembrane system that play a central role in membrane traffic and are therefore likely to be affected by the altered MT organization. Previous work from our lab identified a number of MT associated proteins whose expression is modulated during P. berghei liver infection, suggesting that the expression of these host factors is regulated by the parasite to perturb MT organization and the endomembrane system. Methods We performed a genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 knockout screen to identify host factors whose knockouts are lethal in the presence of P. berghei sporozoites. The knockout library consisted of 8898 barcoded single-guide RNAs targeting 7783 genes. Results We identified 266 genes that are essential for P. berghei sporozoite development in hepatocytes. Among these, we validated a known essential gene, THRAP3, whose knockout leads to an increase in the number of vacuoles containing parasites. We also identified 10 genes whose knockout phenotypes resemble those of the mt1 null mutant, including CENPJ, a gene essential for centrosome function. We also validated two previously uncharacterized genes, TBC1D6 and POMC. Conclusions Our findings suggest that P. berghei modulates the expression of a number of host genes to alter MT organization during early liver-stage infection. Impact The genome-wide knockout screen is a powerful tool for the identification of host factors that are important for controlling parasite invasion and survival. This dynamic organization requires host microtubule polymerization and is abrogated by host microtubule depolymerization. The parasite induces dramatic reorganizations of the host actin cytoskeleton at the LS stage. samples.hyp:
A mosquito carrying the malaria parasite

Malaria remains a major global health challenge, with the World Health Organization reporting 228 million new cases in 2019, the most recent year for which figures are available.

The disease is caused by a genus of single-celled parasites, which are transmitted to humans by the bite of an infected Anopheles mosquito.

Once in the human body, the parasites travel to the liver where they multiply. Some of the parasites then develop into what is known as ‘hypnozoites’, which can lie dormant in the liver for up to a year before turning into ‘trophozoites’, which cause the symptoms of the disease.

Scientists have been investigating how the parasites hijack liver cells to survive and reproduce, as understanding this could lead to the development of treatments that block this process.

Writing in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, scientists at the US National Institutes of Health (NIH) describe how they identified key molecules involved in this process.

They found that a family of molecules called ‘cysteine proteases’ are essential to the parasites’ ability to change into hypnozoites, and have identified one called ‘histone deacetylase’ as being particularly important for this process.

The researchers then tested whether inhibiting the activity of this enzyme would block infection of human liver cells by the malaria parasite, and found that it reduced infection levels by around 90%.

Though at an early stage, the findings suggest a potential new target for anti-malarial drugs, and the researchers hope that further studies could lead to the development of new treatments.

Dr Sara Cherry, who was not involved in the research, told The Scientist: “This is a very nice paper. [It] describes an extensive characterization of a key step in the malaria life cycle that is essential for [malaria] persistence.”

“By targeting this step, the authors suggest a new potential anti-malarial drug target,” she said.

“[This] provides an attractive and promising therapeutic strategy to block this stage of the parasite’s life cycle,” Cherry added.

The present study aimed to examine the prevalence of malaria and the use of malaria prophylaxis among a cohort of international travellers, and to identify risk factors associated with the use of prophylaxis.

Between January 2016 and December 2018, a total of 16,305 international travellers were included in the study. Information on travel-related risk behaviours and the use of malaria prophylaxis was obtained through a computer-assisted interview. Prevalence estimates and risk factors were calculated and multivariable logistic regression was used to adjust for demographic differences between travellers who did and did not use antimalarial drugs.

The word "endoplasmic" refers to the middle part of a cell, and the word "reticulum" refers to a network. The endoplasmic reticulum can be further classified into two types: rough endoplasmic reticulum and smooth endoplasmic reticulum.

Rough endoplasmic reticulum

The rough endoplasmic reticulum is so called because of the presence of numerous ribosomes attached to it, and these ribosomes are involved in the synthesis (or construction) of proteins and other large molecules inside the cell. The rough endoplasmic reticulum is often closely associated with the cell nucleus, where it receives genetic instructions for protein synthesis from the nucleus. These instructions are carried out by the ribosomes attached to the rough endoplasmic reticulum. The rough endoplasmic reticulum is continuous with the outer membrane of the nuclear envelope.

Smooth endoplasmic reticulum

In contrast to the rough endoplasmic reticulum, the smooth endoplasmic reticulum does not have ribosomes attached to it, but it is still involved in the synthesis and transport of lipids, steroid hormones, and proteins. The smooth endoplasmic reticulum also helps in the storage of calcium ions. It is often found in large quantities in cells that need to carry out specialized functions, such as muscle cells and cells of the immune system. For example, in muscle cells, the smooth endoplasmic reticulum stores calcium ions, which are released when a muscle contracts.

The smooth endoplasmic reticulum is often continuous with the inner membrane of the nuclear envelope. The smooth endoplasmic reticulum also extends out from the nuclear envelope to form structures called ER exit sites (ERES), which are involved in the transport of proteins from the rough endoplasmic reticulum to their appropriate destinations in the cell. From the ERES, the proteins are packaged into transport vesicles, which then deliver the proteins to their target locations.

The endoplasmic reticulum is a vital organelle for all cells, and it plays an important role in a variety of cellular processes. Dr. Joanne Nilsson, Postdoctoral Fellow at the Department of Microbiology, Immunology and Hygiene at the University of Toronto, Canada, said: “To successfully establish infection, pathogens must subvert host cell processes to redirect resources towards their own benefit. To do this, they often target the cytoskeleton - the “backbone” of the cell that is essential for many cellular processes. Our knowledge of how different pathogens target the cytoskeleton is critical to understanding how they establish infection. Until now, no one knew how this cytoskeletal manipulation occurs at the molecular level.”
To understand how the parasite manipulates the host cell cytoskeleton, the researchers used a combination of cutting-edge microscopy techniques and genetic approaches in yeast and in parasite-infected mammalian cells. 

The team found that the parasite takes control of a molecular motor that is responsible for moving packages of proteins within the cell. By redirecting the motion of this molecular motor, the parasite is able to change the distribution of microtubules within the host cell and hijack the cellular transport system to generate more energy for itself. 

Dr. Nilsson explained: “Microtubules are like railroad tracks for the cell. They are used to transport a variety of important packages within the cell to where they are needed. The parasite targets a molecular motor called dynein, which is responsible for moving these packages along microtubules. By reorganizing dynein into a different pattern of activity, the parasite changes the structure of microtubules, and this gives them the ability to hijack the dynein to do its own bidding.”

The study also reveals that the parasite accomplishes this by hijacking a signaling pathway normally used by the host cell to coordinate different types of cytoskeletal rearrangements. samples.src: Hundreds of thousands of deaths still occur each year from malaria, with a large number of these in Africa.
samples.ref: Ngwaga ka ngwaga go sa hlaga diketekete tša mahu ka lebaka la malaria, moo palo ya godimo ya mahu a e lego ka Afrika.
samples.hyp:
The most effective way to prevent malaria is to stop the mosquito that transmits the malaria-causing parasite from biting people. The parasite is transmitted through the bite of an infected Anopheles mosquito.

Insecticide-treated bed nets and indoor residual spraying of houses with insecticides are two of the most important strategies used to prevent malaria transmission by reducing the number of bites from mosquitoes that carry the malaria parasite.

Anopheles gambiae is the main mosquito species that transmits the malaria parasite in Africa. This mosquito has developed resistance to the insecticides commonly used for preventing malaria, making it more difficult to stop them from biting people. Insecticide-treated bed nets and indoor spraying with insecticides have significantly reduced mortality from malaria in young children in Africa. However, the longevity of these interventions is limited, with the insecticides losing their effectiveness after about two years. New strategies are urgently needed to protect people in malaria-endemic areas.

Mosquitoes need a blood meal to develop into fertile adults and to be able to transmit parasites to other humans. After taking a blood meal, female mosquitoes seek out sites to lay their eggs, which are usually near water sources, and are commonly found indoors. Once the eggs have hatched, the resulting larvae (wiggly maggots) require access to water to breathe and develop. After a few days the larvae pupate, and then emerge as adult mosquitoes.

If the early stages of a mosquito’s life (from egg to larvae to pupae) could be prevented from accessing water, this would kill them and stop them from developing into adult mosquitoes. Water is a key requirement for all four stages and by targeting early stages, the number of adult mosquitoes that develop would be reduced. This would lead to fewer mosquitoes to transmit malaria parasites to people.

Our recent publication in Nature shows that a synthetic blood cocktail, which mimics a mammalian blood meal, can be used to kill early stage mosquitoes and prevent them from accessing water. The cocktail works by targeting the receptors in the mosquito’s gut that detect the presence of a blood meal. The presence of a blood meal triggers a change in the microenvironment of the mosquito’s gut, which allows certain bacteria that the mosquito has eaten to multiply. These bacteria produce toxins that kill the mosquito. We found that a few bacteria were able to kill the mosquitoes, with one bacterium, Janthina magariotes, being the most effective. The cocktail made from this bacterium is now being developed into a biolarvacise for use against mosquitoes.

The causative agent of malaria is the Plasmodium parasite, which is transmitted to humans by the bite of an infected Anopheles mosquito. These parasites infect and destroy red blood cells, causing symptoms including fever and fatigue. To progress to the next stage of its lifecycle, the parasite infects the mosquito and replicates within its salivary glands. During a mosquito bite, the parasite is transferred to a new human host and continues to replicate within red blood cells, eventually causing the symptoms of malaria. In 2019, there were an estimated 229 million cases of malaria worldwide, with the majority of these cases occurring in the African region. The WHO aims to reduce the global malaria incidence rate by 10% by 2023, which will require continued efforts and research to develop new interventions and control strategies.

The use of genomic data to inform control strategies could help combat infectious diseases, such as malaria, more effectively. Genomic data can be used to understand the genetic variation within a parasite species, which can inform strategies for tracking and preventing drug resistance. For example, the use of genomic data identified areas of resistance to antimalarial drugs in the P. falciparum parasite. This information can be used to guide treatment policies and to develop new drugs that combat resistance. Additionally, genomic data can be used to track the spread of infectious diseases. For example, genomic data has been used to track the spread of the SARS-CoV-2 virus, which caused the COVID-19 pandemic. This information can be used to develop strategies to control the spread of infectious diseases and to prepare for future outbreaks. However, the effective use of genomic data in control strategies requires the development of new bioinformatics tools and methods that are tailored to the specific needs of low and middle-income countries (LMICs), such as Africa. The design and evaluation of these tools and methods must consider the unique challenges and resources available in LMICs.

samples.ref: Go šwahlela ga diphedi tša tlhago bjalo ka Karolo ya Maitapišo a Dinyakišišo tša Afrika Borwa ka ga Phetogo ya Lefaseng ka Bophara
samples.hyp: South Africa, like many other countries, is experiencing rapid environmental change as a consequence of global change. In addition to the well-known and widespread impact of increasing atmospheric carbon dioxide on climate, other important aspects of global change that are of concern to South Africa include increased ultraviolet radiation, increased incidence of extreme weather events such as droughts and floods, rising sea levels, and ocean acidification. These changes are likely to place pressures on the country’s natural resources, and are likely to have significant implications for the country’s economic sectors and its capacity to ensure sustainable development. It is clear that understanding and quantifying biotic and abiotic components of the environmental changes that are occurring as a consequence of global change is essential for sound science-based management of natural resources. Biological invasions are one component of environmental change that is of particular concern because of the ecological and economic damage that invasive species cause. Biological invasions are a global problem that is likely to become more pronounced in the future as a consequence of global change. In order to understand the role of biological invasions as a component of global change it is first necessary to understand the processes that are driving invasions in the natural as well as social sciences. The aim of this paper is to review what is currently known about biological invasions in South Africa in order to establish the knowledge gap that currently exists and to make recommendations for future research based on that gap. The main sources of information for this review were publications in the peer-reviewed literature and reports that are in the public domain that describe studies conducted in South Africa or studies that include data for South Africa in combination with data for other countries. This information was used to conduct a literature survey and a comprehensive database was constructed that includes demographic as well as ecological information for all plant and animal invader species in South Africa for which such information is available. This database will be made available to the public and to the research community. Information on the research capacity in South Africa that is currently active in the field of biological invasions was gathered by contacting all universities and other research institutions in the country and requesting information on who is currently active in the field and what the capacity of each institution in the field might be. From this information, it is clear that there is a strong research effort in the country that is addressing various aspects of biological invasions. samples.src: In this chapter, we assess how much research in South Africa has been directed towards biological invasions relative to other elements of global change.
samples.ref: Ka mo kgaolong ye, re sekaseka ka gore ke dinyakišišo tše kaakang tšeo di dirilwego ka Afrika Borwa tšeo di bego di lebišitšwe go go šwahlela ga diphedi tša tlhago ge go bapetšwa le dikarlo tše dingwe tša phetogo ya lefaseng ka bophara.
samples.hyp:
We do this by examining the published scientific literature on biological invasions and global change in South Africa. Our results show that research on biological invasions in South Africa has increased significantly over the last two and a half decades, and that the number of publications on biological invasions in South Africa has been increasing at a rate similar to the global increase. However, research on biological invasions in South Africa in the context of global change has to our knowledge not been examined before, and we therefore hope to fill this void. We show how the South African scientific literature on biological invasions and global change can be divided into four distinct periods, and examine publication activity in each of these periods in more detail. The results of our study suggest that research on biological invasions in South Africa has thus far been relatively independent from global change research. However, global change research in South Africa has been increasing, and the two research streams are starting to overlap. This is reflected in the final period we identify in the literature, where a significant proportion (~25%) of the publications on biological invasions were published in the context of global change. We conclude that research on biological invasions should continue to increase in South Africa and that more studies are needed where biological invasions are investigated in the context of global change in South Africa. We believe that such studies would be beneficial in developing management strategies for biological invasions in South Africa, since biological invasions in South Africa are likely to be greatly impacted by global change. We believe that the results of such studies could also be beneficial in other countries in Africa that have similar social, economic and climate conditions.

samples.hyp:
For each threat, we identified the most important biotic and abiotic factors that influence South African species’ susceptibility and/or vulnerability to the threat, as well as the most effective strategies to mitigate the threat to South African species.

We found that the majority of literature on the threats to South African ecosystems is descriptive and identifies a need for predictive and mechanistic research. The degree to which South African species are threatened varies depending on the threat, with overharvesting being the most significant and climate change being the least significant threat to species endemic to South Africa. Cold-tolerant species are at higher risk from climate change than species from other parts of the world, because cold spots are likely to disappear faster than warm spots in South Africa. The application of the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species to South African species is also a concern, as many of these species are currently insufficiently known to allow for accurate assessment of their threat status. We identified a need for research to prioritize the application of conservation funding to where it is most needed and to identify knowledge gaps in South African biodiversity.

Indeed, most of the hotspots were detected in Europe and North America, where the majority of the published studies were conducted. However, we also identified several research hotspots in South America, Asia, and Australia. Surprisingly, we found very few research hotspots in Africa, despite the fact that the first case of Ebola virus infection was reported already in 1976. The temporal analysis of the research activity on Ebola virus shed light on the dynamics of the scientific interest around this topic. The first studies on Ebola virus were published in the early ‘90s, with a very low research activity. The interest in studying the Ebola virus suddenly increased in 2007, in parallel with the appearance of the outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and then decreased back to the initial low level. During the 2014–2016 West Africa Ebola virus outbreak, the research activity showed a new peak, which quickly decreased after the announcement of the epidemic’s end.

The first Ebola vaccine was approved for use in August 2019. The vaccine, codenamed “ERVEBO”, is manufactured by the pharmaceutical company “Merieux”, and is based on a weakened and purified strain of the Ebola virus that is unable to cause disease. The safety and effectiveness of the vaccine was demonstrated during the 2014–2016 Ebola outbreak in West Africa, where it was tested on more than 11,000 people. According to the European Medicines Agency, the vaccine is approved for the prevention of Ebola virus disease in adults and children over 1 year old.

The approval of the first Ebola vaccine is a significant milestone, and a major step forward in the protection of populations against this devastating disease. The vaccine will be particularly valuable in areas where the risk of Ebola virus infection is high, such as West Africa. The vaccine will help to protect healthcare workers, humanitarian aid workers, and others at risk of infection, and will contribute to preventing future outbreaks of Ebola virus disease.

These are the most important interactions in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic, as there are multiple drivers of COVID-19 spread, including individual, behavioural, social, and economic drivers, as well as the characteristics of the local environment. Few studies have investigated the effects of multiple drivers, and there is a need to improve our understanding of their joint effects, to be able to effectively design and evaluate interventions that can counteract them. Here, we use a literature review to identify studies that include multiple drivers of the COVID-19 pandemic and describe their main findings. We find that most studies examine changes in a single driver, while only a few consider more than one driver. Among the latter, most studies are observational, and they use correlation and causal inference to explore and understand the effects of the drivers. We also find that the studies tend to examine individual drivers within a specific context, making it hard to infer broader conclusions. We suggest that more integrative research, using experimental and modelling approaches, is needed to understand the relative importance of different drivers and the nature of their interactions. Such research could help design effective interventions to mitigate the COVID-19 pandemic and future outbreaks.

The research that has been conducted to date, however, provides a starting point. We therefore collated and systematically assessed the available evidence on the relative importance of global change drivers in driving ecosystem change in the Greater Mekong Region (GMR) and surrounding countries. The evidence was collated from literature and expert interviews and systematically assessed in an expert workshop. Four drivers were assessed as having a high potential to change ecosystem states and dynamics in the region: (1) land use change, (2) climate change, (3) invasive species, and (4) water infrastructure development and use. samples.hyp:
Most studies on substance use in the country focus on alcohol and tobacco.

The aim of this study was to gain an understanding of the patterns and correlates of marijuana and methamphetamine use among a sample of young adults in Cape Town, South Africa.

Participants were 119 young adults, between the ages of 19 and 29. The Marijuana and Methamphetamine Scale (MMS) was used to measure the use and correlates of the two substances. Correlates included demographic variables, psychological variables (intrinsic and extrinsic aspirations, neuroticism, self-madification, and generalized anxiety and depression), and subjective norms.
Results
Analyses revealed that the sample was split almost evenly between the two substances, with 59% of the sample reporting some marijuana use and 41% some methamphetamine use. Correlates of use for both substances were investigated using regression analyses. For marijuana use, significant positive correlations were found for age, extrinsic aspirations, neuroticism, and subjective norms towards marijuana use, while a significant negative correlation was found for intrinsic aspirations. For methamphetamine use, significant positive correlations were found for age, intrinsic and extrinsic aspirations, self-madification, and generalized anxiety, while a significant negative correlation was found for depression.
Conclusions and Implications
The findings of this study provide an understanding of the patterns and correlates of marijuana and methamphetamine use among young adults in Cape Town, South Africa. The findings also point to the need for the development of preventive interventions that are tailored to the local context and are based on an understanding of the cultural factors that influence the use of these substances among young adults in South Africa. Furthermore, the findings highlight the need for the development of preventive interventions that address the co-occurrence of the use of these substances with other risk behaviors among young adults in South Africa. For example, the high levels of neuroticism among the sample suggest the need for the development of interventions that address emotional management among young adults in South Africa.

For example, the 1995 Conservation and Sustainable Use of Lake Victoria Fisheries Management Plan (Lake Victoria Environmental Management Programme 1995) and the 2000 Regional Fisheries Management Plan for Lake Victoria (Lake Victoria Fisheries Organisation 2000), both of which are still in force, dealt with the effects of habitat change and invasive species such as the Nile perch on the fisheries economy. A number of other studies have also linked changes in the fisheries economy to changes in the fisheries value chain (e.g. Nandonde et al. 2017). 
Other studies have focussed on specific aspects of the fisheries sector. For example, the economics of fish farming have been examined (e.g. Njiraini et al. 2013), as has the performance of the Lake Victoria fisheries complex (Busia et al. 2015). 
A number of studies have examined the role of the informal sector in the Lake Victoria fisheries economy (e.g. Olushayo et al. 2017; Olushayo and Mugoya 2018). 
These studies have provided important information on the informal sector, which is of growing importance in the Lake Victoria fisheries economy. However, there is a lack of information on the role of the formal sector. 
The Lake Victoria fisheries sector is the largest in Tanzania. The formal sector consists of a number of companies involved in fishing, fish farming, fish processing and marketing. The aim of this study is to examine the role of the formal sector in the Lake Victoria fisheries economy. 
The study was based on data collected from structured questionnaires administered to 127 respondents representing the formal sector in the Lake Victoria fisheries economy between February and March 2021. 
The results show that the formal sector is important in the Lake Victoria fisheries economy. However, the sector is facing a number of challenges, including limited access to credit, limited access to markets, and limited access to technology.

This is important because there are often multiple drivers behind a migration decision. 
For example, people migrate for many different reasons, such as to find work, to join family, or to escape natural disasters. 
In this paper, we present a new method to identify the drivers of migration by combining the strengths of three different approaches: 
(1) text mining of migration research (2) expert knowledge from round-table discussions and (3) a database of migration policies. 
Our results show that experts and text mining agree on the top drivers, that is, the ones that need to be considered when developing policies to manage migration. 
However, experts found drivers that require further research, and policy makers can use our results to prioritise future research. 
We also find that experts and text mining agree on the least important drivers. 
This is important because it suggests that we can use text mining to help identify drivers that are not important to policy makers. 
This is the first step in developing an automatic method to identify the drivers of migration that is useful to policy makers.

Temperature sensitivity of SOM decomposition was identified as the most important factor explaining 73% of the variation in SOM across the nine study sites and was not related to the atmospheric CO2 concentration and nitrogen deposition. Our results suggest a global pattern in which the response of SOM to local and global drivers is largely mediated through the temperature sensitivity of SOM decomposition. This is likely to reflect the effect of tree cover on soil organic matter dynamics over different timescales. Tree cover protects the soil surface from physical damage caused by vehicles, feet, and animals and reduces erosion by surface water run-off and increases soil moisture content (Périlleux et al., 2002; Houghton and Nicholls, 2000). Thus, tree cover reduces soil exposure to physical forces that can damage soil organic matter (Six et al., 2004). In areas of our study where trees were present, they formed a dense canopy that also inhibited direct sunlight exposure of the soil surface, a known factor that limits soil organic matter decomposition (Rochson et al., 2004). This effect is generally greater in the top layer (0–10 cm) where organic matter is most susceptible to decomposition. However, in areas of recent tree felling, the exposed soil is subject to increased rates of organic matter decomposition as a result of increased solar radiation and altered soil moisture content (Rochson et al., 2004; Lavelle et al., 2006). This is likely to have the effect of reducing soil organic matter content in the top layer (0–10 cm) in felled areas, as we observed, and increasing the proportion of organic inputs from older, deeper layers, a phenomenon that is known to result in an increase in the relative proportion of lignin (a recalcitrant plant biomass) in soil organic matter (Conrad, 1992; Six et al., 2004). Lignin is relatively recalcitrant to decomposition and is known to promote the formation of soil organic matter aggregates, thereby reducing microbial activity and organic matter turnover (Baldoni et al., 2012). This may explain why, despite apparent increases in soil organic matter content in deeper layers (20–30 cm) in felled areas, microbial biomass and respiration rates were generally lower than in undisturbed areas.

Careful forestry: replanting tree species that will help the soil retain water, rather than planting single species plantations

Sustainable forestry means cutting down less, and cutting down carefully. Now researchers report that forests in Zambia are in serious trouble, and to help them will require not just a more careful axe but a more subtle understanding of the ecology of the region.

Forests in western Zambia are “in rapid decline”, according to a report in the journal Global Change Biology. The reason? The land is over-exploited. And so the researchers recommend “restoration forestry”, a careful balancing of the needs of the human and non-human residents of the region.

samples.ref: Go Maatlafatša Tšweletšo ya dinawa tša Chickpea le Botšweletši ka Mokgwa wa Boitlhamelo wa Batšeakarolo ka Ethiopia
samples.hyp:
The project aims to (i) strengthen capacities of the National Crop Research Institute (NCRI) in conducting research through establishment of chickpea research hub and innovation platform, (ii) develop innovative production technologies for major chickpea constraints, (iii) promote sustainable chickpea production and trade through multi-stakeholder partnerships, and (iv) disseminate and promote technologies through public awareness and media. The project has established a chickpea research hub at NCRI and innovation platform in four regions in Ethiopia. The research hub/innovation platform approach is a novel approach that brings together researchers, development practitioners, private sector, nongovernmental organizations, media, and other stakeholders in an integrated process to conduct research and generate evidence for development of technologies and/or policies. The project has developed a participatory action research agenda and work plan with clearly defined research questions, hypotheses, and methods; innovative and participatory monitoring and evaluation framework; detailed communication and dissemination plan; and financial framework for managing project funds. The research agenda focuses on major biotic and abiotic constraints of chickpea production in Ethiopia. The research will be conducted through multi-actor research process with stakeholders involved in research design, implementation, and dissemination of research findings in a co-learning process. The project has established a gender-balanced project management team and innovation platform steering committee. The project has established collaborative working groups with the private sector, public institutions, and nongovernmental organizations. The project has developed or is developing chickpea variety and agro-inputs; chickpea processing technologies and business plans; and chickpea marketing and trade information systems. The project has conducted or is conducting capacity building workshops for stakeholders, media, and public awareness campaigns. The research-into-development approach of the innovation platform will not only help in evidence generation for development of new technologies and/or policies but also make the technologies developed relevant, acceptable, and usable by end-users. The innovation platform will be sustained beyond the life of the project by establishing a chickpea innovation fund, which will enable the stakeholders to design and implement research and development activities, and attract additional resources from other funding agencies. The innovation platform approach has not been previously used in the research-for-development context in Ethiopia. If successful, the approach will not only help in evidence generation and technology development but also in policy and institutional reforms by creating a new platform that brings together different stakeholders in the country to collectively and collaboratively work together to solve problems that are of national and regional importance.

The study found that:

  • The area used to grow chickpeas increased by 97.6%
  • The yield also increased by 123.6% 
  • The production of chickpeas increased by 202.1%

To achieve this increase in production, the researchers explained that the “area covered by improved chickpea increased from 76.4 to 134,200 hectares,” that the “yield of improved chickpea increased from 362 to 804 kilograms per hectare,” and that “the supply of improved chickpea seed increased from 5,000 to 133,200 kilograms.”

  • The introduction of new varieties of chickpea, and

  • Increased income
  • Chickpea seed as a source of income since farmers were able to sell the seed before harvest
  • Increased diversity in the diet
  • Improved soil fertility
  • Crop rotation

The researchers noted that “the major challenge that constrained increased production and productivity of chickpea in Ethiopia was the limited availability of improved chickpea varieties and poor dissemination of improved chickpea technologies to the large area cultivated.”

English: The SARS-CoV-2 lineage A variant (A.23.1) with altered spike has emerged and is dominating the current Uganda epidemic. The variant has also been detected in other African countries, including Botswana, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Ghana, Kenya, Mozambique, Nigeria, Tanzania, and Zimbabwe. Here, we examined the growth advantage of A.23.1 in vitro and its potential to evade immune responses in vitro and in convalescent sera in comparison to the previously circulating lineage B variants in Uganda. A.23.1 showed a growth advantage over lineage B variants in Vero E6 and in human lung and intestinal epithelial cells. In both cell types, A.23.1 entered the cells 10 min faster than the lineage B variants. The A.23.1 spike protein was not recognized by a set of monoclonal antibodies targeting the receptor-binding domain (RBD) and the N-terminal domain (NTD) of the spike protein. Our results indicate that the in vitro data support the hypothesis that the A.23.1 variant has a growth advantage over previously circulating variants and that the A.23.1 spike protein has undergone functional changes that might affect neutralization by antibodies.

samples.src: Researchers report on SARS-CoV-2 variant evolution in Uganda
samples.ref: Banyakišiši ba bega ka ga phetogo ya mohuta wa SARS-CoV-2 go la Uganda
samples.hyp:
A new preprint paper* reports on the analysis of 151 SARS-CoV-2 whole genome sequences from Uganda, collected between November 2020 and January 2021.

The researchers report that the B.1.1.28 C.35V variant, first detected in Botswana, has also circulated in Uganda, albeit at low frequencies. The B.1.1.28 variant carries the same E484K mutation found in the B.1.351 (South Africa) and B.1.617.2 (India) variants.

The researchers also identify three other variants of concern, the B.1.1.7 (UK), B.1.351 (South Africa) and B.1.617.2 (India). These variants account for 20% of the sequences in their dataset, with the B.1.1.7 variant being the most prevalent.

The researchers used whole genome sequencing to trace the development of the COVID-19 pandemic in Uganda. They found that the B.1.1.28 C.35V variant emerged in Uganda in December 2020, while the B.1.1.7 (UK), B.1.351 (South Africa) and B.1.617.2 (India) variants emerged in January 2021. The B.1.617.2 variant emerged in Uganda earlier than in India, the country where this variant was first identified.

The SARS-CoV-2 coronavirus that causes COVID-19 has many variants, which are different versions of the virus that have developed since the start of the pandemic. Scientists use the Greek alphabet to name variants. The most common variants in the United States are the Alpha, Beta, Gamma, and Delta variants. 

The virus that causes COVID-19 is very good at evolving and mutating. As it spreads through the human population, it picks up random changes in its genetic code. Some of these changes do not affect how the virus works, but others can affect it. Most of the variants that have developed since the start of the pandemic have had at least one significant change that helps the virus spread more easily from one person to another. 

The changes in the virus that make it more contagious can also make it harder for vaccines to prevent infection. Scientists are very concerned about new variants that have several changes that affect how the virus infects cells and can make it harder for vaccines to prevent illness. 

The good news is that scientists are watching for variants of concern. If a variant is able to spread more easily or evade the body’s defenses, scientists can monitor how much it is spreading in different parts of the world. They can also study how well current vaccines work against it. If they find out that a new variant is able to break through a specific vaccine, they can change the vaccine to be more effective against the new variant.

The authors sequence 110 SARS-CoV-2 genomes from 46 patients in Sudan, identifying 13 unique genomes, 12 of which were novel compared to available genome reference sets. The study reports a high rate of deletions in the spike protein in Sudanese isolates, as well as mutations that have been associated with immune evasion and transmissibility.


The authors note that the study has limitations due to small sample size and the sequence data being generated as part of a larger study, which precluded the ability to perform deep sequencing. They acknowledge these limitations, but believe the data provide useful information for tracking the evolution of the virus in Sudan.

The authors’ sequence data and analysis code are available at https://www.mpi.nl/human-genetics/resources/supplementary-material/duaipaper2021. Further information will be made available on an open online repository after approval by the Sudanese authorities, which is pending at the time of this submission.

In our opinion, the study adds to existing knowledge about SARS-CoV-2 variants in global circulation. The authors’ data suggest a pattern in the evolution of SARS-CoV-2 in Sudan, which could inform public health policies and preparedness in the country. The use of open and FAIR data, as well as the authors’ commitment to share data and analysis tools on an open online repository, will allow for further scientific investigation of these sequences in the broader global context. We encourage the authors to share all data, including the full set of 110 sequences, as well as analysis tools and methods, once approved by the Sudanese authorities to allow for maximum benefit of these valuable data. In addition, we encourage the authors to apply labels to the genome reference sets that are consistent with other recent publications on SARS-CoV-2 variants, such as labels from the BEI Resources’ SARS-CoV-2 Genome and Variants track or labels from the COVID-19 Genomics Consortium (CO-GiNv).

samples.src: Case Studies Documenting The Reasons for and Circumstances of Female Genital Mutilation/Cutting in Indonesia, Ethiopia and Kenya
samples.ref: Dinyakišišo tša Tiragalo tšeo di Ngwalago ka ga Mabaka le Maemo ao a bakago go Tloša/go Ripa Ditho tša Bong tša Basadi ka Indonesia, Ethiopia le ka Kenya
samples.hyp:
Publication Date: 2018
Region: Africa, Asia and Pacific
Type: Case Studies
Globally, 200 million girls and women today have undergone female genital mutilation/cutting (FGM/C), with 44 million girls under 15 years of age at risk in the next ten years. The practice is most common in Africa and the Middle East, but it persists in other parts of the world, including Asia and Latin America. While the practice is declining in some countries, the pace is slow, and in other countries, it is on the rise. Even where the practice is declining, the reduction is often due to migration of families with FGM/C traditions to areas where the practice is not done or not as prevalent, or to the aging of women in communities with high FGM/C prevalence. The scale and complexity of FGM/C, particularly the variation in types, the cross-border and -cultural diversity of its practice, and the different migration patterns of FGM/C-affected populations pose considerable challenges for national policy and programming. This series of case studies aims to contribute to a more nuanced and contextually grounded understanding of the factors that influence the continuation of FGM/C. The studies examine the reasons and circumstances surrounding the continuation of FGM/C cuttings in three countries with a high prevalence of FGM/C – Indonesia, Ethiopia, and Kenya – with the working definition of context as “the composite of characteristics that influence and are influenced by the community’s responses to issues and events.” The studies analyze the ways in which community members, including men and boys, women and girls, understand and experience FGM/C, as well as the ways in which FGM/C is practiced and the responses of those who oppose the practice. The studies are based on a review of the available literature on FGM/C, including recent demographic health surveys that contain data on FGM/C, as well as in-country interviews with key informants and experts, community focus groups, and community members. This report is divided into three sections. The first section provides a brief background on FGM/C, the context for the study, and the data and methods used for this series of case studies. The second section contains the findings from the three country case studies, and the last section concludes with cross-country lessons learned, challenges, and recommendations for influencing the factors that influence the continuation of FGM/C, as well as for research and programming.

Female genital cutting/mutilation is defined differently in different parts of the world. The World Health Organization (WHO) defines female genital mutilation/cutting as any procedure that involves altering or causing injury to the female genital organs for non-medical reasons. The WHO differentiates between four types of female genital cutting/mutilation: type 1 involves partial or total removal of the clitoris; type 2 involves partial or total removal of the clitoris and the labia minora, with or without extension to the labia majora; type 3 involves narrowing of the vaginal opening through the creation of a covering seal; and type 4 involves other injury to the female genital organs. Female genital cutting/mutilation is almost always carried out on girls and women by other members of the community, usually by traditional cutters, older women, or health workers in community settings. The procedure is carried out using a blade, knife, or scalpel, and in some cases, the base of a tree branch or a piece of glass is used. The practice is often performed in unhygienic conditions and under traditional beliefs, which may include the belief that female genital cutting/mutilation is a necessary and important tradition to prepare girls for womanhood, marriage, and sexual relations, as well as to increase their fertility. Female genital cutting/mutilation is a violation of the human rights of girls and women and a violation of their rights to health, equality, nondiscrimination, and education. Female genital cutting/mutilation has short- and long-term adverse consequences for girls and women’s health, including severe bleeding, shock, infection, problems in urinary function, and psychological trauma. Female genital cutting/mutilation may also lead to complications during pregnancy and childbirth, including prolonged labor, obstructed birth, maternal hemorrhage, sepsis, and shock. Female genital cutting/mutilation is also associated with an increased risk of female genital infections, such as bacterial vaginosis, and an increased risk of HIV. However, the perspectives of these two groups are often not taken into account when developing interventions to reduce practice.

This study aimed to explore the views of health workers and parents on the acceptability of interventions to reduce FGM/C in two African countries with different cultural and religious contexts; Djibouti and Ethiopia.

In-depth interviews were conducted with 28 health workers and 29 parents, and four focus group discussions with a total of 79 participants were held in each country. Qualitative data were analysed thematically, and quantitative data were descriptively analysed.

All health workers supported the introduction of interventions to reduce FGM/C, while some parents were hesitating. Acceptability was strongly associated with the provision of appropriate alternative ceremonies (Grounded Theory).

In Djibouti, health workers and parents supported the provision of information to the public, a national FGM/C protocol, community mobilization, and the involvement of religious leaders. In Ethiopia, interventions should include information dissemination, the provision of alternative ceremonies, and law enforcement.

Health workers can be key allies in the effort to end FGM/C. To engage parents and enable their support, interventions must address practical and cultural concerns, provide information, and be implemented with the support of religious leaders.

All types of FGM can have serious health consequences. These include:

  • haemorrhage
  • infection
  • ulcers
  • psychological trauma
  • difficulties in later pregnancy, and higher risk of complications during labour and delivery
  • pain and difficulty during sexual intercourse
  • a higher risk of female infertility

The researchers then combined this data with information about the prevalence of FGM, and the legal and health status of FGM in each country. They also included information about gender equality, women’s education, and economic status. They used statistical models to analyse the data and identify which factors were associated with the prevalence of FGM in each country.
They found that in all the countries studied, younger women were more likely to have undergone FGM than older women. Girls aged 15-19 were found to be most at risk: globally, over two-thirds (69%) of all girls who had FGM had undergone it before the age of 15. The researchers also found that national wealth was associated with a higher prevalence of FGM: in the countries with the highest average wealth, 1 in 7 (14%) of women aged 15-49 had undergone FGM compared to 1 in 23 (4%) of women in the countries with the lowest average wealth.
The study also identified several other factors that were associated with a higher prevalence of FGM. These included: having a mother who had undergone FGM, living in a country with an Islamic faith, and living in Eastern or Southern Africa. On the other hand, a higher prevalence of education among women was associated with a lower prevalence of FGM. The study did not find an association between FGM and urban residence or the frequency of religious practice.
The researchers concluded that a range of factors influenced the prevalence of FGM, and that interventions to try and eliminate the practice should be tailored to the specific context in each country.

The effects of sodium metavanadate (NaVO3) on the male reproductive system of African giant rats (Cricetomys gambianus) were investigated. Animals were divided into four groups and treated as follows: group I served as control and received distilled water; group II was administered with NaVO3 at a single dose of 3.5 mg/kg body weight; group III received NaVO3 at an equitoxic dose of 1.5 mg/kg body weight/day for 14 days; and group IV was administered with NaVO3 at a subtoxic dose of 0.7 mg/kg body weight/day for 14 days. Results showed significant (p < 0.05) depletion of testosterone in all treated groups at different time intervals (immediately after treatment, 7, and 14 days) compared to the control group. A dose-related decrease in sperm motility and progressive movement was observed in treated groups. Apoptotic cells were detected in the testis of rats treated with equitoxic and subtoxic doses of NaVO3. Ultrastructural studies showed distortion of the spermatids, sloughing of the spermatids from the spermatogonia, vacuolization of the spermatids, and degeneration of the spermatogonia in treated groups compared to the control. In conclusion, the results of the present study indicate that NaVO3 induces testicular toxicity in the African giant rats, which is characterized by disruption of the spermatogenetic process and apoptosis of germ cells.

samples.ref: Go ba gona ga banadiamo go tikologo go oketšegile mo nakong ye e sa tšwago go feta.
samples.hyp:
This can be attributed to the increase in vanadium ore mining and processing, and the rapidly growing vanadium-consuming industries, especially steel-making. Vanadium is a steel-hardening ingredient used in coal-based ferrovanadium and silicomanganese production. Vanadium is also found in the environment in coal, ash, and petroleum products, and is emitted to the air during combustion processes. The lung is the principal target organ for vanadium, and the route of entry is via inhalation. The current study aimed to (i) review the experimental inhalation studies on vanadium in animals, and (ii) evaluate the toxicity of vanadium in humans from the inhalation studies published in the past 50 years. The results from animal studies show that vanadium is readily absorbed and retained in the lung, and the majority of the inhaled vanadium is eliminated within 48 h. The studies also show that vanadium is a lung irritant and a dose-dependent cytotoxic, genotoxic, and immunotoxic compound. In humans, most studies show that vanadium is also absorbed and retained in the lung, and that it is a lung irritant. Only a few studies, however, show evidence of cytotoxicity, genotoxicity, and immunotoxicity. The studies on the cytotoxicity, genotoxicity, and immunotoxicity of vanadium show conflicting results. This discrepancy between animal and human data may be explained by differences in the toxicity equivilence factors (TEFs) used to calculate the NOAEL values, and the animal studies have used TEFs derived from acute oral toxicity studies. When human equivalent doses (HCEDs) are used to calculate the NOAEL values from the animal studies, the results show that vanadium is a potential cytotoxic, genotoxic, and immunotoxic fume in humans. The studies also show that the long-term exposure to low levels of vanadium is hazardous to human health. The major findings of this review are: (i) the long-term exposure to low levels of vanadium is hazardous to human health; (ii) the inhalation of vanadium is a potential health risk to workers in the vanadium industry, and (iii) there is a need for more long-term inhalation studies on human subjects.

SMV is a known contact allergen, and skin contact can cause allergic contact dermatitis. SMV has a molecular weight of 128.00 g/mol with a melting point of 1015°C and a boiling point > 2000°C. SMV is not known to bioaccumulate, nor is it a recognized teratogen. It is, however, considered potentially mutagenic and genotoxic. SMV is not listed as a known carcinogen, nor is it listed as a reproductive or developmental toxin. SMV is not regulated for occupational exposure in the United States, except in the state of California where it is listed as a Proposition 65 chemical. The Air Quality Management District in California has also listed SMV as a toxic air contaminant. The OSHA permissible exposure limit is 0.3 mg/m³ as a total airborne inhalable particles. The National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) has not established a recommended exposure limit for SMV. The LD50 for SMV in rats after a single oral dose is 653 mg/kg. The no observed adverse effect level (NOAEL) for SMV in humans is 0.49 mg/kg body weight/day. The no observed reproduction effect level (NOEL) for SMV in rats after a 30-day exposure is 1.4 mg/kg body weight/day. The observed adverse effect level (OAEL) for SMV in rats after a 30-day exposure is 2.2 mg/kg body weight/day. The current study was designed to assess the reproductive and genotoxic effects of SMV exposure in male African giant rats (Cricetomys atrimanus) after a 30-day exposure period. Crohn's disease is a long-term condition that causes the immune system to attack the gastrointestinal (GI) tract, which results in inflammation.
This inflammation can damage the GI tract and cause severe abdominal pain, bloody diarrhea, and weight loss.
There is no cure for Crohn's disease, but many effective treatments are available to help reduce inflammation and control the symptoms.
Here are 10 of the most common Crohn's disease treatments.
See more articles in the same category
1.
Diet and lifestyle changes
Diet and lifestyle changes are the first line of defense against Crohn's disease.
A healthy, well-balanced diet can help reduce inflammation and promote healing, while regular exercise can help improve overall health and well-being.
2.
Medications to treat inflammation
Medications are an important part of the treatment plan for Crohn's disease. These medications work to reduce inflammation in the GI tract and include:
- aminosalicylates, such as 5-aminosalicylic acid (5-ASA) or mesalamine, which are taken by mouth and help to reduce inflammation in the colon
- corticosteroids, such as prednisone or hydrocortisone, which are taken by mouth or as an enema and help to reduce inflammation quickly
- immunomodulators, such as azathioprine or 6-mercaptopurine, which are taken by mouth and work to decrease the activity of the immune system
- biologics, which are given by injection and work to target specific proteins involved in the body's immune response
3.
Surgery to remove damaged sections of the GI tract
Surgery may be necessary if medications are unable to control the symptoms of Crohn's disease or if the disease causes complications, such as a blockage or a hole in the GI tract.
The type of surgery performed will depend on the location and severity of the inflammation.
4.
Total parenteral nutrition (TPN)
TPN is a method of providing nutrition to the body through a vein, bypassing the GI tract. It may be necessary in cases where the GI tract is severely damaged and unable to absorb nutrients.
5.
Vitamin and mineral supplements
People with Crohn's disease may have a decreased ability to absorb nutrients from food, which can lead to deficiencies in vitamins and minerals.
